> Super, short documentation. The same pages, without the references to the examples app or the passages marked as secondary. Links are relative to the docs/ folder of the repository.

# Super

A minimalist front-end framework, typed end to end, that governs three things: stores, components and routing. Everything else belongs to your project.

> **Status: exploratory draft**
>
> The API may still change. The packages are not published on npm: they live in the repository, under `packages/`.

## At a glance

A Super feature fits in three files: a **contract** that says what can be read, requested and listened to; a **store** that implements it; a **component** that displays and sends commands. Each one is a class.

```ts title="src/@core/counter/contract.ts"
import { type Outcome, SuperContract } from '@super-ts/core';

export type CounterState = { counts: Readonly<Record<string, number>> };

export type CounterTypes = {
  state: CounterState;
  commands: { increment(input: { id: string }): Outcome<{ count: number }, 'storage'> };
};

export class CounterContract extends SuperContract<CounterTypes> {
  constructor() {
    super({ name: 'counter' });
  }

  // A selector is a method: the state first, then its parameters.
  count(s: CounterState, id: string) {
    return s.counts[id] ?? 0;
  }
}
```

```ts title="src/@core/counter/store.ts"
import { type Commands, SuperStore } from '@super-ts/core';
import type { CounterRepository } from '../../ports/counter-repository';
import type { CounterContract } from './contract';

export class CounterStore extends SuperStore<CounterContract> implements Commands<CounterStore> {
  #repository: CounterRepository;

  constructor({ counterRepository }: { counterRepository: CounterRepository }) {
    super({ contract: 'counter', initialState: { counts: {} } });
    this.#repository = counterRepository;
  }

  // A contract command = a method. The waiting lives in the store.
  async increment({ id }: { id: string }) {
    const count = this.selectors.count(id) + 1;
    await this.#repository.save(id, count).catch(() => this.fail('storage'));
    this.set((s) => ({ counts: { ...s.counts, [id]: count } }));
    return { count }; // Super publishes increment:done; "pending" is tracked automatically
  }
}
```

```ts title="src/@components/shared/counter-button.super"
import { SuperElement } from '@super-ts/dom';

export class CounterButton extends SuperElement {
  // Declared in the class: the tag, and the prop received from the parent (<CounterButton counterId="coffees" />).
  @tag = 'counter-button';
  @prop counterId: string;

  // Prepared once: the store, requested by the name of its contract, and the value read.
  @contract counter;
  @selector count = () => this.counter.selectors.count(this.counterId);

  // On every render: display, send and move on.
  render() {
    <button on:click={() => this.counter.send('increment', { id: this.counterId })}>{this.count.value}</button>
  }
}
```

The component is a `.super` file: TypeScript whose methods write their elements directly, like statements (see [Templates](templates.html)). In its class it declares its tag and its props (`@tag`, `@prop`), the store it reads and the value it takes from it (`@contract`, `@selector`), and reads a prop by its name: `this.counterId`. It imports nothing from `@core/`: it requests the store by the name of its contract, and the compiler knows its selectors and commands. It sends a command and moves on; the store does the asynchronous work and updates its state; Super tracks the command (`this.counter.selectors.pending('increment')`) and publishes its outcome (`increment:done`, `increment:failed`). The component re-renders because the value it reads has changed.

## Principles

- **Two required folders, the rest is free.** Contracts and stores in `src/@core/`, components in `src/@components/`. The `@` prefix marks what belongs to Super. Domain, ports, adapters, routes and composition root are organised however your project sees fit.
- **The contract is the only door to a store.** Its selectors say what is read, its commands what is requested, its events what is listened to. A component requests the store by its name (`@contract counter;`) and imports only types from `@core/`.
- **The view sends and moves on.** A command returns nothing: there is never an `await` in a component. The result comes back through the state or through an event.
- **Props down, events up.** A parent never calls a method of a child.
- **Prepare, then display.** The fields and constructor of a component prepare once (contracts, local state, reads, listeners); `render` displays on every render. Super refuses to prepare anything during render.
- **The compiler does the work.** An unknown command, a missing body, a store method outside the contract, a link without its parameter, a screen with the wrong props or a mistake in a template do not compile.
- **Web standards first.** A store is an `EventTarget`, a component is a custom element. `.super` files are compiled to lit-html, a deliberate but hidden dependency: you never import lit.

## What Super deliberately does not do

- No HTTP client, no injection container: you assemble everything in your composition root.
- No imposed layers beyond `@core/` and `@components/`.
- No shadow DOM: components render in the light DOM, your global styles apply.

## The packages

| Package | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `@super-ts/core` | `SuperContract`, `SuperStore` : contracts, selectors, stores. No dependency on the DOM. |
| `@super-ts/dom` | `SuperElement` : components, rendering, `createApp`, router. |
| `@super-ts/testing` | `mount`, `fakeStore`, `record`, `flush`, `cleanup`. |
| `@super-ts/ui` | The UI kit: fields bound to forms, `CommandButton`, `RouteLink`, toasts, dialogs, menus, table. See [UI kit](ui.html). |
| `@super-ts/vite` | The plugin that compiles `.super` files, enforces the architecture and generates the contract dictionary (`@core/contracts.d.ts`). |
| `@super-ts/lang` | The `.super` language: parser, compilation to lit, type check (`super-tsc`). See [Tooling](tooling.html). |
| `@super-ts/language-server` | The language server for `.super` files in the editor (`packages/lang-server`), command `super-language-server`. |
| `@super-ts/lint` | The Biome configuration that fixes the import order. |

## With an AI assistant

The docs also exist in markdown, in the [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org) format, to give them to an LLM or to a coding agent. These files are generated from these pages on every `npm run check`, and `npm run docs:check` fails if they are out of date.

- [`llms.txt`](llms.txt): the index, one line per page.
- [`llms-full.txt`](llms-full.txt): all the docs in one file, code included.
- [`llms-small.txt`](llms-small.txt): the same, without the FAQ, the examples catalogue or the references to the examples app, for small context windows.

In a project, just give the agent the path, for example in an `AGENTS.md`: "the Super docs are in `docs/llms-full.txt`".

# Getting started

Install the repository, run the example, then write a complete feature end to end.

## Install

Super is not published on npm yet. You work in the repository, which contains the packages and an example app.

```bash
npm install
npm run dev          # the example app on http://localhost:5173
npm test             # the tests (Vitest, happy-dom)
npm run typecheck    # super-tsc: types of .ts and .super files, including *.test-d.ts type tests
npm run lint         # Biome (import order, formatting) and formatting of .super files
npm run format       # formats everything: Biome for .ts files, the .super formatter for .super files
npm run check        # lint, typecheck, tests, then the docs index
```

The packages `@super-ts/core`, `@super-ts/dom`, `@super-ts/testing`, `@super-ts/ui` and `@super-ts/vite` are resolved through aliases declared in the `tsconfig.json` files and `vite.config.ts`. In the app, the Super folders are imported through aliases too, from any file: `'@core/counter/contract'`, `'@components/app-shell'` (see [Architecture](architecture.html#importing-from-core-and-components)).

Components are written in `.super` files: the Vite plugin compiles them, and `npm run typecheck` checks them. To get errors and completion in your editor, plug in the `.super` language server (see [Tooling](tooling.html#editor)).

## Your first feature: a theme button

You are going to add a button that switches between light and dark mode. It is deliberately simple, but it goes through every step: contract, store, component, wiring and test.

### Step 1: the contract

The contract describes what the store can do, without saying how. It is a class, in its own folder under `src/@core/`, that names itself in its constructor: that name is how you will ask for it.

```ts title="src/@core/theme/contract.ts"
import { SuperContract } from '@super-ts/core';

export type ThemeMode = 'light' | 'dark';
export type ThemeState = { mode: ThemeMode };

export type ThemeTypes = {
  state: ThemeState;                        // what the store keeps in memory
  commands: { toggle(): void };             // what you can ask of it
  events: { changed: { mode: ThemeMode } }; // what it announces
};

export class ThemeContract extends SuperContract<ThemeTypes> {
  constructor() {
    super({ name: 'theme' });
  }

  // What you can read: a selector is a method that receives the state.
  isDark(s: ThemeState) {
    return s.mode === 'dark';
  }
}
```

The Vite plugin spots the contract and registers it in `src/@core/contracts.d.ts`, a generated file (to commit, never to write by hand). This is what makes `'theme'` known to the compiler everywhere in the app. See [Contracts](contracts.html) and [Selectors](selectors.html).

### Step 2: the store

The store implements the contract: an initial state, and one method per command.

```ts title="src/@core/theme/store.ts"
import { type Commands, SuperStore } from '@super-ts/core';
import type { ThemeContract } from './contract';

export class ThemeStore extends SuperStore<ThemeContract> implements Commands<ThemeStore> {
  constructor() {
    super({ contract: 'theme', initialState: { mode: 'light' } });
  }

  toggle() {
    const mode = this.selectors.isDark() ? 'light' : 'dark';
    this.set({ mode });
    this.emit('changed', { mode });
  }
}
```

`implements Commands<ThemeStore>` has the compiler check the methods: a forgotten command, a parameter that differs from the contract or a public method outside the contract do not compile. This constructor takes nothing: the store is created with `ThemeStore.create()`. See [Stores](stores.html).

### Step 3: the component

The component asks for the store by its contract's name, reads a selector and sends the command on click. It is reusable: it goes in `src/@components/shared/`, in a `.super` file.

```ts title="src/@components/shared/theme-toggle.super"
import { SuperElement } from '@super-ts/dom';

export class ThemeToggle extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'theme-toggle';

  // Once, at construction: the store, and what you read from it.
  @contract theme;
  @selector isDark = this.theme.selectors.isDark;

  // On each render: display from the current values.
  render() {
    <button type="button" on:click={() => this.theme.send('toggle')}>
      {this.isDark.value ? 'Switch to light mode' : 'Switch to dark mode'}
    </button>
  }
}
```

`render()` returns nothing: the button is written as a statement, `on:click` sets up the listener and `{…}` displays a value (see [Templates](templates.html)). The component imports nothing from `src/@core/`: `@contract theme;` is enough, and the compiler knows the contract's selectors and commands. See [Components](components.html) and [Reading a store](reading-a-store.html).

### Step 4: the wiring

The composition root, `main.ts`, creates the stores and provides them to the app. The component can then be used anywhere under the root, for example in the shell's header: `<ThemeToggle />`, after `import { ThemeToggle } from '@components/shared/theme-toggle'`.

```ts title="src/main.ts (with the theme)"
const counter = CounterStore.create({ counterRepository: createLocalStorageCounterRepository() });
const theme = ThemeStore.create();
const router = createRouter(Router);

createApp({ root: document.querySelector<HTMLElement>('#app')!, stores: [counter, theme], router })
  .mount(AppShell.create());
```

The app finds each store by its contract's name: a component that asks for `'theme'` receives this one. See [Wiring the application](application.html).

### Step 5: the test

```ts title="src/@components/shared/theme-toggle.test.ts"
import { flush, mount } from '@super-ts/testing';
import { ThemeStore } from '@core/theme/store';
import { within } from '@testing-library/dom';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { expect, test } from 'vitest';
import { ThemeToggle } from './theme-toggle';

test('the button toggles the theme', async () => {
  const theme = ThemeStore.create();
  const { container } = await mount(ThemeToggle, { stores: [theme] });

  await userEvent.click(within(container).getByRole('button'));
  await flush();

  expect(theme.selectors.isDark()).toBe(true);
  expect(container.textContent).toContain('Switch to light mode');
});
```

The test stays a `.ts` file: it imports the `.super` component without an extension and mounts it with `mount`. A test may import a store: the plugin does not check `*.test.ts` files. To test the component on its own, replace the real store with `fakeStore('theme', { state: { mode: 'dark' } })`. See [Testing](testing.html).

---

# Architecture

Super imposes two folders and four rules. Everything else in your `src` is user-land: Super does not look at it.

## The structure

```text
src/
├── @core/          IMPOSED BY SUPER: contracts and stores
│   ├── counter/    contract.ts, store.ts, store.test.ts
│   └── contracts.d.ts   generated by the Vite plugin (to commit)
├── @components/    IMPOSED BY SUPER: components (screens included)
│   ├── counter/    index.super, index.css, index.test.ts, counter-controls.super
│   ├── app-shell/  the shell
│   └── shared/     reusable components
├── domain/         user-land (this project's choice)
├── ports/          user-land (this project's choice)
├── adapters/       user-land (this project's choice)
├── routes.ts       user-land
└── main.ts         user-land
```

In `@core/`, the convention is **one folder per contract**: `contract.ts`, `store.ts` and its test. In `@components/`, **one folder per screen**, in kebab-case and without a suffix (`shop/index.super` exports `ShopScreen`), with its sub-components as flat files (`counter/counter-controls.super`); reusable components go in `shared/`. A component is a `.super` file (see [Templates](templates.html#super-files)); its tests stay `.ts`. The plugin's rules only look at the first level: a file is under `@core/`, under `@components/`, or elsewhere.

`src/@core/contracts.d.ts` is generated by the Vite plugin: it is the name → contract class dictionary (plus the router, under `'router'`) that lets you write `@contract counter;` with full types, and the link between each screen and its route (`ScreenRoutes`). You commit it, you never write it.

## The `@` prefix

The prefix reads at a glance: **a prefixed folder belongs to Super**, a folder without a prefix belongs to your project. A `core/` or `components/` folder without `@` is nothing special: it is a user-land folder like any other, which therefore cannot contain a store or a component.

> **Why `@` and not `$`?**
>
> In a shell, `$core` is read as a variable: `cd src/$core` silently lands in `src/`. `@` works fine in the shell, in relative imports and in the dev server's URLs.

> **Not to be confused**
>
> `@super-ts/core` is the framework package. `@core/counter/contract` is a file in your app, in `src/@core/`. One comes from `node_modules`, the other from your `src`.

## Importing from @core and @components

Both Super folders are imported through aliases, from any file, whatever its depth:

```ts
import { AppShell } from '@components/app-shell';
import { CounterStore } from '@core/counter/store';
```

No more `'../../@core/…'` to recount when a file moves folder. Relative imports (`'../@core/counter/store'`) remain possible, and the architecture rules apply to both forms.

**On the Vite and Vitest side, nothing to do**: the `superPlugin` plugin declares these aliases itself, from the `src` folder you give it. An import without an extension also finds a `.super`: `'@components/app-shell'` leads to `app-shell/index.super`.

**On the TypeScript side**, for the IDE and the type check, declare the aliases in your app's `tsconfig.json` (no plugin can inject them into TypeScript). Each alias has two targets: your `src`, and the declarations of the `.super` files, which the tooling writes to `.super/types/` (a folder ignored by git). `rootDirs` merges the trees (your `src`, the declarations, then the virtual TypeScript in `.super/virtual/` from which they draw their types): a `.ts` that imports a `.super` component, like `routes.ts`, sees its types, and "go to definition" opens the `.super`.

```text title="tsconfig.json"
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "paths": {
      // … the @super-ts/… packages
      "@core/*": ["./src/@core/*", "./.super/types/src/@core/*"],
      "@components/*": ["./src/@components/*", "./.super/types/src/@components/*"]
    },
    "rootDirs": ["./src", "./.super/types/src", "./.super/virtual/src"]
  }
}
```

Who writes this virtual TypeScript, and when: see [Tooling](tooling.html#type-check).

## Import order

Super also sets the order of imports, checked by the linter:

1. Super packages: `@super-ts/…`;
2. Super folders: `@components/…` and `@core/…`;
3. everything else: Node modules (`node:…`), npm packages, then relative paths.

Within each group, the order is alphabetical.

```ts title="src/@components/counter/index.test.ts"
import { createRouter } from '@super-ts/dom';
import { type FakeCommands, fakeStore, flush, mount } from '@super-ts/testing';
import type { CounterState } from '@core/counter/contract';
import { within } from '@testing-library/dom';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { describe, expect, test } from 'vitest';
import { Router } from '../../routes';
import { CounterScreen } from '.';
```

You can see at a glance what comes from the framework, what comes from the app's Super building blocks, and the rest. Imports without a name (`import './styles.css'`) are never moved: they act as separators, which preserves the loading order of stylesheets.

### Linting

The rule is enforced by Biome. Super provides its configuration, which your project extends in its `biome.json`:

```text title="biome.json"
{
  "extends": ["@super-ts/lint/config.json"]
}
```

```bash
npm run lint       # checks import order and formatting (also run by npm run check)
npm run lint:fix   # fixes both
```

In this repository, Super's configuration is in `packages/lint/config.json`. Super's configuration only touches the import order: formatting and the other lint rules are left to the project. The repository itself enables Biome's formatter (two spaces, single quotes, 140 columns) and formats `.super` files with the same rules (see [Tooling](tooling.html#formatting)).

> **Other folders have no alias**
>
> Only the Super folders have one. `ports/`, `adapters/` or `routes.ts` are imported with relative paths (`'../routes'`), or with your own aliases if you declare some.

## The four rules

| Rule | What is rejected |
| --- | --- |
| Contracts and stores are defined under `src/@core/`. | A module outside `@core/` that imports `SuperContract` or `SuperStore` from `@super-ts/core`. |
| Components are defined under `src/@components/`. | A module outside `@components/` (`.super` or `.ts`) that imports `SuperElement` from `@super-ts/dom`. |
| A component imports only types from `@core/`. | A component that imports a value from `@core/`: a store, a contract class, a constant, a function, or an `import * as`. |
| Contracts and stores do not depend on the DOM. | A module in `@core/` that imports anything from `@super-ts/dom` (`html`, `SuperElement`, `createApp`…), except types. |

The fourth rule keeps the core of the app independent of the display: a store is tested without the DOM, and could serve another interface. The third rule is the most important: it guarantees that **a component sees a store only through its contract**, which it asks for by name (`@contract counter;`). It reads through the selectors, sends commands, listens to events, and nothing else. This is what lets you test it with a fake store, and keeps domain logic from slipping into the view.

## The Vite plugin

The `@super-ts/vite` plugin compiles `.super` files and enforces these rules. It is declared in `vite.config.ts`, and also serves Vitest:

```ts title="vite.config.ts"
import { superPlugin } from '@super-ts/vite';
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [superPlugin({ src: fileURLToPath(new URL('./src', import.meta.url)) })],
});
```

The same plugin:

- compiles each `.super` to TypeScript (lit-html templates), then strips the types; a compilation error stops the module from loading, with its position in the `.super`;
- provides a source map from the final JS to the `.super`: stack traces and the debugger point to the line and column of the source (see [Source maps](tooling.html#source-maps));
- applies the architecture rules to the compiled code: a `.super` is checked as a `.ts` would be;
- in dev, rewrites the virtual TypeScript of a `.super` on every transform, so that the `.ts` files that import it see up-to-date types;
- declares the `@core/` and `@components/` aliases, and adds `.super` to the resolved extensions (see above);
- reads the contracts in `src/@core/` (the `contract.ts` or `*.contract.ts` files, which declare `export class X extends SuperContract` and are named through `super({ name })`), rejects two contracts with the same name, and registers them so that each store finds its own by name;
- finds the app's router (`export const Router = defineRouter(…)`) and adds it under `'router'`; reads its `.screens(…)` to link each screen's tag to its route (`'counter-screen': 'counter'`), which types `this.router.current` in the screen;
- writes it all to `src/@core/contracts.d.ts`, at startup and then on every file save in dev;
- in dev, makes components hot-replaceable (see below).

### Hot replacement of components

In dev, editing a component does not reload the page: the new version replaces the old one, and the displayed elements **keep their state** (local state, input, store state) and re-render with the new code. Components created afterwards use the new version, including from a parent that was not modified.

This replacement is only safe if the component's fields have not changed: the displayed elements were built with the old ones. Super therefore reloads the whole page when the change:

- adds, removes or renames a field or a setup declaration (`@state extra = …;`);
- modifies a handler written as an arrow field (`onAnswered = () => …`);
- touches a component that has `#private` members, fields or methods such as a `#row()` that emits elements (those of the old class are not those of the new one).

Editing `render`, `renderError`, `mounted` or another method is done hot. For a `.super`, its compiled code replaces the old one. A file in `@core/` (contract, store) always reloads the page. None of this exists in a build: the code added by the plugin is only active under `vite` in dev.

A module that breaks a rule **is not loaded**: Vite refuses to transform it and displays the error (overlay in dev, build or test failure).

```text
[super] src/shared/badge.ts imports SuperElement from @super-ts/dom.
Components can only be defined under src/@components/: this module is not loaded.

[super] src/@components/counter-list/counter-list-item.super imports CounterContract from @core/counter/contract.
A component imports only types from src/@core/: it talks to stores through their contract (@contract cart;).
This module is not loaded.
```

### What the plugin does not check

- **Tests** (`*.test.ts`, `*.test-d.ts`): the app does not load them, so they can import a real store or define test doubles wherever they like.
- **Type imports** (`import type { CounterState } from '@core/counter/contract'`): they disappear at compile time, so they are allowed everywhere.
- **User-land**: `domain/`, `ports/`, `adapters/`, `routes.ts`, `main.ts` import whatever they like.

The plugin reads the code as text (for a `.super`, the compiled code): it recognises named imports (including those renamed with `as`), a contract by its declaration `export class X extends SuperContract` and the router by `export const Router = defineRouter(…)`. See [Limitations](limitations.html).

## User-land

Outside `@core/` and `@components/`, you organise things as you like. In the [examples app](examples.html):

- **[`domain/`](../examples/demo/src/domain/)**: the domain types and rules (`Product`, `CartLine`, the counter catalogue, the page of products requested from an API), without Super or the DOM. Contracts use them; a component can import their types.
- **[`ports/`](../examples/demo/src/ports/)**: the interfaces the stores need (here `CounterRepository`, `ProfileClient`, `OrderClient`, `ProductCatalog`). This is a choice inspired by hexagonal architecture; another project could put these interfaces next to the store, in `@core/`.
- **[`adapters/`](../examples/demo/src/adapters/)**: the concrete implementations of these ports (`localStorage`, in-memory, a simulated server, the dummyjson.com HTTP API…).
- **[`routes.ts`](../examples/demo/src/routes.ts)**: the routes and screens, declared in a single export, `Router`. A component accesses it through `this.router`, which also builds links (`this.router.href(…)`); `Router.href` is for code outside components.
- **[`main.ts`](../examples/demo/src/main.ts)**: the composition root, the only place that chooses the adapters and assembles everything.

## Who imports what

| From | Can import |
| --- | --- |
| `@core/` (contracts, stores) | Other contracts and stores, the domain, the ports, `@super-ts/core`; from `@super-ts/dom`, only types. |
| `@components/` | Types from `@core/`, other components, the domain and the rest of user-land, `@super-ts/dom`, and the `@super-ts/ui` kit. |
| User-land | Everything. |

> **One dependency rule to remember**
>
> A component depends on a store's contract, never on its implementation.

---

# Contracts

A contract describes a store from the outside: what you can read, what you can ask of it, what it announces. It is the only thing a component knows about a store.

## Declaring a contract

```ts title="src/@core/counter/contract.ts"
import { type Outcome, SuperContract } from '@super-ts/core';
import { COUNTERS, MIN_COUNT } from '../../domain/counter';

export type CounterState = {
  counts: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
  loadErrorMessage: string | null;
};

export type CounterTypes = {
  state: CounterState;
  commands: {
    load(): void;
    increment(input: { id: string }): Outcome<{ count: number }, 'unknown' | 'storage'>;
    decrement(input: { id: string }): Outcome<{ count: number }, 'unknown' | 'below-min' | 'storage'>;
    reset(input: { id: string }): Outcome<{ count: number }, 'unknown' | 'storage'>;
  };
};

export class CounterContract extends SuperContract<CounterTypes> {
  constructor() {
    super({ name: 'counter' });
  }

  count(s: CounterState, id: string) {
    return s.counts[id] ?? 0;
  }
  canDecrement(s: CounterState, id: string) {
    return (s.counts[id] ?? 0) > MIN_COUNT;
  }
  // …
}
```

A contract comes in three pieces:

1. **A type** (`CounterTypes`) that describes its state, its commands and its events, for the compiler.
2. **A class** that extends `SuperContract<CounterTypes>` and names itself in its constructor: `super({ name: 'counter' })`. This name is the contract's key throughout the app: a component declares `@contract counter;`, a store declares `super({ contract: 'counter', … })`.
3. **Methods**, optional: each one is a selector, a permitted read of the state (see [Selectors](selectors.html)).

A contract lives in `src/@core/<name>/contract.ts`, one folder per contract, next to its store. The Vite plugin reads these files and generates `src/@core/contracts.d.ts`, the name → class dictionary that types `@contract counter;`, `@on('counter', …)` and `StoreOfContract<'counter'>`. This file is committed, but never written by hand.

## The three keys: state, commands, events

| Key | Required | What it describes | If omitted |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `state` | yes | The interface of the state the store keeps in memory. An object. | Does not compile. |
| `commands` | no | What you can ask of the store: `name(body): void`. | The store accepts no commands. |
| `events` | no | What the store announces: `name: payload`. | The store emits nothing. |

This minimal contract is valid:

```ts
export class ClockContract extends SuperContract<{ state: { now: number } }> {
  constructor() {
    super({ name: 'clock' });
  }
}
```

### state: the interface of the state

`state` is the type of what the store keeps in memory. It sets the shape of the `initialState` passed to the store's constructor, what the store reads with `this.get()` and changes with `this.set()`, and the first parameter of the selectors. Components never see this interface: they read through the selectors.

### commands: the requests

A command is a request addressed to the store. It takes **at most one parameter**, the **body** (an object, more readable and extensible than several arguments), and **nothing comes back to whoever sends it**. In practice, a command often changes the state, but not necessarily. The rule that matters goes the other way: only the store changes its state.

```ts
commands: {
  load(): void;                                                    // no body: send('load')
  increment(input: { id: string }): Outcome<{ count: number }, 'unknown' | 'storage'>;
}
```

A command declares one or the other:

- **`void`**: it has no particular outcome to publish (apart from an unexpected failure).
- **`Outcome<Result, Reasons>`**: what its success produces (published in `increment:done`), and the closed list of its failure reasons (published in `increment:failed`). See [Declaring the outcome](commands-and-events.html#declaring-the-outcome).

> **Nothing comes back to the caller**
>
> A direct response, or several parameters, do not compile:
>
> ```ts
> // @ts-expect-error a command does not return data
> class Async extends SuperContract<{ state: {}; commands: { add(): Promise<number> } }> {}
> // @ts-expect-error two parameters: a command only has one body
> class Bad extends SuperContract<{ state: {}; commands: { add(a: number, b: number): void } }> {}
> ```
>
> This is a design choice: the component sends and moves on, and Super publishes the outcome to everyone who listens to it. `void` is enough even if the store's method is `async`.

### events: the announcements

Each command already has its events, published by Super: `increment:done` and `increment:failed`. The `events` key is for the other facts the store announces, those that are not the outcome of a single command. An event pairs a name with its payload. **Only the store emits** (with `this.emit`); **anyone can listen**: components, other stores, tests.

```ts title="src/@core/cart/contract.ts"
// A hand-written event: a fact that is not the outcome of a single command.
// The cart becomes empty after `clear`, or after the `remove` of the last item.
events: {
  emptied: void;          // this.emit('emptied'), no payload
};
```

An event with a payload is written `synced: { at: number }` and emitted with `this.emit('synced', { at: Date.now() })`.

## What a contract is not

- **Not an implementation.** It does not say how commands are handled: that is the [store](stores.html)'s role.
- **Not an instance.** A contract holds no state. There can be several stores for the same contract (one per test, for example).
- **Not the store's dependencies.** The `CounterRepository` does not appear in the contract: it is an implementation detail, declared by the store's constructor.

At runtime, Super only reads a contract's name and methods (the selectors). The types `state`, `commands` and `events` exist only for the compiler.

## Who uses the contract

| Who | What for |
| --- | --- |
| The store | `class CounterStore extends SuperStore<CounterContract> implements Commands<CounterStore>`: the compiler requires one method per command and checks the emitted events. |
| Components | `@contract counter;` to read through the selectors and send, `@on('counter', …)` to listen (see [the declarations](components.html#preparing-stores-reads-state-form-references-listeners)). |
| `createApp` | Finds the right store for a component: the contract's name serves as the key. |
| The Vite plugin | Reads the contracts in `src/@core/`, generates `contracts.d.ts`, rejects two contracts with the same name. |
| Tests | `fakeStore('counter', …)` for a component; `store.selectors.count('coffees')` on a real store's handle. |

## Pitfalls

> **A misspelt key is rejected**
>
> `command` instead of `commands` (or `event` instead of `events`) does not compile: the error appears on `super({ name })`, with the offending key and the expected keys ("unknown key in the contract types: command (expected: state, commands, events)").

> **The name is written out in full**
>
> The plugin reads `super({ name: 'counter' })` in the source: the name must be a string literal. Two contracts with the same name are rejected, and `'router'` is reserved for the app's router.

> **The selectors' state is annotated by hand**
>
> TypeScript does not infer a method's parameters: write `count(s: CounterState, id: string)`. This first parameter is checked at the store's declaration (`SuperStore<CounterContract>`): a type that does not accept the contract's state does not compile.

---

# Selectors

Selectors are the permitted reads of the state. They are the contract's methods, used as they are by components, the store and tests. You write them with the state as the first parameter, and Super supplies it at call time: you write `count(s, id)` in the contract, then `selectors.count(id)` everywhere else.

## Declaring selectors

```ts title="src/@core/counter/contract.ts"
// The only allowed reads of the state. A component reads through these (plus `pending`, provided by Super).
export class CounterContract extends SuperContract<CounterTypes> {
  constructor() {
    super({ name: 'counter' });
  }

  catalog(_s: CounterState) {
    return COUNTERS;
  }
  find(_s: CounterState, id: string) {
    return COUNTERS.find((counter) => counter.id === id) ?? null;
  }
  count(s: CounterState, id: string) {
    return s.counts[id] ?? 0;
  }
  label(_s: CounterState, id: string) {
    return COUNTERS.find((counter) => counter.id === id)?.label ?? null;
  }
  loadErrorMessage(s: CounterState) {
    return s.loadErrorMessage;
  }
  canDecrement(s: CounterState, id: string) {
    return (s.counts[id] ?? 0) > MIN_COUNT;
  }
}
```

- Each selector receives **the state as its first parameter**. Annotate it (`s: CounterState`): TypeScript does not infer a method's parameters.
- It can take **other parameters** after the state: `count(s, id: string)` is used as `selectors.count('coffees')`.
- It can **ignore the state**: `catalog` returns static data. This is useful so that components have nothing to ask for other than the contract.
- It must be **pure**: no side effects, no network calls, only a read.
- `pending` is reserved: Super adds it to the selectors, to tell whether a command is pending (`selectors.pending('load')`). A `pending` method in the contract does not compile (error at the store's declaration). A selector only reads the state; pending commands are not part of it.

### A selector without parameters

A selector only takes a parameter if the answer depends on it. `canDecrement` needs the `id` (you need to know whether *this* counter is above 0). `loadErrorMessage` does not: the answer only depends on the global state. On the component side, the difference shows: a selector without parameters is passed as is to `@selector loadErrorMessage = this.counter.selectors.loadErrorMessage;`, a selector with parameters is called inside a function (see [In a component](selectors.html#in-a-component)).

## Why selectors

- **A single definition.** "A missing counter is worth 0" is written once. The store, components and tests apply the same rule; changing it in the contract changes it everywhere.
- **A closed door.** A component never sees the raw state: `this.counter` has no `state()`, and `this.counter.selectors.counts` does not compile, since `counts` is not a selector. The view cannot reinvent a reading rule on its own.
- **Less noise.** The state is supplied by Super: no `s` to carry around.

## Using them

| Where | How | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Component | The contract's view, usually in a `@selector` (see [the declarations](components.html#preparing-stores-reads-state-form-references-listeners)) | `@selector count = () => this.counter.selectors.count(this.counterId);` |
| Store | The protected tool `this.selectors` | `this.selectors.count(id) + 1` |
| Test, other store, `main.ts` | The store's handle | `store.selectors.count('coffees')` |

### In a component

```ts title="src/@components/counter/index.super"
// The route parameter, read on call: `this.counterId()`.
counterId = this.router.current.params.id;

// Reads only what concerns the displayed counter: the other counters do not re-render the screen.
@contract counter;
@selector label = () => this.counter.selectors.label(this.counterId());
@selector count = () => this.counter.selectors.count(this.counterId());
@selector canDecrement = () => this.counter.selectors.canDecrement(this.counterId());
// A load or a write is pending: wait before starting another one.
@selector busy = () => this.counter.selectors.pending();
```

An `@selector` reads a selector's value as is; the condition or the computation happens in `render`, or in a new selector in the contract. See [Reading a store](reading-a-store.html) for the re-render rules.

### In the store

```ts title="src/@core/counter/store.ts"
increment({ id }: { id: string }) {
  return this.#write(id, this.selectors.count(id) + 1);
}

decrement({ id }: { id: string }) {
  if (this.selectors.find(id) && this.selectors.count(id) <= MIN_COUNT) this.fail('below-min');
  return this.#write(id, this.selectors.count(id) - 1);
}
```

Each call rereads the current state: right after a `this.set`, `this.selectors.count(id)` already returns the new value.

### In a test

```ts title="src/@core/counter/store.test.ts"
const store = CounterStore.create({ counterRepository });
await store.send('load');

await store.send('increment', { id: 'coffees' });

expect(store.selectors.count('coffees')).toBe(2);
```

> **Why on the handle, and not on the contract?**
>
> A contract has no state: it describes a store, it is not one. There can be several stores for the same contract. Selectors are therefore read on a specific store: its handle (`store.selectors`), its view in a component (`this.counter.selectors`), or `this.selectors` in the store itself. Each one supplies that store's state, and its cache.

## What to put in a selector

- **Yes**: any read that a component or the store does more than once, or that contains a rule ("worth 0 if missing", "possible if nothing is pending").
- **Yes**: the data that components need and cannot import from `@core/` (catalogue, labels).
- **Yes**: a value the screen displays after a condition or a computation, when that computation deserves a name. `@selector` only accepts a selector as is; one more selector keeps the component simple.
- **No**: a selector that returns the whole state (`all(s: CounterState) { return s; }`). That reopens the door selectors close.
- **Yes**: derivations (a cart's lines, total, filtered list). They belong in the contract rather than in components: they are shared, testable without a DOM, and Super stabilises their result (see below).

## Deriving in a selector

A selector can filter, sort or build new objects without any particular precaution. Each store keeps a cache of its selectors, and Super avoids needless recomputations and re-renders in two steps.

- **Recompute or not**: Super records the top-level fields of the state that the selector reads. On the next state change, if none of these fields has changed reference, the previous result is returned without recomputing.
- **Keep the reference**: after a recomputation, the result is deeply compared with the previous one. If it is equal, the old reference is returned. Otherwise, the unchanged parts (a line that has not moved) keep theirs.

Example: a messaging app whose state contains the messages and the reply being typed.

```ts
type InboxState = { messages: Message[]; folder: 'inbox' | 'archive'; draft: string };

export class InboxContract extends SuperContract<{ state: InboxState }> {
  constructor() {
    super({ name: 'inbox' });
  }

  visible(s: InboxState) {
    return s.messages.filter((m) => m.folder === s.folder).sort((a, b) => b.date - a.date);
  }
}
```

`visible` reads `messages` and `folder`. A keystroke in `draft` creates a new state, but triggers no filter, no sort and no re-render. A received message triggers the recomputation; the list re-renders, and only the new message's line is new.

What you need to know:

- Tracking stops at the top level: a selector that returns `s.messages[3].subject` is recomputed as soon as any message changes. The recomputation has no consequence, the comparison of the result avoids the re-render.
- A selector that walks the whole state (`Object.keys(s)`, `{ ...s }`) depends on everything: it is recomputed on every change.
- The comparison only descends into arrays and plain objects: a `Date`, a `Map` or a class instance is compared by reference.
- A selector only reads its state and its arguments: what it would read elsewhere (a module variable, `Date.now()`) is not tracked.

## A contract without selectors

Selectors are optional, but they are the only reads a component has. Without them, a component can send commands to the store and listen to its events, nothing more: it never sees the raw state. The full handle, for its part, keeps `state()` for tests, the composition root and the other stores. The router follows the same rule: components read the active route through `this.router.current` (`name()`, `path()`, `params`, `query`), never its raw state (see [Router](router.html#the-active-route-and-the-router-state)).

---

# Stores

A store implements a contract. It holds the state, handles the commands, waits for what it has to wait for (an adapter, the network), then updates its state and announces what happened.

## Defining a store

```ts title="src/@core/counter/store.ts"
import { type Commands, SuperStore } from '@super-ts/core';
import { MIN_COUNT } from '../../domain/counter';
import type { CounterRepository } from '../../ports/counter-repository';
import type { CounterContract } from './contract';

/** Dependencies are whatever you want: Super never inspects them. */
type Deps = { counterRepository: CounterRepository };

const message = (error: unknown) => (error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error));

// No "pending" flag and no event to emit: Super tracks each command and publishes its
// outcome. The handler does its work, fails with `this.fail(reason)`, or returns its result.
export class CounterStore extends SuperStore<CounterContract> implements Commands<CounterStore> {
  #repository: CounterRepository;

  constructor({ counterRepository }: Deps) {
    super({ contract: 'counter', initialState: { counts: {}, loadErrorMessage: null } });
    this.#repository = counterRepository;
  }

  // The load error stays in the state: it must remain visible, even for a screen mounted later.
  async load() {
    this.set({ loadErrorMessage: null });
    try {
      this.set({ counts: await this.#repository.loadAll() });
    } catch (error) {
      this.set({ loadErrorMessage: message(error) });
    }
  }

  increment({ id }: { id: string }) {
    return this.#write(id, this.selectors.count(id) + 1);
  }

  decrement({ id }: { id: string }) {
    if (this.selectors.find(id) && this.selectors.count(id) <= MIN_COUNT) this.fail('below-min');
    return this.#write(id, this.selectors.count(id) - 1);
  }

  reset({ id }: { id: string }) {
    return this.#write(id, MIN_COUNT);
  }

  /** The code shared by the three writes: a private method, not a command. */
  async #write(id: string, next: number) {
    if (!this.selectors.find(id)) this.fail('unknown');
    await this.#repository.save(id, next).catch(() => this.fail('storage'));
    this.set((s) => ({ counts: { ...s.counts, [id]: next } }));
    return { count: next };
  }
}
```

A store lives in `src/@core/<name>/store.ts`, next to its contract. It extends `SuperStore<CounterContract>`: the contract class is only imported as a type, the runtime link goes through the name given to `super({ contract: 'counter' })`.

## The constructor: contract, initial state, dependencies

The constructor receives the dependencies and calls `super` with two things:

- **`contract`**: the name of the implemented contract, the one in its `super({ name })`. An unknown name, or another contract's name, does not compile.
- **`initialState`**: the starting state, matching the contract's `state`. It is copied on every `create()`: two instances never share their state.

The constructor stores its dependencies in `#private` fields and can listen to the stores it receives (see [below](stores.html#a-store-that-depends-on-another-store)). It neither reads nor changes the state: `this.get()`, `this.set()` or `this.send()` throw an error there. The state only exists once the store is created.

## Commands: one method per command

Each command of the contract is a **public method** of the store, with the same name. `implements Commands<CounterStore>` has the compiler check it all:

- **One method for each command**: forgetting one does not compile.
- **Exactly the contract's parameters**: `increment({ id }: { id: string })`. Annotate them by hand, TypeScript does not infer the parameters of a class method. A narrower parameter (`{ id: 'coffees' }`) does not compile.
- **Synchronous or asynchronous**: a method can be `async`. The store, and only the store, is where you wait for an adapter.
- **It returns the result declared** by its command's `Outcome` (nothing for a `void` command), or fails with `this.fail(reason)`. Super publishes the outcome (`increment:done`, `increment:failed`) and tracks the pending command: no flag to manage. See [Declaring the outcome](commands-and-events.html#declaring-the-outcome).
- **No other public method**: code shared between commands is written as a `#private` method, like `#write`. A public method outside the contract does not compile.

Without `implements Commands<Self>`, none of this is checked: Super would take any public method for a command. Keep it on every store.

### The tools

The store inherits `protected` tools, usable in its methods. These names are reserved.

| Tool | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `this.get()` | The current state, deeply frozen: an in-place mutation (`this.get().items.push(x)`) throws an error. You replace it with `set`. |
| `this.selectors` | The contract's selectors, with the state supplied: `this.selectors.count(id)`. Each call rereads the current state. Plus `this.selectors.pending(…)` for pending commands. |
| `this.set(patch)` | Merges the patch into the state (one level). Fields the patch does not touch keep their reference: that is how Super knows what changed. Accepts an object or a function `(state) => patch`. The state is updated right away; subscribers are notified only once at the end of the task, even after several `set` calls. |
| `this.emit(name, payload?)` | Announces an event declared in `events` (not a command's outcome: Super publishes that). The payload is typed; a `void` event is emitted without an argument. |
| `this.send(name, body?)` | Sends a command of this same store, tracked by Super like any other (pending, `:done`, `:failed`). To share code without this tracking, call a `#private` method. |
| `this.fail(reason)` | Fails the pending command with a declared reason. Does not return. The compiler accepts the reasons of every command in the contract, not only those of the pending command. |
| `this.signal` | `AbortSignal` aborted by `dispose()`. Not needed for stores received as dependencies (see below); it is for listeners added outside Super, such as `window.addEventListener('online', …, { signal: this.signal })`. |

```ts
this.set({ loadErrorMessage: null });                            // partial object
this.set((s) => ({ counts: { ...s.counts, [id]: next } }));      // function of the current state
```

### Dependencies

Dependencies are **the constructor's parameters**. `create(…)` takes exactly these arguments, with their types.

```ts
CounterStore.create({ counterRepository: createLocalStorageCounterRepository() }); // ok
// @ts-expect-error missing dependency
CounterStore.create();
```

A store without dependencies has a constructor without parameters and is created with `create()`, like `CartStore.create()`.

## Creating an instance: the handle

Declaring the class creates nothing. `CounterStore.create(deps)` is what builds an instance, usually in `main.ts` or in a test. It returns a **handle**, never the instance: the store's methods are not called directly, they are triggered by `send`.

```ts
const counter = CounterStore.create({ counterRepository });

counter.state();                                   // Readonly<CounterState>
counter.selectors.count('coffees');                  // the contract's selectors
await counter.send('increment', { id: 'coffees' });  // Promise<void>: resolved if the command succeeds
const off = counter.on('increment:done', ({ input, result }) => {});
counter.pending('increment');                      // is a command pending?
const unsubscribe = counter.subscribe((state) => {});
counter.dispose();                                 // later sends are rejected
```

| Member | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `state()` | The current state, frozen. |
| `selectors` | The contract's selectors, read on the current state, plus `pending(…)`. |
| `send(name, body?)` | Sends a command. The promise carries no data: it resolves if the command succeeds, and rejects if it fails (with a `CommandFailure` carrying the reason for a declared failure), if the command is unknown or if the store is disposed. |
| `on(name, listener, { signal }?)` | Listens to a declared event, or to a command's lifecycle (`increment:done`, `increment:failed`). Returns the unsubscribe function. |
| `pending(command?, body?)` | Is a command pending? Any command, one command, or one command for a body. |
| `subscribe(listener, { signal }?)` | Listens to every state change (batched per task). |
| `dispose()` | Removes the internal listeners; later `send` calls are rejected. |
| `contract` | The contract read by Super (its name), useful to the `createApp` provider. |

> **The full handle is not for components**
>
> Components receive a reduced view through `@contract counter;`: `selectors`, `send()` (which returns `void`) and `on()`, never the raw state; they listen to its events through an `@on('counter', 'increment:done')` method. The full handle is for tests, the composition root and other stores. Its type is inferred from the contract's name: `StoreOfContract<'counter'>`.

### subscribe: being notified of every state change

`subscribe` calls your function after every state change, with the new state (several `set` calls in the same task give only one call). It returns a function that stops listening.

```ts title="src/main.ts (excerpt)"
const savedCart = createSavedCart(); // adapters/saved-cart.ts
const cart = CartStore.create({ quantities: savedCart.load() }); // the cart from before the reload

// subscribe: the cart is saved on every change, and survives a page reload.
// The store knows nothing about storage: the composition root wires it in.
cart.subscribe((state) => savedCart.save(state.quantities));
```

This is the typical use of `subscribe`: syncing the state with an external system (a storage, an analytics tool, another tab), outside any component, without the store knowing. `CartStore` only receives its starting quantities (`{ quantities }`) and does not know where they are kept; changing storage only touches `main.ts` and the adapter.

The counter does it differently, and rightly so: its store talks to a port, `CounterRepository` (see [Dependencies](stores.html#dependencies)), because persistence is part of its job. Loading is asynchronous, a write can fail, and the screen must show it: these cases go through the store's commands and state. When storage is only a reflection of the state, with no error to report and no data to wait for, `subscribe` is enough.

In a component, you do not need it: `@selector` does the same thing more finely (only when the value read changes) and unsubscribes by itself on unmount. `subscribe` is for code outside components: `main.ts`, a logging tool during development, a test that counts changes.

### dispose: ending the store's life

`dispose` removes the store's internal listeners and aborts its `signal`: if it was listening to another store, that listening stops. Commands sent afterwards are rejected.

```ts
counter.dispose();
await counter.send('increment', { id: 'coffees' }); // rejected: "[super] store "counter" disposed: command "increment" rejected"
```

In a typical app, stores live as long as the page: you never call `dispose`. It is for stores that live shorter lives: a widget created with its own application then removed from the page, a store created for a session and released at its end, or a test that checks that a released store refuses commands.

```ts title="src/widgets/timer-widget.ts"
export function mountTimerWidget(root: HTMLElement): () => void {
  const timer = TimerStore.create();
  const app = createApp({ root, stores: [timer] });
  app.mount(TimerWidget.create());
  return () => {
    app.dispose();   // removes the application and empties the root
    timer.dispose(); // releases the store
  };
}
```

## A store that depends on another store

A store can receive another store as a dependency, listen to its events or send it commands. The type of the dependency is inferred from the contract's name: `StoreOfContract<'cart'>`. Nothing to clean up: Super ties the `on` and `subscribe` of stores received as dependencies to the lifetime of the store receiving them. Listening stops by itself on its `dispose()`.

```ts title="src/@core/checkout/store.ts"
import { type Commands, type StoreOfContract, SuperStore } from '@super-ts/core';
import type { OrderClient } from '../../ports/order-client';
import type { CheckoutContract } from './contract';

type Deps = { cart: StoreOfContract<'cart'>; orderClient: OrderClient };

export class CheckoutStore extends SuperStore<CheckoutContract> implements Commands<CheckoutStore> {
  #cart: Deps['cart'];
  #orderClient: OrderClient;

  constructor({ cart, orderClient }: Deps) {
    super({ contract: 'checkout', initialState: { lastOrder: null } });
    this.#cart = cart;
    this.#orderClient = orderClient;
    // A new purchase starts: the confirmation of the previous order is no longer relevant.
    cart.on('add:done', () => this.set({ lastOrder: null }));
  }
  // …
}

// main.ts
const cart = CartStore.create();
const checkout = CheckoutStore.create({ cart, orderClient: createFakeOrderClient() });
```

The listener is added in the constructor, but it only runs after `create`: it can then call `this.set`.

### Sending a command to another store

A store can also send commands to the store it receives, and wait for the processing to finish: we are in a store, the only place where you wait.

```ts title="src/@core/checkout/store.ts"
async placeOrder({ address }: { address: string }) {
  const cart = this.#cart.selectors; // the cart state, read through its selectors
  if (cart.isEmpty()) return this.fail('empty-cart');

  const lines = cart.lines().map((line) => ({ sku: line.product.sku, quantity: line.quantity }));
  const total = cart.total();
  const result = await this.#orderClient.place({ address, lines, total }).catch(() => this.fail('network'));
  if (!result.ok) return this.fail(result.reason);

  await this.#cart.send('clear'); // a command sent to the other store, awaited until it finishes
  const order = { orderId: result.orderId, total };
  this.set({ lastOrder: order });
  return order;
}
```

- **No data in return**: the promise from `send` only says "it is done" (and rejects if the command fails). To know the result, read the other store afterwards, or listen to its events.
- **Reading the other store**: `this.#cart.selectors` goes through its selectors. `this.selectors` only covers the store itself.
- **One direction only**: the cart is created first and passed at creation. Two stores cannot depend on each other; if the cart must react to the checkout, it listens to a checkout event instead of receiving it as a dependency.

> **At the top level of the dependencies**
>
> Super recognises the stores passed directly in the dependency object, the constructor's first argument (`{ cart }`). A store nested deeper (`{ stores: { cart } }`) is not tied: keep stores at the top level.

## Errors

A component sends its commands without waiting: so the store decides how an error is published.

- **An expected refusal** (unknown counter, already at 0, storage full): `this.fail(reason)`, with a reason declared in the `Outcome`. The component listens to `:failed` and shows the message of its choice.
- **An error that must stay visible**, even for a screen mounted later: in the state, like `loadErrorMessage`.
- **An unexpected exception**: nothing to do. The command fails with the reason `'error'`, `pending` becomes false again, and the exception goes to the console.

| Situation | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Command missing from the store | `send` rejects: "[super] unknown command "x" on the store "counter"". |
| Store disposed | `send` rejects: "[super] store "counter" disposed: command "x" rejected". |
| Method that calls `this.fail('storage')` | `:failed` with `reason: 'storage'`; the promise from `send` rejects with a `CommandFailure`. |
| Method that throws an exception | `:failed` with `reason: 'error'` and the exception; the promise from `send` rejects with it. |
| `this.get()`, `this.set()` or `this.send()` in the constructor | Error on `create`: the state only exists once the store is created. |

---

# Commands and events

The view sends and lets go. The store does the work, waits for what it has to wait for, then succeeds or fails. Super tracks each command from end to end: it knows when it is pending, and publishes its outcome.

## The journey of a click

What happens when you click "+" on a counter's screen:

1. `CounterControls` emits `increment` to its parent (component event).
2. `CounterScreen` sends the command: `this.counter.send('increment', { id: 'coffees' })`. It waits for nothing.
3. Super notes that `increment` is **pending**: `this.counter.selectors.pending()` becomes true, the screen re-renders with the buttons disabled.
4. The store's `increment` method awaits `this.#repository.save(…)`, updates `counts` and returns `{ count: 3 }`.
5. Super notes that the command is finished (the buttons are enabled again) and publishes `increment:done` with `{ input: { id: 'coffees' }, result: { count: 3 } }`.
6. The screen shows the new value (it changed in the state) and "Incremented: 3" (thanks to the event, received by its `@on('counter', 'increment:done')` method).

## Sending a command

```ts title="src/@components/counter/index.super (excerpt)"
export class CounterScreen extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'counter-screen';

  counterId = this.router.current.params.id;
  @contract counter;

  run = (command: CounterChange) => this.counter.send(command, { id: this.counterId() }); // and moves on
}
```

In a component, `send` returns `void`. There is nothing to wait for: writing `await this.counter.send(…)` makes no sense, and no data comes back to the caller.

## Why no await in a component

- **One place for asynchrony.** Waiting and errors live in the store; the "pending / succeeded / failed" tracking is done by Super. The view stays a function of what it reads.
- **No view waiting for a reply that will never come.** If the screen is unmounted during the save, nothing breaks: the store finishes its work and Super publishes the outcome to whoever listens.
- **Everyone sees the outcome.** A reply only benefits the caller; an event benefits every component concerned.

## The lifecycle of a command

Each command goes through three moments, which Super tracks without the store having to write anything:

| Moment | What Super exposes | Component side |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pending | The store's method has started and has not finished. | `this.counter.selectors.pending('increment')` is `true`: automatic re-render. |
| Succeeded | The method finished without error. `increment:done` event, with the body (`input`) and the result (`result`). | `@on('counter', 'increment:done') onIncremented({ input, result }) { … }` |
| Failed | The method called `this.fail(reason)`, or threw an exception. `increment:failed` event, with the body, the reason and the error. | `@on('counter', 'increment:failed') onIncrementFailed({ input, reason }) { … }` |

`pending` becomes false again before `:done` or `:failed` is emitted: a listener already sees the command as finished.

## Declaring the outcome in the contract

A command declares what its success produces and why it can fail, with `Outcome<Result, Reasons>`:

```ts title="src/@core/counter/contract.ts"
commands: {
  load(): void;
  increment(input: { id: string }): Outcome<{ count: number }, 'unknown' | 'storage'>;
  decrement(input: { id: string }): Outcome<{ count: number }, 'unknown' | 'below-min' | 'storage'>;
  reset(input: { id: string }): Outcome<{ count: number }, 'unknown' | 'storage'>;
};
```

- **The result** (`{ count: number }`) is what Super publishes in `increment:done`. It never comes back to whoever sent the command.
- **The reasons** are a closed list of codes, specific to this contract. They describe the expected refusals: `'unknown'` for a counter outside the catalogue, `'below-min'` for a counter already at 0, `'storage'` when saving fails.
- **A command without an `Outcome`** (`load(): void`) still has its lifecycle: `load:done` without a result, and `load:failed` for an unexpected exception.

### In the store: return or fail

```ts title="src/@core/counter/store.ts"
increment({ id }: { id: string }) {
  return this.#write(id, this.selectors.count(id) + 1);
}

decrement({ id }: { id: string }) {
  if (this.selectors.find(id) && this.selectors.count(id) <= MIN_COUNT) this.fail('below-min');
  return this.#write(id, this.selectors.count(id) - 1);
}

/** The code shared by the three writes: a private method, not a command. */
async #write(id: string, next: number) {
  if (!this.selectors.find(id)) this.fail('unknown');                   // expected refusal, typed
  await this.#repository.save(id, next).catch(() => this.fail('storage'));
  this.set((s) => ({ counts: { ...s.counts, [id]: next } }));
  return { count: next };                                                 // published in increment:done
}
```

- Each command of the contract is a store method, which receives the body. `implements Commands<CounterStore>` checks that none is missing and that their parameters are exactly the contract's.
- `this.fail(reason)` fails the command and does not return. Only the reasons declared by the contract are accepted: `this.fail('nope')` does not compile.
- The method returns the declared result. Forgetting it, or returning something else, does not compile.
- Shared code is written as a `#private` method: a public method outside the contract is refused by the compiler.
- No more "pending" flag to reset in a `catch`, and no outcome event to emit: Super takes care of it.

### return this.fail(…) or this.fail(…)

`this.fail` is declared as never returning (`never`), and the compiler takes it into account: after a conditional `this.fail(…)`, the type narrows. The profile store writes it with `return`, which makes the exit visible when reading:

```ts title="src/@core/profile/store.ts"
async save(input: ProfileInput) {
  const result = await this.#client.save(input).catch(() => this.fail('network'));
  if (!result.ok) return this.fail(result.reason); // fail does not return: afterwards, the compiler knows result.ok is true
  return { id: result.id };
}
```

- Both forms do exactly the same thing, at compile time as at runtime: `this.fail` interrupts the method in every case.
- `return this.fail(…)` reads better when what follows depends on the condition, as here; a plain `this.fail(…)` is enough for a guard, like `if (!this.selectors.find(id)) this.fail('unknown')`.
- A call to `this.fail` inside an arrow function (the `.catch(() => this.fail('network'))` above) also fails the command: the exception propagates up to it.

## Failure reasons: codes, not messages

The store says *what happened*; the component chooses *what to display*. The text, and so the language, stays in the view, and the compiler flags a forgotten reason:

```ts title="src/@components/counter/index.super"
const FAILED: Record<CounterFailure | 'error', string> = {
  unknown: 'This counter does not exist.',
  'below-min': 'The counter is already at zero.',
  storage: 'Could not save: storage is unavailable.',
  error: 'An unexpected error occurred.',
};
```

With a code, the component can also react differently depending on the case: offering to free up space for `'storage'`, or displaying nothing for `'below-min'`.

### The unexpected failure: the 'error' reason

An exception the store did not expect (a bug, an `undefined.x`) also fails the command, with the reason `'error'` and the exception in `error`. So the interface never stays stuck "pending". It also goes to the console, whereas a declared, expected failure does not show up there.

## Knowing that a command is pending: pending

```ts
@contract counter;
@selector isLoading = () => this.counter.selectors.pending('load');                         // one command
@selector isSaving = () => this.counter.selectors.pending('increment', { id: this.counterId() }); // for this body
@selector isBusy = () => this.counter.selectors.pending();                                   // any command
```

- `pending` is supplied by Super with the contract's selectors: read in a `@selector` (or in `render`), it re-renders the component when a command starts or finishes.
- The body is filtered field by field: `{ id: 'coffees' }` matches any command whose body has `id === 'coffees'`.
- If two identical commands are pending, `pending` stays true until the last one finishes.
- In the store, `this.selectors.pending(…)` gives the same information; outside a component, `store.pending(…)`.
- `pending` is reserved: a contract cannot declare a selector with that name.

## Listening to the outcome

```ts title="src/@components/counter/index.super"
counterId = this.router.current.params.id;
@contract counter;
@state local = { message: null as string | null };

// The screen sends a command and moves on; Super publishes the outcome of each one.
@on('counter', 'increment:done')
onIncremented({ input, result }) {
  this.#done('increment', input.id, result.count);
}

@on('counter', 'increment:failed')
onIncrementFailed({ input, reason }) {
  this.#failed(input.id, reason);
}
// … likewise for decrement and reset

// Only the outcomes of the displayed counter become a message.
#done(change: CounterChange, id: string, count: number) {
  if (id === this.counterId()) this.local.set({ message: `${DONE[change]}: ${count}` });
}

#failed(id: string, reason: CounterFailure | 'error') {
  if (id === this.counterId()) this.local.set({ message: FAILED[reason] });
}
```

- **One method per event**: `@on('counter', 'increment:done')` calls the method on each outcome, with a parameter typed by the event (`{ input, result }`). The event name is written as is, without a pattern: for several commands, one method each, delegating to a private method. `@on` does not require a `@contract` (see [the declarations](components.html#preparing-stores-reads-state-form-references-listeners)).
- **The body is attached to the outcome** (`input`): the "Coffees" screen recognises its own commands, without the store having to copy the `id`.
- **The route is read in the method** (`this.counterId()`), when the outcome arrives: it sees the up-to-date route.
- **Turn the outcome into local state** to display it: an event does not last, local state does (see [Local state](local-state.html)).
- **Nothing to clean up**: an `@on` method is called as long as the component is mounted, and not after. In a component written in `.ts`, the equivalent is `this.counter.on(…)` in a field or the constructor; `on` is forbidden during `render`.

## A lasting outcome: the state

An event is one-off: a component mounted later does not see it. What must last goes in the state.

|  | Through the state | Through a command's outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | Data that lasts: a value, a load error. | A one-off fact: "it is saved", "it is refused". |
| Example | `counts`, `loadErrorMessage` | `increment:done`, `increment:failed` |
| Component side | Read with `@selector x = () => this.counter.selectors.…;`. | Listened to with `@on('counter', '…')` on a method. |
| A component mounted later | Sees the value. | Sees nothing: the event has passed. |

In the counters example, a load error must stay displayed on the list, even if you come back to it later: the [store](../examples/demo/src/@core/counter/store.ts) keeps it in `loadErrorMessage` rather than failing `load`. A write refusal, on the other hand, only makes sense at the moment: it is the command's outcome.

## Hand-written events

The lifecycle covers the outcome of commands. For a fact that is not a command's outcome (a background sync that finished, data arriving from a server), the contract declares its own events, and the store emits them:

```ts
// contract
events: { synced: { at: number } };

// store
this.emit('synced', { at: Date.now() });
```

## Who can emit, who can listen

|  | Emit a store event | Listen to it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Super | The command lifecycle (`:done`, `:failed`). |  |
| The store | Its declared events, with `this.emit` in its methods. | Those of stores received as dependencies (`cart.on(…)` in its constructor). |
| A component | **No.** The view given by `@contract` has no `emit`. | Yes, with `@on('counter', '…')` on a method. |
| A test | Yes, with `fakeStore(…).emit(…)`, to play the store. | Yes, with `record(store, 'increment:done')`. |

> **A component's `emit` is not a store's**
>
> A component also has a `this.emit`, but it emits *the component's* events to its parent (those declared in its `emits` type). The store and its subscribers never see it. This is intended: a component cannot announce a write that never happened.

## The two kinds of events

|  | Store event | Component event |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Declared in | the contract: a command's `Outcome`, or `events: { synced: … }` | the component: `@emit increment: void;` |
| Emitted by | Super (a command's outcome) or the store (`this.emit`) | the component: `this.emit('increment')` |
| Listened to by | anything with access to the store: `@on('counter', 'increment:done')` in a component, `counter.on('increment:done', …)` elsewhere | the parent only: `<CounterControls … on:increment={…} />` |
| Used to | announce what happened in the store | signal an interaction to the parent |

See [Parents and children](parents-and-children.html) for component events.

## Commands in tests

Outside a component (tests, other stores, composition root), `send` returns a promise: it resolves when the command has succeeded, and rejects when it fails, with a `CommandFailure` carrying the reason.

```ts
const failed = record(store, 'decrement:failed');

await expect(store.send('decrement', { id: 'coffees' })).rejects.toMatchObject({ reason: 'below-min' });

expect(failed.last).toEqual({ input: { id: 'coffees' }, reason: 'below-min', error: null });
```

---

# Components

A component is a typed custom element, written as a class that extends `SuperElement`. Its declarations and fields prepare the instance once; `render()` displays on every render.

## Defining a component

A component lives in a `.super` file under `src/@components/`, for example `src/@components/shop/index.super`. It is an ordinary TypeScript module, with one difference: in its methods, HTML is written directly, as elements placed like statements (see [Templates](templates.html#super-files)). An import without an extension finds it: `@components/shop` refers to `shop/index.super`.

```ts title="src/@components/counter/index.super"
import { SuperElement } from '@super-ts/dom';
import type { CounterChange, CounterFailure } from '../../domain/counter';
import { CounterControls } from './counter-controls';
import './index.css';

const DONE: Record<CounterChange, string> = {
  increment: 'Incremented',
  decrement: 'Decremented',
  reset: 'Reset to zero',
};

// The screen chooses the text for each failure reason (the compiler flags a forgotten reason).
const FAILED: Record<CounterFailure | 'error', string> = {
  unknown: 'This counter does not exist.',
  'below-min': 'The counter is already at zero.',
  storage: 'Could not save: storage is unavailable.',
  error: 'An unexpected error occurred.',
};

/** Screen of the `/counters/:id` route: it reads `id` from its route. */
export class CounterScreen extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'counter-screen';
  // Tracked: renaming the counter also changes the tab title.
  @title = () => this.label.value ?? 'Counter not found';

  // The route parameter, read on call: `this.counterId()`.
  counterId = this.router.current.params.id;

  // Reads only what concerns the displayed counter: the other counters do not re-render the screen.
  @contract counter;
  @selector label = () => this.counter.selectors.label(this.counterId());
  @selector count = () => this.counter.selectors.count(this.counterId());
  @selector canDecrement = () => this.counter.selectors.canDecrement(this.counterId());
  // A load or a write is pending: wait before starting another one.
  @selector busy = () => this.counter.selectors.pending();
  @state local = { message: null as string | null };

  // The screen sends a command and moves on; Super publishes the outcome of each one.
  @on('counter', 'increment:done')
  onIncremented({ input, result }) {
    this.#done('increment', input.id, result.count);
  }

  @on('counter', 'decrement:done')
  onDecremented({ input, result }) {
    this.#done('decrement', input.id, result.count);
  }

  @on('counter', 'reset:done')
  onReset({ input, result }) {
    this.#done('reset', input.id, result.count);
  }

  @on('counter', 'increment:failed')
  onIncrementFailed({ input, reason }) {
    this.#failed(input.id, reason);
  }

  @on('counter', 'decrement:failed')
  onDecrementFailed({ input, reason }) {
    this.#failed(input.id, reason);
  }

  @on('counter', 'reset:failed')
  onResetFailed({ input, reason }) {
    this.#failed(input.id, reason);
  }

  // Only the outcomes of the displayed counter become a message.
  #done(change: CounterChange, id: string, count: number) {
    if (id === this.counterId()) this.local.set({ message: `${DONE[change]}: ${count}` });
  }

  #failed(id: string, reason: CounterFailure | 'error') {
    if (id === this.counterId()) this.local.set({ message: FAILED[reason] });
  }

  run = (command: CounterChange) => this.counter.send(command, { id: this.counterId() });

  #back() {
    <a class="back-link" href={this.router.href('counters')}>← All counters</a>
  }

  render() {
    const label = this.label.value;
    if (label === null) {
      <main class="screen">{this.#back()}<h1>Counter not found</h1><p>No counter "{this.counterId()}".</p></main>
      return;
    }

    const count = this.count.value;
    const busy = this.busy.value;
    <main class="screen counter-screen">
      {this.#back()}
      <h1>{label}</h1>
      <CounterControls
        count={count}
        canDecrement={this.canDecrement.value && !busy}
        canIncrement={!busy}
        on:increment={() => this.run('increment')}
        on:decrement={() => this.run('decrement')}
      />
      <button type="button" class="counter-reset" disabled={count === 0 || busy} on:click={() => this.run('reset')}>Reset to zero</button>
      <p class="counter-message" role="status">{this.local.get().message}</p>
    </main>
  }
}
```

A component class is made of four parts:

| Part | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `extends SuperElement` | The base class, with no generic in a `.super` file: the compiler derives the component's types from its declarations. |
| The declarations | `@tag` (the custom element name, required, with a hyphen), then as needed `@prop` for the props received, `@emit` for the events emitted to the parent, `@title` for the page title. See [Component declarations](components.html#component-declarations). A screen receives no props from the router: it reads its route through `this.router.current`, typed from its route without declaring anything (see [The screen and its route](router.html#the-screen-and-its-route)). |
| The preparation | Contracts (`@contract`), read values (`@selector`), local state (`@state`), the form (`@form`), references (`@ref`), listeners (`@on` on a method), and actions as fields. See [Preparing](components.html#preparing-stores-reads-state-form-references-listeners). |
| `render()` | The component's HTML, required, written as elements in the method body, with no `return`. An optional `renderError(error)` method replaces it if the component or a descendant crashes (see [Handling errors](errors.html#render-error)). |

The component imports nothing from `@core/`, except types: it talks to stores through `@contract name;` (and to the router through `this.router`), and the Vite plugin checks this.

## Component declarations

What describes the component from the outside is written at the top of its class body: its tag, its props, its events, and the page title while it is mounted. No generic on `SuperElement`, no `type Props` above the class: the compiler derives the component's types from these lines, and checks them at every tag that uses it. What the component prepares once (contracts, reads, state, form, references, listeners) is declared the same way: see [Preparing](components.html#preparing-stores-reads-state-form-references-listeners).

```ts title="Example"
export class ConfirmDialog extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'confirm-dialog';
  @title = 'Confirmation';
  @prop question: string;
  @prop tone: 'neutral' | 'danger' = 'neutral';
  @prop note?: string;
  @emit answered: { confirmed: boolean };

  render() {
    <p>{this.question}</p>
    <button on:click={() => this.emit('answered', { confirmed: true })}>Confirm</button>
  }
}
```

| Declaration | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
