| `@tag = 'x-y';` | The custom element name. Required (except for an `abstract` class), a lowercase string with a hyphen. Unique in the app: a second component with the same tag throws an error on its first `create`. |
| `@prop name: T;` | A required prop, read through `this.name`. |
| `@prop name?: T;` | An optional prop (`T \| undefined`). |
| `@prop name: T = value;` | An optional prop with a default value, computed once per instance. |
| `@emit name: T;` | An event, emitted through `this.emit('name', payload)` (`void` if it carries nothing). |
| `@title = …;` | The page title while the component is mounted: a string, or a tracked function. See [The page title](components.html#the-page-title). |

### Props

A prop is read by its name, `this.question`, anywhere in the class and from the fields onwards. Reading always gives the current value, and a prop change re-renders the component. `this.props` still exists (all the props, read-only), but you write `this.name`. The three forms are detailed in [Parents and children](parents-and-children.html#declaring-props).

- **The content written between the tags fills the `content` prop.** It is declared like the others (`@prop content: Children;`) and read through `this.content`. See [Composing: children](parents-and-children.html#composing).
- **Native property names are rejected.** The component is a DOM element: a prop cannot be called `id`, `title`, `hidden`, `slot`… The type error says so: "`title` is already a property of HTML elements: choose another name". In the demo, `title` became `heading` (`KitPage`, `Card`) and `id` became `counterId` (`CounterListItem`). A route parameter `id` is likewise read into a field with a different name: `counterId = this.router.current.params.id;`.
- **`page` is reserved**: it is `this.page`, which holds the page title.

### Events

`@emit name: T;` declares an event and what it carries (`void` if it carries nothing). The component emits it through `this.emit('name', payload)`, the parent listens to it through `on:name={…}` on the tag. See [emit in the child, on in the parent](parents-and-children.html#emit-in-the-child-on-in-the-parent).

### What the compiler rejects

- A missing tag, one written `static tag = …` (a quick fix rewrites it as `@tag`), or one that is not a lowercase string with a hyphen.
- A hand-written generic: "In a `.super` file, props and events are declared in the class: `@prop name: Type;` and `@emit name: Type;`".
- A duplicate declaration, a prop without a type, a `?` with a default value, an `@emit` with a value, a declaration outside a component.

A component written in a `.ts` file (`RouterOutlet`, the components of `@super-ts/ui`, the framework's tests) does not have these declarations: it keeps `static tag` and the generic, and reads its props through `this.props`. It also prepares through methods (`this.contract(…)`, `this.selector(…)`, `this.state(…)`, `this.form(…)`, `this.ref<T>()`, `.on(…)` in the constructor).

```ts title="A component in a .ts file"
type Props = { question: string };
type Emits = { answered: { confirmed: boolean } };

export class ConfirmDialog extends SuperElement<{ props: Props; emits: Emits }> {
  static tag = 'confirm-dialog';
  // …
}
```

### Preparing: stores, reads, state, form, references, listeners

What the component prepares once, when it is constructed, is also declared in its class body: the contracts it reads, its read values, its local state, its form, its references and its listeners. Most components therefore no longer have a constructor.

```ts title="Example"
export class ProfileScreen extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'profile-screen';
  @contract profile;
  @contract shop = 'catalog';                       // a field name different from the contract's
  @selector saving = () => this.profile.selectors.pending('save');
  @state local = { saved: null as string | null };
  @form edit = { initial: { name: '' }, submit: { to: this.profile, command: 'save' } };
  @ref nameInput: HTMLInputElement;

  @on('profile', 'save:done')
  onSaved({ result }) {
    this.local.set({ saved: result.id });
  }

  render() {
    <form {this.edit.bind()}>
      <input ref={this.nameInput} {this.edit.field('name')} />
      <button type="submit" disabled={this.saving.value}>Save</button>
    </form>
  }
}
```

| In a `.super` file | Before, and still in a `.ts` file | Read through |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@contract cart;` | `cart = this.contract('cart');` | `this.cart.selectors.x()`, `this.cart.send(…)` |
| `@contract shop = 'catalog';` | `shop = this.contract('catalog');` | the same, under the name `this.shop` |
| `@selector lines = this.cart.selectors.lines;` | `lines = this.selector(this.cart.selectors.lines);` | `this.lines.value` |
| `@selector count = () => …;` | `count = this.selector(() => …);` | `this.count.value` |
| `@state local = { … };` | `local = this.state({ … });` | `this.local.get()`, `this.local.set(…)` |
| `@form edit = { … };` | `edit = this.form({ … });` | `this.edit.bind()`, `this.edit.field('name')`… |
| `@ref input: HTMLInputElement;` | `input = this.ref<HTMLInputElement>();` | `ref={this.input}`, then `this.input.value` |
| `@on('profile', 'save:done') onSaved(p) { … }` | `this.profile.on('save:done', (p) => …)` in the constructor | the method, called on every event while the component is mounted |

Only the declaration changes: reading stays the same (`this.lines.value`, `this.local.get()`, `this.edit.bind()`, `this.input.value`, `this.cart.send(…)`).

- **No type on `@contract`, `@selector`, `@state`, `@form`**: it comes from the value. To widen it, write `as` in the value (`null as string | null`). `@ref`, conversely, declares the type of its element and has no value.
- **The value of `@contract x = '…'` is a string written as is**, the contract name: `@contract log = 'error-log';` reads the `error-log` contract under the name `this.log`.
- **Order matters**, as with fields: a `@selector` or a `@form` that reads `this.cart` comes after `@contract cart`.

### Listeners: `@on`

A listener is declared on a method: `@on('contract', 'event')` above it, and the method is called on every event while the component is mounted. No more need for a constructor to set up a listener.

- **`@on` does not require `@contract`**: it opens access to the contract itself. A component that only listens to `profile` does not need `@contract profile;`.
- **The method's parameter is typed by the event**: for `save:done`, `{ input, result }`; for `save:failed`, `{ input, reason }`. No need to annotate it.
- **`@on('router', 'navigated')` listens to the router**, like `this.router.on('navigated', …)`.
- **The event name is a string written as is**, with no template literal (`` `${change}:done` ``): one method per event. In the demo, `CounterScreen` declares `onIncremented`, `onDecremented`, `onReset`, `onIncrementFailed`…, which all call `#done` or `#failed` (see the excerpt at the [top of the page](components.html#defining-a-component)).

### Why `@form` and not a `<Form>` component

A form is component state: its values, its errors, its checks, its submission, read throughout the template (`this.edit.field('name')`, `this.edit.values()`, the "Saving…" button). The tag itself already exists: it is the native `<form>`, bound through `<form {this.edit.bind()}>`. A `<Form>` would hide this state and lose the typing of the fields. `<Table>`, on the other hand, is a component because it only displays.

### Preparation errors

- A contract declared twice: "The contract `cart` is already declared by `@contract cart`".
- `@contract router`: "The router is read through `this.router`, without `@contract`".
- A type on `@contract`, `@selector`, `@state` or `@form`: "No type on `@selector`: it comes from the value".
- The old forms, in a `.super` file: `local = this.state({ … })` gives "In a `.super` file, `this.state(…)` is declared with `@state`: `@state local = …;`", with a quick fix that rewrites the line (likewise for `this.contract`, `this.selector`, `this.form` and `this.ref`).
- A `this.x.on(…)` in the constructor: "In a `.super` file, a listener is declared on a method: `@on('x', 'event') onEvent(payload) { … }`". No automatic fix: the method has to be written.

Outside a component, nothing changes: a store that listens to another store keeps `cart.on('add:done', …)` in its constructor, `main.ts` keeps `cart.subscribe(…)`, and a store's handle, in a test, keeps `counter.on('increment:done', …)`.

### In the editor

An `@` typed in a component body suggests `tag`, `title`, `prop`, `emit`, `contract`, `selector`, `state`, `form`, `ref` and `on`, with a template to fill in; `@t` only suggests `tag` and `title`, and an `@tag` or `@title` already written is no longer suggested. Hovering each declaration shows its documentation. After `@contract `, the editor suggests the app's contracts that the component does not declare yet. In `@contract x = '…'` and `@on('…', '…')`, the editor completes the names of the app's contracts, then those of the events of the chosen contract. `@prop` and `@emit` are valid TypeScript (decorated fields); `@tag = …` and `@title = …` are not, but the formatter and Zed's Tree-sitter grammar know them (see [Tooling](tooling.html#editor)).

## Prepare, then render

|  | Declarations and fields | `render()` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When | Once, when the instance is created. | On mount, then on every change of props, local state or a value read from a store. |
| Role | Prepare: declare the contracts read, the reactive values, local state, the form, references, listeners, actions. | Describe the HTML from the current values. |
| Written with | `@contract`, `@selector`, `@state`, `@form`, `@ref`, `@on`, `@title` (in a `.ts` file: `this.contract`, `this.selector`, `this.state`, `this.form`, `this.ref`, a contract's `on`, `this.page.title`). | The prepared fields: `.value`, `get()`, selectors, props (`this.name`). |
| Produces | Nothing. | The elements it emits, or nothing at all (`render() {}`). |

**Preparation is blocked during render.** In a `.super` file, it is only written through declarations, outside `render`. The methods they call (`contract`, `state`, `selector`, `ref` and `form`, written as is in a `.ts` file) throw an error if they are called during `render`: you cannot resolve a store or create state on every render. A contract's `on` listener is allowed in a handler or in `mounted`, but throws an error during a render; so does `this.page.title` (see [The page title](components.html#the-page-title)). The error goes through the component's [renderError](errors.html#render-error), like any render error.

**Props are readable from the declarations and fields onwards**: Super sets them before constructing the instance. A value copied at that point (`@state local = { draft: this.text };`, the initial values of an edit form) does not follow later changes: for an always up-to-date value, read the prop (`this.text`) in `render`, in a `selector` function or in a listener, like the `@on` methods of `CounterScreen`, which call `this.counterId()` when the event arrives and so read the current route.

## Where to put what: preparation or render?

The question to ask: **should this exist only once for the instance, or is it recomputed from the current values?**

| Line | Where | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@tag`, `@prop`, `@emit` | declaration | What the component is from the outside: at the top of the class, once and for all. |
| `@title = () => …` | declaration | The title is set once; the function itself is recomputed after every render. |
| `@contract counter;` | declaration | Resolving a store is wiring, done once. During a render, it throws an error. |
| `@selector count = …;` | declaration | Declares what the component reads. The value itself is recomputed on every read of `.value`. |
| `@state local = { message: null };` | declaration | Local state must survive renders. Recreated on every render, it would start from scratch. |
| `@form edit = { … };`, `@ref input: HTMLInputElement;` | declaration | A form and a reference are instance state: created once, read on every render. |
| `@on('counter', 'increment:done') onIncremented(…) { … }` | decorated method | A listener is set up once, and lives as long as the component is mounted. No constructor. |
| `run = (command) => …` | arrow field | A stable action, created once, with `this` bound. |
| `this.count.value` | `render` | Values change: you read them at render time. |
| `if (label === null)` | `render` | A display decision depends on the current value. The branch emits its elements, then `return;` stops the render: what has already been emitted is kept. |
| `<main>…</main>` | `render` | The elements are the display itself. |
| `#back() { <a …>…</a> }` | method | A reused piece of HTML is written in a method that emits its elements, called through `{this.#back()}` in `render`. |

In short: preparation carries the verbs *declare, subscribe, listen, prepare*; `render` carries the verbs *read, decide, display*. `render` must be callable ten times in a row with no consequence.

> **The classic mistake: reading a value in a field**
>
> A field is initialised when the instance is created: props are readable, but the store is not resolved yet, and a value read at that point would not follow changes.
>
> ```ts
> // ✗ throws an error: the contract can only be read once the component is mounted
> count = this.counter.selectors.count(this.counterId);
>
> // ✓ declare the read, read the value in render
> @selector count = () => this.counter.selectors.count(this.counterId);
> render() {
>   <output>{this.count.value}</output>
> }
> ```

## A component without a store

A presentational component, which displays its props and emits events, only needs `render`:

```ts title="src/@components/counter/counter-controls.super (excerpt)"
/** Pure presentational component: it knows no store. */
export class CounterControls extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'counter-controls';
  @prop count: number;
  @prop canDecrement: boolean;
  @prop canIncrement: boolean;
  @emit increment: void;
  @emit decrement: void;

  render() {
    <div class="counter-controls" role="group" aria-label="Counter">
      <button type="button" aria-label="Decrement" disabled={!this.canDecrement} on:click={() => this.emit('decrement')}>−</button>
      <output class="counter-value" aria-label="Counter value">{this.count}</output>
      <button type="button" aria-label="Increment" disabled={!this.canIncrement} on:click={() => this.emit('increment')}>+</button>
    </div>
  }
}
```

It knows no store: it stays reusable and can be tested on its own.

## A component for a side effect

Some components exist mainly for what they do on mount, not for what they display. Everything they set up with `this.signal`, or through an `@on` listener, is cleaned up on unmount.

```ts title="src/@components/widget/timer-shortcuts.super"
import { SuperElement } from '@super-ts/dom';

/** A keyboard shortcut added on window on mount, removed by `signal` on unmount. */
export class TimerShortcuts extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'timer-shortcuts';

  @contract timer;

  protected override mounted() {
    window.addEventListener(
      'keydown',
      (event) => {
        const typing = event.target instanceof HTMLInputElement || event.target instanceof HTMLTextAreaElement;
        if (event.code !== 'Space' || typing) return;
        event.preventDefault();
        this.timer.send('toggle');
      },
      { signal: this.signal },
    );
  }

  render() {
    <p class="shortcut">Space bar: start or pause.</p>
  }
}
```

Typical cases: sending a command on mount, listening to an event to trigger an action elsewhere (analytics, sound, focus), setting a listener on `window`. A component that displays nothing keeps an empty `render`: `render() {}` (see [Rendering nothing](templates.html#rendering-nothing)).

## The tools of a component

Everything goes through `this`. What the class declares, what it uses (the preparation tools are protected: only the class has access to them), and what Super calls on the class itself.

| Member | Where | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What the class declares |
| `@tag = 'x-y';` | at the top of the class | The custom element name, required, with a hyphen (`'counter-screen'`). Checked on the first `create`. See [Component declarations](components.html#component-declarations). |
| `@prop name: T;` | at the top of the class | A prop received from the parent: required, optional (`name?: T`) or with a default value (`name: T = value`). |
| `@emit name: T;` | at the top of the class | An event emitted to the parent (`void` if it carries nothing). |
| `@title = …;` | at the top of the class | The page title while the component is mounted: a string, or a tracked function. See [The page title](components.html#the-page-title). |
| `@contract name;`, `@contract name = 'contract';` | in the class | The store provided for this contract, seen through its selectors, `send` and `on`. All contracts except the router. In a `.ts` file: `this.contract(name)`. See [Reading a store](reading-a-store.html). |
| `@selector name = …;` | in the class | A value read from a selector, read through `.value` in `render`; the component only re-renders if it changes. In a `.ts` file: `this.selector(read)`. See [Reading a store](reading-a-store.html). |
| `@state name = { … };` | in the class | Local state, read through `get()`, changed through `set(…)`. In a `.ts` file: `this.state(initial)`. See [Local state](local-state.html). |
| `@form name = { … };` | in the class | A form: bound fields, rules, checks, submission through a command. In a `.ts` file: `this.form(options)`. See [Forms](forms.html). |
| `@ref name: T;` | in the class | A reference to a template element: `<input ref={this.input} />`, then `this.input.value` once mounted. The compiler rejects the reference if `T` is not the tag's type (see [References](templates.html#references)). In a `.ts` file: `this.ref<T>()`. |
| `@on('contract', 'event') method(payload) { … }` | on a method | A listener, called on every event while the component is mounted, with no `@contract` needed; `'router'` listens to the router. In a `.ts` file: `.on(…)` in the constructor. See [Listeners](components.html#listeners-on). |
| `render()` | required method | Describes the HTML, on every render. Can neither read a new contract nor create state. |
| `renderError(error)` | optional method | Displayed instead of `render` if `render`, a descendant, or resolving a store on mount crashes. If it crashes itself, the error bubbles up to the parent. See [Handling errors](errors.html#render-error). |
| `mounted()`, `unmounted()` | optional methods | Called after the first render of each mount, and on unmount. |
| What the class uses |
| `this.name` | everywhere, from the fields onwards | A prop declared with `@prop`, always at its current value. A prop change re-renders the component; a copy made at construction does not follow it. `this.props` gives them all, read-only. |
| `this.emit(name, payload?)` | everywhere | Emits an event declared with `@emit`, to the parent. See [Parents and children](parents-and-children.html). |
| `this.router` | everywhere | The app's router, without a declaration: its selectors, `send`, `on` and `href`. See [The router in a component](router.html#the-router-in-a-component). |
| `this.page.title = …` | everywhere except `render` | Sets the page title while the component is mounted, like `@title`: a string, or a tracked function. Write-only. See [The page title](components.html#the-page-title). |
| `this.signal` | once mounted | `AbortSignal` aborted on unmount, for listeners set up outside Super (`window.addEventListener(…, { signal: this.signal })`). Unnecessary for stores: `@on` listeners clean themselves up. |
| `this` | everywhere | The element itself, for the cases the API does not cover (focus, measurements). |
| On the class |
| `<Class prop={…} on:name={…} />` | template | Mounts the child at this position (same instance from one render to the next). Props are checked against its `@prop`, listeners against its `@emit`. See [Parents and children](parents-and-children.html). |
| `Class.create(props?, { on }?)` | outside a template | Returns the element, for the initial mount, the router or a test. Props and listeners are typed the same way. |
| `Class.eventName(name)` | outside a template | The DOM name of an emitted event (`'confirm-dialog:answered'`), for a listener set up by hand. |

A field or a prop cannot have the name of a native `HTMLElement` property (`slot`, `title`, `hidden`, `id`…): the component is a DOM element, and that name is already taken. `page` is likewise reserved, for `this.page`. Do not override `connectedCallback` or `disconnectedCallback` either: Super throws an error on the first `create`. Use `mounted` and `unmounted`.

### mounted and unmounted

```ts title="src/@components/app-shell/index.super"
import { RouterOutlet, SuperElement } from '@super-ts/dom';
import { RouteLink } from '@super-ts/ui';
import './index.css';

/** Shared layout: the navigation between the examples, then the screen of the active route. */
export class AppShell extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'app-shell';

  @contract counter;

  protected override mounted() {
    this.counter.send('load');
  }

  render() {
    // Each link marks itself `aria-current="page"` on the displayed page; `activeFor`
    // extends a section to its other routes (the counter list and a single counter).
    <header class="app-header">
      <nav aria-label="Examples">
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'examples' }}>
          Examples
        </RouteLink>
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'counters' }} activeFor={['counter']}>
          Counters
        </RouteLink>
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'profile' }}>
          Form
        </RouteLink>
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'shop' }} activeFor={['checkout']}>
          Shop
        </RouteLink>
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'errors' }}>
          Errors
        </RouteLink>
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'widget' }}>
          Widget
        </RouteLink>
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'composition' }}>
          Composition
        </RouteLink>
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'kit' }}>
          Kit
        </RouteLink>
      </nav>
    </header>
    <RouterOutlet />
  }
}
```

The shell reads nothing from the counter store: it never re-renders for it. It only uses it to load the counters once, on mount.

Use `mounted` when you need the already rendered DOM (measuring, giving focus) or to start an action on mount. What must stop on unmount stops in `unmounted`:

```ts title="src/@components/widget/timer-widget.super (excerpt)"
#interval: ReturnType<typeof setInterval> | undefined;

// The interval lives between the widget's mount and unmount.
protected override mounted() {
  this.#interval = setInterval(() => this.timer.send('tick'), 1000);
}

protected override unmounted() {
  clearInterval(this.#interval);
}
```

## Lifecycle

1. **Creation**: the parent's tag (or `create`) sets the props, then constructs the instance (declarations and fields, in order, then the constructor if there is one), which already reads them.
2. **Mount**: the element enters the DOM. Super resolves the declared contracts, wires the `@on` listeners, performs the first `render`, sets its title if it declares one, then calls `mounted`.
3. **Renders**: on every change of props, local state or a value read from a store. Several changes in the same task give only one render.
4. **Move**: an element moved in the DOM (for example by a `for` loop with `key`) is not restarted: it keeps its state.
5. **Unmount**: a real removal from the DOM aborts `signal`, unsubscribes the component from its stores (reads and `@on` listeners), removes its title, then calls `unmounted`. If it is reinserted later, the same instance mounts again: its contracts are resolved again, its `@on` listeners rewired, its title set again, and `mounted` called again. Its local state is kept.

## The page title

The tab title (`document.title`) belongs to the mounted components: a component sets it through `@title`, and removes it when it unmounts. Nobody writes `document.title` by hand.

### A fixed or tracked title

A string gives a fixed title, set on mount and removed on unmount: `@title = 'Widget';`. A function gives a **tracked** title: it is recomputed after every render, with the same reads as `render`. The shop's title therefore changes with the cart:

```ts title="src/@components/shop/index.super (excerpt)"
export class ShopScreen extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'shop-screen';
  // Tracked: the tab title changes with the cart, like the render.
  @title = () => {
    const count = this.cart.selectors.count();
    return count > 0 ? `Shop (${count} in cart)` : 'Shop';
  };

  @contract cart;
  // …
}
```

The computation is free (a condition, formatting), unlike the function of a `@selector`. In a counter's screen, `@title = () => this.label.value ?? 'Counter not found';` follows the counter's name: renaming it also changes the tab title.

### this.page.title

`@title` is a shortcut: `this.page.title = …` does the same thing imperatively, with a string or a function. What changes is when you write it.

| Set in | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| A field or the constructor, in a `.ts` file (what `@title` does) | The component's title, applied again on every mount. |
| `mounted`, a handler | Replaces the component's title until it unmounts. |
| `render` | Forbidden: throws an error. |

```ts
onSaved = () => {
  this.page.title = 'Profile saved';
};
```

### The title stack

Several mounted components can set a title at the same time. The last one mounted wins; those below keep following their data without being displayed; when it unmounts, the previous title comes back. Any component can set a title, not just a screen: in the demo, `KitPage`, the shared layout of the kit, gives all the kit pages their title with `@title = () => this.heading;`.

The sequence, for the shop and a confirmation dialog that would declare `@title = 'Confirmation';`, with the demo's settings (`suffix: ' · Super'`, `default: 'Super · examples'`):

| Moment | Titles set (oldest to newest) | Tab title |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The shop mounts, empty cart | `Shop` | Shop · Super |
| A product added to the cart | `Shop (1 in cart)` | Shop (1 in cart) · Super |
| "Empty the cart" opens the dialog | `Shop (1 in cart)`, `Confirmation` | Confirmation · Super |
| "Confirm": the cart empties, the dialog unmounts | `Shop` | Shop · Super |
| Navigation to a screen without a title | none | Super · examples |

On the second-to-last line, the shop followed the emptied cart while the dialog was on top: its title is already up to date when it comes back.

### What is forbidden

- Setting the title during `render`: `this.page.title` throws an error ("cannot be set during render").
- Reading the title: `this.page.title` is set, not read; reading it throws an error.
- A prop named `title`: it is a property of HTML elements (the demo calls it `heading`). `page` is reserved.

### Default title and suffix

The router configures what surrounds the titles set, in the options of `createRouter` (not in `defineRouter`, whose keys are routes):

```ts title="src/main.ts (excerpt)"
const router = createRouter(Router, { title: { default: 'Super · examples', suffix: ' · Super' } });
```

`default` is displayed when no component sets a title; `suffix` is appended to the title set. Without `default`, the document's original title comes back. See [The page title](router.html#the-page-title) in the router page.

## Creating an element outside a template

In a `.super` file, `<CounterControls count={count} … />` mounts the child at this position (see [Parents and children](parents-and-children.html)); the tooling translates it into `CounterControls.create(props, { on })`. Outside a template, for the initial mount or a test, you call this `create(props?, { on }?)` directly: it returns the element.

```ts
createApp({ root, stores, router }).mount(AppShell.create());
```

A component is not written by its tag: `<counter-screen>` typed in a template or in `index.html` is not supported. It always goes through its class, as a tag (`<CounterControls count={count} … />`) or through `create`.

---

# Reading a store

`@contract name;` gives the component the view of the store provided by the application. `@selector` chooses what it reads from it: the component only re-renders if that value changes.

## @contract and @selector

```ts title="src/@components/counter-list/counter-list-item.super (excerpt)"
/** A row of the home list: only re-renders if its counter's value changes. */
export class CounterListItem extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'counter-list-item';
  @prop counterId: string;
  @prop label: string;

  @contract counter;
  @selector count = () => this.counter.selectors.count(this.counterId);

  render() {
    <a href={this.router.href('counter', { params: { id: this.counterId } })}>{this.label}</a>
    <span class="counter-list-value">{this.count.value}</span>
  }
}
```

- `@contract counter;` is declared in the class body, once per store used, and is read through `this.counter`. The name is the contract's, checked by the compiler: `@contract compteur;` does not compile. For a different field name: `@contract shop = 'catalog';`.
- `@selector count = …;` is also declared in the class body, after the `@contract` it reads. Its value is the reading of **one** selector; it is read through `.value` in `render`, with the selector's type. No type to write: it comes from the value.
- All these declarations are described in [Components](components.html#preparing-stores-reads-state-form-references-listeners). A component written in a `.ts` file keeps the methods: `counter = this.contract('counter')`, `count = this.selector(…)`.
- The selectors are the contract's, with the state already supplied, plus `pending(…)` to know whether a command is pending (see [pending](commands-and-events.html#pending)).
- The component does not import the contract: it names it. Only types may come from `@core/` (`import type`).

### A selector, as is

The value of a `@selector` is the value of a selector **as is**. Two ways to write it, depending on whether the selector takes a parameter:

```ts title="src/@components/counter-list/index.super (excerpt)"
@contract counter;
@selector catalog = this.counter.selectors.catalog;                  // no parameter: passed as is
@selector isLoading = () => this.counter.selectors.pending('load');  // with a parameter: a function
@selector loadErrorMessage = this.counter.selectors.loadErrorMessage;
```

A condition, a computation or a mix of two selectors do not go in a `@selector`. They go in `render`, or in a new contract selector if they make sense for the domain:

```ts
// ✗ does not compile: the function does not return a selector's value
@selector canDecrement = () => this.counter.selectors.canDecrement(this.counterId) && !this.counter.selectors.pending();

// ✓ two readings, combined in render
@selector canDecrement = () => this.counter.selectors.canDecrement(this.counterId);
@selector busy = () => this.counter.selectors.pending();
render() {
  <button disabled={!this.canDecrement.value || this.busy.value}>−</button>
}
```

The rule is checked at compile time: a selector value carries a type brand that `@selector` requires. `null` and `undefined` cannot carry a brand: for them, Super checks at runtime, and throws an error explaining what to do. The reason: a `@selector` that computes might depend on no store and stay frozen, or mix the store with something else without Super knowing.

## What @contract gives

| Member | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `selectors` | The contract's selectors, plus `pending`, read on the current state at each call. To pass to `@selector`, or to read directly in `render`. |
| `send(name, body?)` | Sends a command and lets it run. Returns `void`; the outcome comes back through the selectors, or through `name:done` / `name:failed`. |
| `on(name, listener)` | Listens to a store event, or a command's outcome. In a `.super` file, it is written on a method, `@on('counter', 'increment:done')`, which is called as long as the component is mounted: no `signal` to pass (see [Listening to the outcome](commands-and-events.html#listening-to-the-outcome)). In a `.ts` file, it is declared in the constructor; it is forbidden during `render`. |
| `href(route, { params, query }?)` | For the router only: builds a typed link, without subscribing the component (see [below](reading-a-store.html#the-router)). |

The component does not receive the store itself: no raw state, no `subscribe`, no `dispose`, no `emit`. These capabilities stay with whoever created the store.

## When the component re-renders

On every store state change, Super recomputes the `@selector`s read during the last render and compares each value with the one displayed. **If nothing has changed, the component does not re-render.**

Example: the "Coffees" screen reads `count('coffees')`. Incrementing "Push-ups" changes the store's state, but not the value read by the screen: it does not re-render.

### What counts as a change

The value read is deeply compared with the previous one. It does not matter if a selector rebuilds it: only its content counts, and Super keeps the old reference as long as it is equal (structural sharing). Plain arrays and objects are compared element by element; a `Date`, a `Map` or a class instance, by reference.

| Reading | Re-render when… |
| --- | --- |
| `@selector count = () => this.counter.selectors.count(this.counterId)` | the number changes. |
| `@selector busy = () => this.counter.selectors.pending()` | a command starts or finishes. |
| `@selector lines = this.cart.selectors.lines` | a line changes. Unchanged lines keep their reference. |
| `@selector catalog = this.counter.selectors.catalog` | never, if the catalogue does not change. |

The value of `.value` is the same reference as long as its content does not change: passing it as props to a child does not re-render it needlessly. A child only re-renders if one of its props changes.

> **For a list: one component per row**
>
> On the counter list, each row is a small component (`CounterListItem`, above) that reads its own value. When a counter changes, only its row re-renders: the list does not move, and the DOM of the other rows is not recomputed.

### Reading props in the reading

A `@selector` function can read props (`this.counterId`). It is recomputed on every render, so on every props change: if the screen goes from "Coffees" to "Push-ups", the reading follows, with no missed update. That is also why a selector with a parameter is written in a function: props are readable when the declaration initialises, but a value read at that moment would stay the one from creation.

## Reading a selector directly in render

A selector called directly in `render` (`{this.counter.selectors.count('coffees')}`) also subscribes the component, as finely as a `@selector`: Super remembers each reading and its value, and on every store change, it redoes these readings. The component only re-renders if one of them gives a different value (deeply compared: a new array with the same content does not count).

The reading is recorded on the component **that renders**, even if the contract view comes from another one: a child that receives its parent's view as a prop and reads it in its own `render` subscribes itself, and re-renders on its own. That is what the kit's [`CommandButton`](ui.html#commandbutton) does, reading `pending` on the contract of the screen that prepared it.

`@selector` is still useful to read a value outside `render` through `.value`, to name it once and reuse it, and for `isValid()` on a route value. Only what is read counts: what `render` shows without going through a selector (a module variable, `Date.now()`) triggers no render.

## Showing nothing from a store

A component that sends commands or listens to events, but shows nothing from the store, declares the contract without `@selector`: it never re-renders for that store.

```ts title="src/@components/app-shell/index.super (excerpt)"
@contract counter;

protected override mounted() {
  this.counter.send('load');
}
```

## The router

The router is read through `this.router`, without declaring it: a view that is always available. The active route is read through `this.router.current`: `name()` (the active route's name), `path()`, `params.<key>()`, `query.<key>()`. Each one is passed as is to `@selector`, like a selector without a parameter.

```ts
@selector route = this.router.current.name;   // 'examples' | 'counters' | 'counter' | … | null
```

`this.router.href('counter', { params: { id: 'coffees' } })` builds a link, with the route and its parameters checked. It does not read the active route: a component that only shows links does not re-render on every navigation. See [Router](router.html).

## The raw state stays hidden

A component only reads a store's state through its contract's selectors:

```ts
// @ts-expect-error `counts` is not a selector of the contract
this.counter.selectors.counts;
// @ts-expect-error a contract view has no state
this.counter.state();
```

It is not just a matter of types: at runtime, the view only passes the selectors, never the state object. The only ways round it are deliberate: a selector that would return the whole state, a store exported from a user-land module, or an `as any`.

## Several stores, or several readings

Declare as many `@contract` and `@selector` as needed. Each `@selector` is compared on its own: the component re-renders if any of them changes.

```ts title="src/@components/shop/index.super (excerpt)"
@contract cart;
@selector catalog = this.cart.selectors.catalog;
@selector lines = this.cart.selectors.lines;
@selector total = this.cart.selectors.total;
@selector isEmpty = this.cart.selectors.isEmpty;
```

## When the store is not provided

Super resolves contracts at mount. If no application (and no test) has provided a store for that contract, the component is not shown (its `renderError`, if it has one, takes its place) and the error is reported (`setup` phase, see [Errors](errors.html#who-catches-what)):

```text
[super] <counter-screen>: no store provided for the contract "counter".
Add it to createApp({ stores }) or to mount(..., { stores }).
```

---

# Local state

Local state belongs to a component instance: private, created with it, lost with it. It is for interface data; the app's data lives in a store.

## Creating local state

```ts
export class StatusLine extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'status-line';

  @state local = { message: null as string | null };

  render() {
    <p role="status">{this.local.get().message}</p>
  }
}
```

| Syntax | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `@state local = initial;` | Declares the state in the class body, which is then read through `this.local` (see [the declarations](components.html#preparing-stores-reads-state-form-references-listeners)). The initial value is copied. In a component written in `.ts`, the equivalent is `local = this.state(initial)`, in a field or the constructor only (during `render`, it throws an error). |
| `get()` | The current value, frozen. Call it in `render` to reflect the latest change. |
| `set(patch)` | Merges the patch (one level), then re-renders the component. Accepts a partial object or a function `(current) => patch`. |

```ts
this.local.set({ message: 'Incremented: 3' });
this.local.set((current) => ({ clicks: current.clicks + 1 }));
```

Several `set` calls in a row give only one render.

## The type, and `null as string | null`

`@state` carries no type: it comes from the initial value (writing `@state local: … = …` is an error). `@state local = { message: null };` would give a field of type `null`, and `this.local.set({ message: 'ok' })` would not compile. So you widen with `as` the fields that will change type:

```ts
@state local = { message: null as string | null, open: false, selectedId: null as string | null };
```

## Local state or store?

| In local state | In a store |
| --- | --- |
| A confirmation message shown under buttons | The counters' values |
| A panel open or closed, an active tab | A "loading" indicator that several components display |
| Input in progress, before submission | Submitted and persisted data |
| The question of an open dialog | A load error to show on several screens |

The questions to ask yourself:

- **Does another component need it?** If so, store.
- **Must it survive navigation?** If so, store. Local state disappears with the screen: when you come back to "Coffees", the message from the previous visit is gone, and that is what you want.
- **Is it app data or a display detail?** App data: store.

## An event turned into local state

A command's outcome is one-off: to display it, the screen copies it into its local state. That is the case for the "Incremented: 3" message, in an `@on` method of a counter's screen:

```ts title="src/@components/counter/index.super (excerpt)"
counterId = this.router.current.params.id;
@contract counter;
// …
@state local = { message: null as string | null };

// The screen sends a command and moves on; Super publishes the outcome of each one.
@on('counter', 'increment:done')
onIncremented({ input, result }) {
  this.#done('increment', input.id, result.count);
}
// …

// Only the outcomes of the displayed counter become a message.
#done(change: CounterChange, id: string, count: number) {
  if (id === this.counterId()) this.local.set({ message: `${DONE[change]}: ${count}` });
}
```

The method reads the route param (`this.counterId()`) when the event arrives: so it sees the up-to-date value, not the one from when the component was created.

## What you need to know

- **Private**: only this component reads and writes it. Neither the store, nor the parent, nor other components have access to it.
- **Per instance**: two screens mounted at the same time each have their own.
- **Tied to the instance**: it is born with the component and disappears with it. An element moved by a `for` loop with `key` keeps it; a component that the parent stops rendering then renders again is a new instance, with fresh state.
- **Reactive**: `set` re-renders the component, like a store change.
- It is the equivalent of React's `useState`, grouped in a single object.

---

# Parents and children

Props go down, events go up. A parent never drives a child by calling its methods: it passes it props, and the child answers with events.

## Using a child component

In a template, a child is placed as a tag, named after its class: a tag that starts with a capital letter is a component, imported like any class (`import { CounterControls } from './counter-controls'`).

```ts title="src/@components/counter/index.super (excerpt)"
<CounterControls
  count={count}
  canDecrement={this.canDecrement.value && !busy}
  canIncrement={!busy}
  on:increment={() => this.run('increment')}
  on:decrement={() => this.run('decrement')}
/>
```

- **The attributes are the props.** The compiler checks them against the child's `@prop`s: a missing required prop, an extra prop or a wrongly typed value is an error. A fixed value is written in quotes (`question="Empty the cart?"`, a string), a computed value in braces.
- **`on:name`** wires a child event to a parent function. The name and the payload are checked against the child's `@emit`s.
- The tag is the equivalent of `CounterControls.create({ count, … }, { on: { increment, … } })`, the call used outside a template (see [Creating an element outside a template](components.html#creating-an-element-outside-a-template)).
- The child element is **created once** per position, then its props are updated on each parent render. It keeps its local state. If it receives equal props (compared key by key), it does not re-render.
- A component can also receive elements between its tags, if it declares them (see [Composing: children](parents-and-children.html#composing)).

## Declaring props

A prop is declared in the class body with `@prop`, with its type, and is read through `this.name`. The tag, the props and the events are written in the same place, without a generic (the details of each declaration are in [Components: declarations](components.html#component-declarations)):

```ts title="src/@components/counter-list/counter-list-item.super (excerpt)"
export class CounterListItem extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'counter-list-item';
  @prop counterId: string;
  @prop label: string;

  render() {
    <a href={this.router.href('counter', { params: { id: this.counterId } })}>{this.label}</a>
    // …
  }
}
```

A prop takes one of these three forms:

```ts
@prop question: string;                          // required
@prop note?: string;                             // optional: string | undefined
@prop tone: 'neutral' | 'danger' = 'neutral';    // optional, with a default value
```

- A **required** prop missing from the parent's tag is a compile error.
- An **optional** prop (`?`) is `undefined` when the parent does not pass it. `?` and a default value do not go together: it is an error.
- The **default value** makes the prop optional; it is computed once per instance (a default `[]` is not shared between two elements).
- A component whose props are all optional is placed without attributes (`<RouterOutlet />`).

- `this.counterId` is read-only, and always up to date: a prop change re-renders the child. `this.props` still exists (all the props, read-only), but you write `this.name`.
- Props are **readable from construction** (to initialise a `@state`, for example). A copy made at that moment does not follow later changes: read `this.name` in `render` or in a `@selector` function for an always up-to-date value.

### Names already taken by HTML elements

A component is an HTML element: `this.id`, `this.title`, `this.hidden` or `this.slot` already exist. A prop therefore cannot have one of these names, and the compiler says so:

```ts
@prop title: string;
// ✗ "title" is already a property of HTML elements: choose another name
```

In the demo app, `title` became `heading` (`Card`, `KitPage`) and `id` became `counterId` (`CounterListItem`). An `id` route parameter is likewise read into a field with another name: `counterId = this.router.current.params.id;`. The name `page` is reserved too (it is `this.page`). For the same reason, the content written between the tags fills a `content` prop (`children` is native), see [Composing: children](parents-and-children.html#composing).

## emit in the child, on in the parent

Each side uses its own vocabulary. `on:` is the prefix used on the parent side to listen; the child never sees it.

|  | Child side (`CounterControls`) | Parent side (`CounterScreen`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Declare | `@emit increment: void;` and `@emit decrement: void;`, in the class body | nothing |
| Act | `this.emit('increment')`: "I announce that someone clicked" | `on:increment={…}`: "when you announce that, I do this" |

The child speaks, the parent listens. The child does not know who listens to it, or even whether anyone does. It is the same principle as an HTML `<button>`: it emits `click`, and it is the page that writes `on:click={…}`, with the same prefix. Elsewhere, it is `$emit` / `@increment` in Vue, `dispatch` / `on:increment` in Svelte.

### Declaring a component's events

```ts
export class ItemPicker extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'item-picker';
  @emit picked: { id: string };
  @emit closed: void;

  render() {
    <button on:click={() => this.emit('picked', { id: 'a' })}>Choose A</button>
    <button on:click={() => this.emit('closed')}>Close</button>
  }
}
```

`@emit name: T;` declares an event and the type of what it carries (`void` if it carries nothing). It has no value: `@emit closed: void = …` is an error. A `void` event is emitted without an argument. The compiler rejects an unknown name, a wrongly typed payload, or a forgotten payload.

### The full journey of a click on "+"

1. `CounterControls` emits `increment`.
2. `CounterScreen` receives the event and calls `this.run('increment')`.
3. `run` sends `this.counter.send('increment', { id: 'coffees' })` to the store.
4. The store saves and updates its state; Super publishes `increment:done`.
5. The screen re-renders; the new value flows back down into `CounterControls` through the `count` prop.

`CounterControls` knows neither the store, nor the `id`, nor the command: it stays reusable. It is the screen that decides what "increment" means.

## A dialog: the parent renders it, it answers with an event

Even a confirmation dialog follows this rule. The parent opens it by rendering it, with its question as a prop; the dialog emits the answer. Mounted, it is open: no nullable prop that would mean "closed". Nobody waits for anything, there is no `await`.

```ts title="src/@components/shared/confirm-dialog.super (excerpt)"
export class ConfirmDialog extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'confirm-dialog';
  @prop question: string;
  @emit answered: { confirmed: boolean };

  render() {
    <div class="backdrop">
      <div role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-label="Confirmation">
        <p>{this.question}</p>
        <div class="actions">
          <button type="button" on:click={() => this.emit('answered', { confirmed: false })}>Cancel</button>
          <button type="button" class="danger" on:click={() => this.emit('answered', { confirmed: true })}>Confirm</button>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  }
}
```

```ts title="src/@components/shop/index.super (excerpt)"
@contract cart;
// The open dialog (none: null), and a one-off message.
@state local = { dialog: null as 'confirm-clear' | null, message: null as string | null };

// The dialog answers with an event: the parent decides what happens next.
onClearAnswered = ({ confirmed }: { confirmed: boolean }) => {
  this.local.set({ dialog: null });                                  // closes the dialog
  if (confirmed) this.cart.send('clear');
};

render() {
  <main class="screen">
    {/* … */}
    <button type="button" on:click={() => this.local.set({ dialog: 'confirm-clear' })}>Empty the cart</button>
    {/* … */}
    if (this.local.get().dialog === 'confirm-clear') {
      <ConfirmDialog question="Empty the cart?" on:answered={this.onClearAnswered} />
    }
  </main>
}
```

1. Click on "Empty the cart": the parent puts `dialog: 'confirm-clear'` in its local state.
2. The parent re-renders; the condition is true, the dialog is mounted with its question and shows.
3. Click on "Confirm": the dialog emits `answered { confirmed: true }`.
4. `onClearAnswered` sets `dialog` back to `null` (the dialog is unmounted) and sends the command.

Opening and closing a dialog means changing a value in the parent's state. With several dialogs, keep a single field (`dialog: 'confirm-clear' | 'confirm-delete' | null`) and one condition per dialog: each has its question and its handler, and two modals cannot be open at the same time. The same pattern works for a drawer or a menu.

### A handler passed to a child: an arrow field

`onClearAnswered` is a field holding an arrow function, not a method. An arrow function keeps the component's `this`; a method passed as is (`on:answered={this.onAnswered}` with `onAnswered() { … }`) would lose it, and `this.local` would be `undefined` at call time. Same rule for an action passed to `on:click` without a wrapping function.

```ts
onAnswered = ({ confirmed }: { confirmed: boolean }) => { … };   // ✓ this bound
onAnswered({ confirmed }: { confirmed: boolean }) { … }          // ✗ this lost once passed to on:answered
```

## Lists

For a list of children, use a `for` loop with a key, written after `key`: a moved element keeps its DOM and its local state. Without a key, rendering follows the position (see [Lists](templates.html#lists)).

```ts title="src/@components/counter-list/index.super (excerpt)"
<ul class="counter-list">
  for (const c of shown; key c.id) {
    <li><CounterListItem counterId={c.id} label={c.label} /></li>
  }
</ul>
```

## Composing: children

A card, a modal, tabs: layout components whose content comes from the parent. The component declares what it accepts through props of type `Children`, and places them where it wants:

```ts title="src/@components/composition/card.super (excerpt)"
import { type Children, SuperElement } from '@super-ts/dom';

/** A card: a heading, content (the children written between its tags) and optional actions. */
export class Card extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'composition-card';
  @prop heading: string;
  @prop content: Children;
  @prop actions?: Children;

  render() {
    <section class="card" aria-label={this.heading}>
      <h2>{this.heading}</h2>
      <div class="content">{this.content}</div>
      if (this.actions) {
        <div class="actions">{this.actions}</div>
      }
    </section>
  }
}
```



The parent fills `content` with the elements written between the tags, and `actions` with a named slot, or with a method:

```ts
// A slot, written where the card is used.
<Card heading={this.label.value}>
  <p>Value: {this.count.value}</p>
  <:actions>
    <button on:click={() => this.run('reset')}>Reset to zero</button>
  </:actions>
</Card>

// Or a method, handy in a loop (the variable is passed as a parameter).
#actions(c: Counter) {
  <button on:click={() => this.rename(c.id)}>Rename</button>
}
// …
for (const c of this.counters.value; key c.id) {
  <Card heading={c.label} actions={this.#actions(c)}>
    <p>{c.count}</p>
  </Card>
}
```

- **The children belong to the parent**: the click on "Reset to zero" calls a parent method, and `this.count` is read by the parent. The children follow its render; the card keeps them when it re-renders on its own.
- **The compiler checks the contract**: children for a component that does not declare `content`, missing required children, a slot that is not a prop of the component are errors.
- The full syntax is in [Templates: children](templates.html#content) and [named slots](templates.html#named-slots). The [Composition](examples.html#composition) example in the demo app shows both ways side by side.

## What does not exist, on purpose

- **No reference to a child** to call its methods: a child exposes no API. In a template, `<CounterControls … />` mounts the child, it does not give you an instance to keep.
- **No callback prop to pass information up**: nothing technically prevents it, but you use an event, declared with `@emit` and typed. The child stays decoupled, and the test can listen to the event with `mount(…, { on })`.
- **No access from a child to its parent's stores** through props: a child that needs a store declares `@contract name;` itself.
- **No hand-written tag**: `<counter-controls>` in raw HTML is not supported. A child always goes through its class, `<CounterControls … />` (or `create` outside a template).

---

# Templates: .super files

A component is written in a `.super` file: TypeScript whose methods contain HTML elements written as statements. Control flow is TypeScript's (`if`, `for`, `switch`), and the whole template is checked by the compiler: props, events, attributes, references.

## A .super file

```ts title="src/@components/counter-list/counter-list-item.super"
import { SuperElement } from '@super-ts/dom';
import './counter-list-item.css';

/** A row of the home list: only re-renders if its counter's value changes. */
export class CounterListItem extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'counter-list-item';
  @prop counterId: string;
  @prop label: string;

  @contract counter;
  @selector count = () => this.counter.selectors.count(this.counterId);

  render() {
    <a href={this.router.href('counter', { params: { id: this.counterId } })}>{this.label}</a>
    <span class="counter-list-value">{this.count.value}</span>
  }
}
```

- **The component is declared in its class**: `@tag` for its tag, `@prop` for its props (read through `this.label`), `@emit` for its events, without generics. See [Components: declarations](components.html#component-declarations).
- **What it prepares once is declared too**: `@contract` for a store, `@selector` for a reading (read through `this.count.value`), and likewise `@state`, `@form`, `@ref` and the `@on('contract', 'event')` listeners. See [Components: setup declarations](components.html#preparing-stores-reads-state-form-references-listeners).
- **Everything else is TypeScript**: imports, types, fields, methods. Only the elements and these declarations are new.
- **You import it without an extension**, like a `.ts`: `import { ConfirmDialog } from '../shared/confirm-dialog'`, or `@components/shop` for `shop/index.super`.
- **A module without a template stays a `.ts`**: contracts, stores, domain, routes, tests.

The Vite plugin compiles the file, `npm run typecheck` checks it and the editor understands it: see [Tooling for .super files](tooling.html).

## Elements written as statements

An element is written where TypeScript expects a statement, in a method of the class, and it is emitted at that point. `render()` returns nothing: it emits. Several elements in a row are allowed, without a common root.

```ts
render() {
  const label = this.label.value;
  if (label === null) {
    <p>Counter not found</p>
    return;
  }
  <h1>{label}</h1>
  <p>Value: {this.count.value}</p>
}
```

- **No element inside an expression**: `const x = <p />` or `() => <p />` are refused. To reuse a piece, write a method (see [Fragments](templates.html#fragments)).
- **`return;` stops the render** while keeping what is already emitted. `return x;` is refused in a method that emits elements: it returns what it emits.
- **An element without children is closed with `/>`** (`<div />`), except HTML void elements (`<br>`, `<input>`, `<img>`…).

## Text

Text is written as is between the tags. A child is read as a statement only if it starts with a reserved form:

| Start of the child | Read as |
| --- | --- |
| `if (`, `for (`, `switch (` | A control statement |
| `const` or `let`, a name or a destructuring, then `=` | A declaration |
| Everything else (`Total:`, `if you need help`, `let me know`) | Text |

Text that starts with a reserved form without being one is an error, never a guess. The editor offers the fix: wrapping it in braces.

```ts
<p>for (more info) see below</p>          // error: text read as a for loop
<p>{'for (more info) see below'}</p>     // correct
```

`<`, `{` and `}` are not written in text: `{'<'}`, `{'{'}`, `{'}'}`. Between tags, `//` is text: a comment is written `{/* … */}`.

### Whitespace

It follows HTML rules, like an HTML template written by hand:

- **Each run of whitespace counts as one space**, line breaks included: `containing` then `<code>offline</code>` on the next line displays "containing offline".
- **Whitespace at the start and end of an element or block renders nothing**: `<button>`, a line break, `−`, a line break, `</button>` gives a "−" button.
- **Two elements of the method separated only by whitespace are separated by a space**; if there is code between them, they are not.

## Interpolations

`{expression}` displays a string, a number or a boolean. `null` and `undefined` display nothing. An object is refused by the compiler, which avoids `[object Object]`.

```ts
<p role="status">Order no. {lastOrder.orderId}, {formatPrice(lastOrder.total)}.</p>
<p>{count} item{count > 1 ? 's' : ''}</p>
```

> **Everything is escaped**
>
> `{'<b>Ada</b>'}` displays the text "<b>Ada</b>", without creating a tag. Data entered by a user cannot inject HTML.

## Attributes

| Syntax | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `class="screen"` | Static attribute. |
| `href={url}` | Computed attribute. `null` or `undefined` remove it. |
| `disabled={busy}` | HTML boolean attribute (`disabled`, `hidden`, `checked`…): present if true. |
| `disabled` | Boolean attribute, always present. |
| `prop:value={v}` | DOM property rather than attribute (`el.value = v`). |
| `on:click={handler}` | Event listener (see [Events](templates.html#events)). |
| `ref={this.input}` | Reference to the element (see [References](templates.html#references)). |
| `{order.field('address')}` in the tag | Element directive: `form.bind()`, `form.field(…)` (see [Forms](forms.html)). |

```ts
render() {
  const name = this.route.value;
  // `null` removes the attribute.
  const current = (active: boolean) => (active ? 'page' : null);
  <header class="app-header">
    <nav aria-label="Examples">
      <a href={this.router.href('examples')} aria-current={current(name === 'examples')}>Examples</a>
      <a href={this.router.href('counters')} aria-current={current(name === 'counters' || name === 'counter')}>Counters</a>
      {/* … */}
    </nav>
  </header>
  <RouterOutlet />
}
```

- **An attribute value** is a string, a number, a boolean, `null` or `undefined`.
- **A tag without a hyphen must exist in HTML or SVG**: `<dvi>` is an error. A tag with a hyphen is a custom element.
- **lit syntax is refused**, with the form to use: `@click` → `on:click`, `?disabled` → `disabled`, `.value` → `prop:value`.

## Events

`on:event={handler}` adds a listener. On an HTML tag, the name must be an event of that tag (`on:clik` is an error) and the handler receives the typed event, with `currentTarget` typed as the element.

```ts
<input on:input={(event) => this.local.set({ draft: event.currentTarget.value })} />
<button type="button" on:click={() => this.run('reset')}>Reset to zero</button>
```

On a child component, `on:` subscribes to its events, declared with `@emit` (see [Child components](templates.html#child-components)). An error thrown in a handler is reported to `onError` (see [Handling errors](errors.html)).

## Showing or not: if

An `if` in the template is TypeScript's `if`, with its type narrowing: after `if (user)`, `user` is no longer `null`.

```ts title="src/@components/counter-list/index.super"
if (this.isLoading.value) {
  <p>Loading…</p>
}
if (loadErrorMessage) {
  <div role="alert">
    <p>Could not load the counters: {loadErrorMessage}</p>
    <button type="button" on:click={() => this.counter.send('load')}>Retry</button>
  </div>
}
```

`else if` and `else` are written as in TypeScript. The body of a block follows the same rules as an element's children.

## Lists: for

Only `for…of` is accepted. `key`, after a `;` inside the parentheses, identifies each item: when the order changes, elements are moved rather than recreated, and child components keep their local state.

```ts title="src/@components/counter-list/index.super"
<ul class="counter-list">
  for (const c of shown; key c.id) {
    <li><CounterListItem counterId={c.id} label={c.label} /></li>
  }
</ul>
```

Without `key`, rendering is positional: that is enough for a list whose order never changes. A loop over a single key recreates an area when the key changes: `for (const _round of [round]; key _round) { … }` in the [errors screen](errors.html).

## Choosing: switch

Each `case` stops at the next `case` or `default`: no fall-through, and `break` is not needed. On a union, a `default` that calls a function expecting `never` makes the choice exhaustive: TypeScript flags a forgotten case.

```ts
switch (status) {
  case 'idle': <p>Idle</p>
  case 'busy': <p>Busy</p>
  case 'done': <p>Done</p>
  default: {assertNever(status)}
}
```

## Declarations in the template

A `const` or `let` declaration can be written among the children, ended with `;`. It is visible to the children that follow it, in the same element or the same block.

```ts
for (const l of this.lines.value; key l.product.sku) {
  const { product, quantity } = l;
  <li>{product.label} × {quantity}</li>
}
```

## Child components

A tag that starts with a capital letter is a component, a `SuperElement` class in scope:

```ts title="src/@components/counter/index.super"
<CounterControls
  count={count}
  canDecrement={this.canDecrement.value && !busy}
  canIncrement={!busy}
  on:increment={() => this.run('increment')}
  on:decrement={() => this.run('decrement')}
/>
```

- **The attributes are its props**, checked against its `@prop` declarations: a missing, extra or wrongly typed prop is an error.
- **`on:x` subscribes to its `@emit`**, with the type of the emitted data.
- **No directive on a component**: `{…}` in the tag goes on an HTML element.

See [Parents and children](parents-and-children.html).

### Children: content

A component that accepts children declares it with a `content` prop of type `Children` from `@super-ts/dom`, and places them wherever it wants with an interpolation: `{this.content}`.

```ts title="src/@components/shared/modal.super"
import { type Children, SuperElement } from '@super-ts/dom';

export class Modal extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'ui-modal';
  @prop heading: string;
  @prop content: Children;
  @prop footer?: Children;
  @emit closed: void;

  render() {
    <div role="dialog" aria-label={this.heading}>
      <h2>{this.heading}</h2>
      {this.content}
      if (this.footer) {
        <footer>{this.footer}</footer>
      }
    </div>
  }
}
```

The children written between its tags fill `content`:

```ts
<Modal heading="Delete the counter?" on:closed={this.cancel}>
  <p>"{this.label.value}" will be permanently deleted.</p>
</Modal>
```

### Named slots

A named slot (the modal's footer) is another prop of type `Children`, declared like the others (`@prop footer?: Children;`) and read through `this.footer`. It can be filled in two ways, as you prefer.

**With a `<:name>` slot**, written between the component's tags, where it is used:

```ts
<Modal heading="Delete the counter?" on:closed={this.cancel}>
  <p>"{this.label.value}" will be permanently deleted.</p>
  <:footer>
    <button on:click={this.cancel}>Cancel</button>
    <button class="danger" on:click={this.confirm}>Delete</button>
  </:footer>
</Modal>
```

**With a method that emits elements**: such a method returns `Children` (see [Fragments](templates.html#fragments)).

```ts
#footer() {
  <button on:click={this.cancel}>Cancel</button>
  <button class="danger" on:click={this.confirm}>Delete</button>
}

render() {
  <Modal heading="Delete the counter?" footer={this.#footer()} on:closed={this.cancel}>
    <p>"{this.label.value}" will be permanently deleted.</p>
  </Modal>
}
```

The method is mostly useful for a list of slots, such as tabs whose panels are a `panels: Children[]` prop: `<Tabs labels={['Profile', 'Security']} panels={[this.#profile(), this.#security()]} />`.

- **Everything is checked against the component's `@prop` declarations**: children for a component that declares none, required children or slots that are missing, an unknown slot.
- **The children stay the parent's**: their listeners, their store readings and their state are the parent's, and they follow its render. The component receiving them keeps them when it re-renders on its own.
- **A `<:name>` slot** goes directly inside a component, without attributes, once per name. `<:content>` does not exist: the direct children already fill `content`.
- **In the editor**, `<:` inside a component suggests its slots.
- **A complete example**: the [Composition](examples.html#composition) screen of the examples app.

## References

`ref={…}` links an element to a reference declared with `@ref name: T;`. The element's type is checked: an `HTMLInputElement` reference put on a `<div>` is an error.

```ts title="src/@components/widget/index.super"
@ref widgetSlot: HTMLElement;
// …
<div class="widget-slot" ref={this.widgetSlot}></div>
```

## Reusable fragments

Not everything needs to be a component. A method that emits elements is reused in `render` through an interpolation of its call. It returns what it emits, of type `Children`: `return x;` is refused there, and its call can also fill a component's [named slot](templates.html#named-slots).

```ts title="src/@components/counter/index.super"
#back() {
  <a class="back-link" href={this.router.href('counters')}>← All counters</a>
}

render() {
  const label = this.label.value;
  if (label === null) {
    <main class="screen">{this.#back()}<h1>Counter not found</h1><p>No counter "{this.counterId()}".</p></main>
    return;
  }
  // …
}
```

Create a component when you need local state, a store, events or an independent re-render (like a list row).

## Rendering nothing

A method that emits no element renders nothing: `render() {}` is an empty component, and an `if` without `else` renders nothing when its condition is false.

## DOM and styles

- **The DOM is patched, not replaced**: focus and ongoing input survive a re-render.
- **Light DOM**: no shadow DOM. Your global styles apply to components, and you can target their tag in CSS (`counter-list-item { display: contents; }`).
- **A root element is not needed**: `render` can emit several top-level elements.

## Component styles

Super has no styling system: a component is a DOM element like any other. The [examples app](examples.html) follows a simple convention you can reuse: **one stylesheet per component**, placed next to it (`index.css` for a screen, `counter-controls.css` for a child component), imported by the component, with its rules nested under its tag.

```text title="src/@components/app-shell/index.css"
app-shell {
  .app-header { padding: 1rem 1.5rem; border-bottom: 1px solid color-mix(in srgb, currentColor 15%, transparent); }
  .app-header nav { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.5rem 1.5rem; }
  .app-header a { font-weight: 600; text-decoration: none; opacity: 0.6; }
  .app-header a[aria-current='page'] { opacity: 1; }
}
```

```ts title="src/@components/app-shell/index.super"
import { RouterOutlet, SuperElement } from '@super-ts/dom';
import { RouteLink } from '@super-ts/ui';
import './index.css';
```

```ts title="src/main.ts"
import './styles.css'; // global references first: component stylesheets come after
```

- **The tag acts as a scope**: nesting under `app-shell` keeps an `.app-header` class from affecting the rest of the page, without shadow DOM.
- **The component loads what it needs**: Vite includes the stylesheet as soon as the component is imported, and drops it once it no longer is.
- **Global styles first**: `main.ts` imports `styles.css` (variables, typography, base elements) before any component, so that the component stylesheets come after.

## What about html, nothing, repeat?

`@super-ts/dom` still exports `html`, `nothing` and `repeat`, the lit-html building blocks the compiler relies on. A component written in `.ts` whose `render` returns an `` html`…` `` still works, but its template is not checked by the compiler. Write your components in `.super`.

---

# Forms

`@form` binds fields to typed values, applies your rules, checks with the server while the user types when needed, and submits through a store command. "Pending" and server errors come from that command's lifecycle.

## A first form

```ts title="src/@core/account/contract.ts"
import { type Outcome, SuperContract } from '@super-ts/core';

export type AccountState = { userId: string | null };

export class AccountContract extends SuperContract<{
  state: AccountState;
  commands: {
    register(input: { email: string; password: string }): Outcome<{ userId: string }, 'email-taken' | 'network'>;
  };
}> {
  constructor() {
    super({ name: 'account' });
  }
  userId(s: AccountState) {
    return s.userId;
  }
}
```

```ts title="src/@components/signup/index.super"
import { SuperElement } from '@super-ts/dom';

export class SignupScreen extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'signup-screen';
  @title = 'Sign up';

  @contract account;   // the store that will receive the command

  @form signup = {
    initial: { email: '', password: '' },
    rules: {
      email: (v) => /.+@.+\..+/.test(v) || 'Invalid address',
      password: (v) => v.length >= 8 || '8 characters minimum',
    },
    submit: { to: this.account, command: 'register', toInput: (values) => values },
    failures: {
      fields: { 'email-taken': { email: 'Address already in use' } },
      form: { network: 'Could not connect, try again.' },
    },
  };

  render() {
    const { signup } = this;
    <form {signup.bind()}>
      <label>Email <input type="email" {signup.field('email')} /></label>
      <p class="error">{signup.error('email')}</p>

      <label>Password <input type="password" {signup.field('password')} /></label>
      <p class="error">{signup.error('password')}</p>

      <p role="alert">{signup.formError()}</p>
      <button disabled={signup.submitting()}>Create my account</button>
    </form>
  }
}
```

- `@form signup = { … };` is declared once in the class body, like the other [setup declarations](components.html#preparing-stores-reads-state-form-references-listeners). The field types come from the value: no annotation on `@form`. In a component written in `.ts`, the equivalent is `signup = this.form({ … })`, which throws if called during `render`.
- The form is ready from construction: `render` can read its values and errors on the first render. It connects to the store when the component mounts, and disconnects when it unmounts.
- `signup.bind()` and `signup.field('email')` are element directives: they are written in braces inside the tag, `<form {signup.bind()}>` for the form, `<input {signup.field('email')} />` for a field (see [Attributes](templates.html#attributes)).
- `disabled={signup.submitting()}` sets the attribute while the submission is pending, and removes it afterwards.
- `@contract account;` gives a view of the store without reading anything from it: the form has its own values. It only needs the store to send `register` and follow its outcome. `submit.to` must be a view declared by `@contract`, **before** the form in the class: declarations are initialised in order.

### Why a declaration and not a <Form> component

A form is component state: its values, errors, checks and submission are read all over the template (`this.edit.field('name')`, `this.edit.values()`, the "Saving…" button). The tag already exists: it is the native `<form>`, bound with `<form {this.edit.bind()}>`. A `<Form>` component would hide that state behind its props and lose the field typing. `<Table>` is a different case: it is a display component.

## Initial values give the types

The type of each field is inferred from `initial`. Widen whatever will change type:

```ts
initial: {
  name: '',                                   // string
  age: null as number | null,                 // optional number: null when the field is empty
  plan: 'free' as 'free' | 'pro' | 'team',    // a union: only these choices are accepted
  languages: [] as string[],                  // several values
  avatar: null as File | null,                // file
  phones: [{ label: 'mobile', number: '' }],  // a list of rows (see Dynamic lists)
},
```

An array of objects is a [dynamic list](forms.html#dynamic-lists). An array of simple values (`string[]`) is a multi-value field: a multiple-choice list or a group of checkboxes.

## Binding fields: field

`field(name)` goes on an `<input>`, a `<select>` or a `<textarea>`. It writes the value into the field, listens to input, and records the first time the user leaves the field. It picks the right property by itself according to the element type.

| Field | Markup | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| text, email, password, search, telephone, URL | `<input type="email" {f.field('email')} />` | `string` |
| text area | `<textarea {f.field('bio')}></textarea>` | `string` |
| date, time, date and time, month, week, colour | `<input type="date" {f.field('birthdate')} />` | `string` (browser format: `1906-12-09`, `#ff0000`) |
| number | `<input type="number" {f.field('age')} />` | `number`, or `null` if the field is cleared |
| slider | `<input type="range" min="0" max="100" {f.field('volume')} />` | `number` |
| drop-down list | `<select {f.field('country')}>…</select>` | `string` (the option's `value`) |
| multiple-choice list | `<select multiple {f.field('languages')}>…</select>` | `string[]` |
| radio buttons | `<input type="radio" {f.field('plan', 'pro')} />` | the value of the checked button |
| single checkbox | `<input type="checkbox" {f.field('newsletter')} />` | `boolean` |
| group of checkboxes | `<input type="checkbox" {f.field('interests', 'sport')} />` | `string[]` of the checked boxes |
| file | `<input type="file" {f.field('avatar')} />` | `File \| null` |
| several files | `<input type="file" multiple {f.field('photos')} />` | `File[]` |

The [UI kit](ui.html#fields) provides ready-wired fields (`Field`, `Select`, `Checkbox`, `RadioGroup`): label, hint, error and ARIA attributes included, bound with `fieldOf(edit, 'email')`.

In the snippets below, `initial` comes from the `@form edit = { … };` declaration, and the tags from the body of `render()`, where `const { edit } = this;` gives the form.

### Text fields

```ts
initial: { name: '', email: '', password: '', search: '', phone: '', website: '', bio: '' },

// in render()
<input {edit.field('name')} />
<input type="email" {edit.field('email')} />
<input type="password" {edit.field('password')} />
<input type="search" {edit.field('search')} />
<input type="tel" {edit.field('phone')} />
<input type="url" {edit.field('website')} />
<textarea {edit.field('bio')}></textarea>
```

The value follows every keystroke; the field is marked "touched" when the user leaves it.

### Numbers and sliders

```ts
initial: { age: null as number | null, quantity: 1, volume: 50 },

// in render()
<input type="number" {edit.field('age')} />                       // null if cleared
<input type="number" min="1" step="1" {edit.field('quantity')} />
<input type="range" min="0" max="100" {edit.field('volume')} />
```

A cleared number field gives `null`: declare `null as number | null` for an optional number. The `min`, `max` and `step` attributes guide input, but do not replace a rule: the form turns off the browser's native validation in favour of your rules.

### Dates, times and colours

```ts
initial: { birthdate: '', alarm: '', meeting: '', month: '', week: '', color: '#3b82f6' },

// in render()
<input type="date" {edit.field('birthdate')} />            // '1906-12-09'
<input type="time" {edit.field('alarm')} />                // '07:30'
<input type="datetime-local" {edit.field('meeting')} />    // '2026-11-25T14:00'
<input type="month" {edit.field('month')} />               // '2026-11'
<input type="week" {edit.field('week')} />                 // '2026-W48'
<input type="color" {edit.field('color')} />               // '#3b82f6'
```

These fields give strings, in the browser's format. Convert them in `submit.toInput` if the command expects another format.

### Drop-down lists

```ts
initial: { country: 'FR', languages: [] as string[] },

// in render()
<select {edit.field('country')}>
  <option value="FR">France</option>
  <option value="BE">Belgium</option>
</select>

<select multiple {edit.field('languages')}>
  for (const l of LANGUAGES; key l.code) {
    <option value={l.code}>{l.label}</option>
  }
</select>
```

The options can come from an array, rendered by a keyed `for` loop: the selection is restored once the options are in place.

### Radio buttons

```ts
initial: { plan: 'free' as 'free' | 'pro' | 'team' },

// in render()
<label><input type="radio" {edit.field('plan', 'free')} /> Free</label>
<label><input type="radio" {edit.field('plan', 'pro')} /> Pro</label>
<label><input type="radio" {edit.field('plan', 'team')} /> Team</label>
```

Each button gets its value as the second argument; the form checks the matching one. The value is typed by the union: `field('plan', 'gold')` does not compile. No need for a `name` or `value` attribute.

### Checkboxes

```ts
initial: { newsletter: false, interests: [] as string[] },
```
