```ts title="src/routes.ts (excerpt)"
  checkout: () => !read('cart').isEmpty() || { to: 'shop' },
}))
.screens(() => ({ /* … */ checkout: CheckoutScreen }));
```

### When guards apply

- On every navigation: `navigate`, `visit`, intercepted links, the browser's back button.
- On the current path, when the router joins the application (`createApp` or `mount`): the application provides the stores. Before that, they are not evaluated.
- A redirect decided by a guard follows the same rules as a [declared redirect](router.html#redirects): the refused path does not enter the history.
- A guard that redirects to the current page simply cancels the navigation.

> **A store read by a guard must be provided**
>
> If a guard reads a contract the application does not provide, an error is thrown: "router guard: no store provided for the contract "session"". In tests, pass the store (real or fake) to `mount(…, { stores, router })`.

```ts title="Testing a guard"
const session = fakeStore('session', { state: { user: null } });
const router = createRouter(Router, { mode: 'memory' });
await mount(RouterOutlet, { stores: [session], router });

await router.send('navigate', { to: 'account' });
expect(router.state().name).toBe('login');

session.setState({ user: 'ada' });
await router.send('navigate', { to: 'account' });
expect(router.state().name).toBe('account');
```

## Links: this.router.href

```ts
// href="/counters/coffees"
<a href={this.router.href('counter', { params: { id: c.id } })}>{c.label}</a>
// href="/"
<a href={this.router.href('examples')}>Examples</a>
```

- `this.router.href(name, { params, query })` builds the path and encodes the values (`'a b'` becomes `'a%20b'`). `params` is required if the path has parameters, `query` always optional.
- **It does not subscribe the component**: it does not read the active route, and a route change does not re-render a component that only builds links.
- Values are typed by the route: `{ params: { id: '42' } }` does not compile if `id` is described `Number`. The query follows the rules of [Query](router.html#query).
- `this.router.href('counter')` without `id`, or `this.router.href('counterz', …)`, do not compile. A route without parameters or query rejects any value.
- **Outside a component** (a test, a user-land module), `Router.href`, imported from `routes.ts`, does the same: `Router.href('counter', { params: { id: 'coffees' } })`.

### Link interception

The application intercepts clicks on internal links (`href` starting with `/`) and turns them into navigation, without a reload. The browser keeps control in these cases:

- external link (`https://…`, `//…`) or relative link (`../x`);
- `target` attribute other than `_self` (`target="_blank"`);
- `download` or `data-native` attribute;
- click with Cmd, Ctrl, Shift or Alt, or a button other than the left one;
- event already cancelled by another listener.

```ts
// The browser really loads the URL.
<a href="/export.csv" data-native>Download</a>
```

## Showing the screen: RouterOutlet

`RouterOutlet` shows the screen of the active route, which reads its values through `this.router.current`. It is a component like any other: you write `<RouterOutlet />` in a shared layout, after importing it from `@super-ts/dom`.

```ts title="src/@components/app-shell/index.super"
import { RouterOutlet, SuperElement } from '@super-ts/dom';
import { RouteLink } from '@super-ts/ui';
import './index.css';

/** Shared layout: the navigation between the examples, then the screen of the active route. */
export class AppShell extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'app-shell';

  @contract counter;

  protected override mounted() {
    this.counter.send('load');
  }

  render() {
    // Each link marks itself `aria-current="page"` on the displayed page; `activeFor`
    // extends a section to its other routes (the counter list and a single counter).
    <header class="app-header">
      <nav aria-label="Examples">
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'examples' }}>
          Examples
        </RouteLink>
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'counters' }} activeFor={['counter']}>
          Counters
        </RouteLink>
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'profile' }}>
          Form
        </RouteLink>
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'shop' }} activeFor={['checkout']}>
          Shop
        </RouteLink>
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'errors' }}>
          Errors
        </RouteLink>
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'widget' }}>
          Widget
        </RouteLink>
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'composition' }}>
          Composition
        </RouteLink>
        <RouteLink to={{ to: 'kit' }}>
          Kit
        </RouteLink>
      </nav>
    </header>
    <RouterOutlet />
  }
}
```

The shell's links are `RouteLink`s, from the [UI kit](ui.html#routelink): the target is written as for `navigate`, and each link sets `aria-current="page"` itself when it leads to the displayed page. `activeFor` keeps "Counters" active on a counter, and "Shop" on the checkout.

Without the kit, the shell would read the name of the active route through `this.router.current.name` (it would re-render when the route changes) and build its links through `this.router.href` (which does not subscribe). `aria-current` would be `'page'` on the link of the active route and `null` on the others: a computed attribute set to `null` is removed (see [Attributes](templates.html#attributes)).

```ts
@selector route = this.router.current.name;

render() {
  const name = this.route.value;
  const current = (active: boolean) => (active ? 'page' : null);   // `null` removes the attribute
  <nav aria-label="Examples">
    <a href={this.router.href('counters')} aria-current={current(name === 'counters' || name === 'counter')}>Counters</a>
    // …
  </nav>
}
```

Each path change mounts a **new instance** of the screen: going from `/counters/coffees` to `/counters/pushups` builds a new screen, and its local state starts from scratch. A change of query or hash alone (`/counters` to `/counters?sort=label`) keeps the screen mounted: a filter or one more page does not lose the local state, and the screen re-renders if it reads a value that changed.

Pending renders run **parents first**. When the outlet replaces a screen, the old one therefore does not re-render with a route that is no longer its own: it is removed before.

## Creating the router

```ts title="src/main.ts (excerpt)"
import { createApp, createRouter } from '@super-ts/dom';
import { AppShell } from '@components/app-shell';
import { Router } from './routes';

// The tab title: the one set by the displayed screen (`@title`), followed by the app name.
const router = createRouter(Router, { title: { default: 'Super · examples', suffix: ' · Super' } });
createApp({ root, stores: [counter, profile, cart, checkout, errorLog, catalog], router }).mount(AppShell.create());
```

| Option | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `mode` | `'browser'` (default) syncs the URL with the browser's history. `'memory'` keeps the history in memory, for tests. |
| `initialPath` | Starting path in `memory` mode (default `'/'`). |
| `title` | `{ default, suffix }`: the page title when no component sets one, and the text appended to the set title. See [The page title](router.html#the-page-title). |

`createRouter` only accepts a router whose screens are declared: passing it `defineRouter({ … })` without `.screens(...)` does not compile. It returns the router handle, to pass to `createApp({ router })`, or to `mount(…, { router })` in tests. This handle reads like a store's: `router.state()` gives [the full state](router.html#the-active-route-and-the-router-state), and `router.send('navigate', …)` navigates.

## The page title

The tab title follows the displayed screen. The router sets the frame, through the `title` option of `createRouter` (and not of `defineRouter`, whose keys are routes); the screen sets its own title through `@title`.

```ts title="src/main.ts (excerpt)"
// The tab title: the one set by the displayed screen (`@title`), followed by the app name.
const router = createRouter(Router, { title: { default: 'Super · examples', suffix: ' · Super' } });
```

- **`default`** is the title when no component sets one (the examples home page, for example). Without `default`, the document's original title comes back.
- **`suffix`** is appended to the set title: the shop screen sets "Shop", the tab shows "Shop · Super".

In the screen, `@title` receives a string (a fixed title) or a function (a **tracked** title), recomputed after each render with the same reads as `render`:

```ts title="src/@components/shop/index.super (excerpt)"
export class ShopScreen extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'shop-screen';
  // Tracked: the tab title changes with the cart, like the render.
  @title = () => {
    const count = this.cart.selectors.count();
    return count > 0 ? `Shop (${count} in cart)` : 'Shop';
  };

  @contract cart;
  // …
}
```

- **The title is set on mount and removed on unmount**: when the route changes, the old screen hands over and the new one sets its own.
- **Any component can set a title**, not only a screen: titles form a stack, the last mounted component that sets one wins, and on its unmount the previous title comes back. In the demo, `KitPage` gives all the kit pages their title (`@title = () => this.heading;`).
- **Outside the declaration** (`mounted`, a handler), `this.page.title = …` does the same.

The details (stack, imperative title, rules) are in [Components: the page title](components.html#the-page-title).

## The router in a component

A component reads and drives the router through `this.router`, without declaring anything: the active route (`current`), a specific route (`at`), navigation (`send`) and links (`href`); its events are listened to through a `@on('router', 'navigated')` method. Nothing to import from `routes.ts`: the view is typed by the app's routes. It can be read anywhere, `render` included, and a component that does not read it mounts without a router. `@contract router` is rejected: the router is read through `this.router`. See [Components: the setup declarations](components.html#preparing-stores-reads-state-form-references-listeners).

```ts
@selector route = this.router.current.name;   // 'examples' | 'counters' | … | null
@selector sort = this.router.current.query.sort;

@on('router', 'navigated')
onNavigated({ from, to }) { /* … */ }

this.router.send('navigate', { to: 'counter', params: { id: 'coffees' } });   // typed by the routes
this.router.send('navigate', { to: 'counters', query: { sort: 'label' } });
this.router.send('navigate', { to: 'examples' });
this.router.send('visit', '/counters/coffees');                              // raw path
this.router.send('back');
this.router.href('counter', { params: { id: 'coffees' } });                  // a link, without subscription
```

### The active route and the router state

A component reads the active route through `this.router.current`. Each value is called, or given to a `@selector`:

| Value | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `current.name()` | The name of the active route (`'examples' \| 'counters' \| 'counter' \| …`, `'form'` being redirected), or `null` if none matches. |
| `current.path()` | The current path, as navigated (query and hash included). |
| `current.params.<key>()` | A path parameter, decoded and converted: `'café'` for `/counters/caf%C3%A9`. `undefined` if it is invalid, or if the active route does not have it. |
| `current.query.<key>()` | A query key declared by the active route, converted: its value, its default, `undefined`, or `[]` for a list. |
| `….isValid()` | On a parameter or a query key: the URL did not carry a non-conforming value, and the active route declares that key. |

The handle returned by `createRouter` (in `main.ts` or a test) gives the full state through `router.state()`: `path`, `name`, `params` and `query` (converted), `invalid` (the keys for which the URL carried an invalid value: `{ params: ['id'], query: [] }`), and two fields only `RouterOutlet` uses: `screen`, the screen to show (the `'*'` screen if no route matches; never a redirect, those are followed before), and `errorScreen`, the `'!'` screen. A component has no access to those two.

### Router commands

| Command | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `navigate({ to, params, query })` | Navigation typed by route name. `params` carries the path parameters, required if the path has any; `query`, optional, the declared query. |
| `visit(path)` | Navigation by raw path (this is what intercepted links use). |
| `back()` | Goes back to the previous history entry. |

Each navigation emits `navigated { from, to }`. Navigating to the current path (clicking again on the link of the displayed page) adds nothing to the history and does not remount the screen, but still emits `navigated`, with `from === to`: this is what lets you leave the `'!'` screen by clicking again on the link of the page in error.

### Path resolution

- The trailing slash is ignored: `/counters/coffees/` matches `counter`.
- The query and hash are ignored to find the route, but kept in `path`. Declared query keys are read into `query`.
- Only the shape of the path counts to find the route: `/counters/abc` matches `counter` even if `id` is described `Number`, with an invalid `id`.
- A path with no match gives a `null` route and the `'*'` screen (nothing is shown if it is not declared).
- Declared redirects and those from guards are followed before showing: `path` and the active route are those of the final destination.

## Testing with the router

A component that reads `this.router` needs a router. In tests, create it in `memory` mode, on the desired path: the screen reads its route there, without props.

```ts title="src/@components/counter/index.test.ts (illustration)"
import { Router } from '../../routes';

const router = createRouter(Router, { mode: 'memory', initialPath: '/counters/coffees' });
const { container } = await mount(CounterScreen, { stores: [counter], router });

await userEvent.click(within(container).getByRole('link', { name: '← All counters' }));
expect(router.state().name).toBe('counters');
```

---

# Errors

When a component crashes, Super can show a fallback render in place of the broken part, and report the error in a single place. Three levels, from the most local to the most global: a component's `renderError`, the router's `'!'` screen, and `onError` in the application.

## Without declaring anything

Example: a counter screen calls `label.toUpperCase()` while `label` is `null`. Without an error boundary, the screen stays empty (or frozen on its last display if the error happens later), the error goes to the console, and the rest of the page keeps working. The user sees a blank area, with no explanation.

## A component's renderError

`renderError(error)` is an optional method, next to `render`. It is shown in place of `render` when the component, or one of its descendants, crashes. It is written like `render`: it emits its elements, without `return`.

```ts title="src/@components/errors/fragile-card.super"
import { SuperElement } from '@super-ts/dom';

/** 1. A block that crashes on render when you break it: its own renderError replaces only its area. */
export class FragileCard extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'fragile-card';
  @prop broken: boolean;

  render() {
    if (this.broken) throw new Error('the block read missing data');
    <p class="ok">This block renders normally.</p>
  }

  override renderError(error: Error) {
    <p class="fallback">This block crashed ({error.message}): its renderError replaces it, the rest of the page carries on.</p>
  }
}
```

- **It receives the error**, always an `Error`: a thrown value that is not one is converted. It has access to the props (`this.broken`) and the component's fields, like `render`.
- **It catches the descendants' errors**: if a child crashes, on render as in its constructor, the whole parent switches to its `renderError`.
- **It catches a store not found at mount** (`setup` phase): the instance exists, it can show a replacement. If it reads that store itself, it crashes in turn and the error goes up.
- **It does not catch the error of its own constructor**: if the constructor (or a field) crashes, the instance does not exist. The error (`setup` phase) goes up to an ancestor's `renderError`.
- **Once in `renderError`, the component stays there** until it is unmounted. It keeps re-rendering if its props change. A screen is remounted on each navigation, which resets it. To reset a block, you recreate it: the Errors example places its blocks in `for (const _round of [round]; key _round)`, and "Start over" increments `round`, which changes the key and recreates the components (see [Lists](templates.html#lists)).
- **If it crashes itself**, the error goes up to the next parent: no loop.

```ts title="src/@components/errors/guarded-panel.super (excerpt)"
/** 2. (continued) The parent of BrokenChild: its renderError catches the child's error. */
export class GuardedPanel extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'guarded-panel';
  @prop withChild: boolean;

  render() {
    <p class="ok">Parent panel.</p>
    if (this.withChild) {
      <BrokenChild />
    }
  }

  override renderError(error: Error) {
    <p class="fallback">The parent caught its child's error ({error.message}).</p>
  }
}
```

`BrokenChild`, written `<BrokenChild />` in the panel's `render`, throws an error in its constructor. It is reported under the child's name (`tag: 'broken-child'`, `phase: 'setup'`) and caught by `GuardedPanel` (`caughtBy: 'guarded-panel'`).

> **Why a separate method, and not an error passed to `render`**
>
> If it is `render` that crashed, calling it again could crash at the same place. `renderError` is a second render, written to depend only on the error and the bare minimum.

### Where to put a renderError

- On a **screen**, for a message suited to the page ("Unable to show this counter").
- On a **self-contained part** of a screen (a chart, a widget), so that the rest of the screen stays usable.
- On the **shell** (`AppShell`), to cover errors outside the active screen, such as in the header.
- No need to put them everywhere: the `'!'` screen acts as the default safety net for all screens.

## The router's '!' screen

If a screen's error goes up to the `RouterOutlet` without being caught, the outlet shows the `'!'` screen in place of the active screen. The shell and the navigation stay usable.

```ts title="src/routes.ts (excerpt)"
.screens(() => ({
  examples: ExamplesScreen,
  // …
  errors: ErrorsScreen,
  widget: WidgetScreen,
  composition: CompositionScreen,
  // …
  '*': NotFoundScreen,
  '!': ErrorScreen,
}));
```

```ts title="src/@components/error/index.super"
import { SuperElement } from '@super-ts/dom';

/** The '!' screen: shown by the router when a screen crashes without being caught. */
export class ErrorScreen extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'error-screen';
  @title = 'Error';
  @prop error: Error;
  @prop path: string;

  render() {
    <main class="screen">
      <h1>This page ran into a problem</h1>
      <p>{this.error.message}</p>
      <button type="button" on:click={() => this.router.send('navigate', { to: 'examples' })}>Back to the examples</button>
    </main>
  }
}
```

- The `'!'` screen receives **the error and the path** as props: it is the only screen that receives props from the router. The compiler requires its props to be `{ error: Error; path: string }`: `@prop error: Error;` and `@prop path: string;`.
- **Any navigation closes it** and mounts a fresh screen: going to another page then coming back, or simply clicking the link of the failed page again. If the screen crashes again, the `'!'` screen reappears.
- If it crashes itself, the error keeps going up.

```ts title="src/@components/errors/double-failure.super (excerpt)"
/** 3. A block whose renderError crashes too: the error bubbles up to the router's '!' screen. */
export class DoubleFailure extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'double-failure';
  @prop armed: boolean;

  render() {
    if (this.armed) throw new Error('broken render');
    <p class="ok">Ready.</p>
  }

  override renderError(): unknown {
    throw new Error('the renderError crashed too');
  }
}
```

## Reporting: onError

`onError`, in `createApp`, receives **every** error from a component rendered under the root, whether it was caught or not. It is the single place to log or notify a monitoring tool.

```ts title="src/main.ts (excerpt)"
createApp({
  root: document.querySelector<HTMLElement>('#app')!,
  stores: [counter, profile, cart, checkout, errorLog, catalog],
  router,
  // Every component error, caught or not: the console, and the log shown by the "Errors" example.
  onError: (error, { tag, phase, caughtBy }) => {
    console.error(`[${tag}] ${phase}`, { caughtBy }, error);
    errorLog.send('record', { message: error.message, tag, phase, caughtBy });
  },
}).mount(AppShell.create());
```

In production, you would rather plug a monitoring tool in there:

```ts title="src/monitoring.ts (user-land)"
export function reportToMonitoring(error: Error, context: { tag: string; phase: string; caughtBy: string | null }) {
  if (import.meta.env.DEV) console.error(`[${context.tag}] ${context.phase}`, error, context);
  else navigator.sendBeacon('/api/errors', JSON.stringify({ message: error.message, stack: error.stack, ...context }));
}
```

`reportToMonitoring` is a function of your project: Super calls it through `onError`, it does not implement it.

| Information | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `error` | The error, always an `Error`. |
| `tag` | The component that crashed (`'fragile-card'`). |
| `phase` | `'setup'` (constructor, or store not found at mount), `'render'` or `'renderError'`: the display was broken. `'event'`, `'listener'` or `'mount'`: an action failed (see below). |
| `caughtBy` | What caught it: the tag of a component with `renderError`, `'super-router-outlet'` for the `'!'` screen, or `null`. |

Without `onError`, a caught error goes to the console, and an uncaught error is thrown. With nested applications, the one closest to the component reports it, once.

## Who catches what

An error goes up the component tree from the one that crashed. The first one able to handle it keeps it:

1. the component that crashed, if it has a `renderError` (except for the error of its own constructor);
2. otherwise its parent, then the parent's parent, up to the first one that has a `renderError`;
3. otherwise, if it reaches the `RouterOutlet`, the `'!'` screen;
4. otherwise nobody: the component stays empty.

In every case, `onError` is called once. The blocks of the Errors example cover each row:

| What crashes | What is shown |
| --- | --- |
| `FragileCard` on render, with its own `renderError` | Its `renderError`, in place of the block only. `caughtBy: 'fragile-card'`. |
| `BrokenChild` in its constructor, under `GuardedPanel` (with `renderError`) | `GuardedPanel`'s `renderError`, in place of the whole panel. `tag: 'broken-child'`, `phase: 'setup'`, `caughtBy: 'guarded-panel'`. |
| `DoubleFailure` on render, then its `renderError` | The error carries on up to the `RouterOutlet`: `'!'` screen in place of the Errors screen. The navigation stays usable. |
| A screen without `renderError` (`CounterListScreen`) | The `'!'` screen, in place of the counter list. |
| The header in `AppShell`, without `renderError` | Nothing is caught: the header stays empty, `onError` is called. A `renderError` on `AppShell` covers this case. |

## Action errors: on:event, on, mounted

An error in a template event handler, in a contract's `on` listener, or in `mounted` / `unmounted` is also reported to `onError`, with the component it comes from. Nothing to write: Super wraps these functions itself.

```ts title="src/@components/errors/index.super (excerpt)"
<section>
  <h2>4. A click that crashes</h2>
  <p>The display does not change: the error is only reported (phase <code>event</code>).</p>
  <button type="button" on:click={() => { throw new Error('the click handler crashed'); }}>Click that crashes</button>
</section>
```

| An error in… | `phase` | On screen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| an `on:click={…}` handler (synchronous or asynchronous) | `'event'` | Nothing changes. |
| an `@on('counter', '…')` listener (`this.counter.on(…)` in a `.ts` file) | `'listener'` | Nothing changes. |
| `mounted()` or `unmounted()` | `'mount'` | Nothing changes. |

**The component does not switch to its `renderError`**: when an action fails, the display is usually still correct. Replacing the whole screen for a failed click would be out of proportion. The error is only reported (to the console without `onError`), and `caughtBy` is `null`.

## What is not covered

- **Code Super does not see go by**: a `setTimeout`, or the function of a `window.addEventListener` set up by hand in `mounted`. An error there goes to the console.
- **`unmounted` of a component removed from the DOM**: the error can no longer go up to the application. It goes to the console.
- **A handler built outside a component**, in an `html` template created when a `.ts` module loads, for example: it is not attached to any component.
- **The constructor of a component created outside a template** (`AppShell.create()` in `main.ts`): the error is thrown at the `create` call, as for any code.
- **Store errors**: they do not go through here. A store catches its errors and publishes them through its state or an event (see [Stores: errors](stores.html#errors)).
- **Configuration errors** thrown by Super itself (two stores for one contract, unknown route in `href`, missing `static tag` in a `.ts` component): these are programming errors, to be fixed.

## Testing errors

`mount` also accepts `onError`:

```ts
const onError = vi.fn();
const { container } = await mount(FragileCard, { props: { broken: true }, onError });

expect(container.textContent).toContain('This block crashed (the block read missing data)');
expect(onError).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.any(Error), { tag: 'fragile-card', phase: 'render', caughtBy: 'fragile-card' });
```

---

# Application

The composition root, `main.ts`, is the only place that chooses the adapters, creates the stores and the router, and provides them to the components.

## The composition root

```ts title="src/main.ts"
import './styles.css'; // global references first: component stylesheets come after
import './kit-theme.css'; // the @super-ts/ui theme for the whole app
import { createApp, createRouter } from '@super-ts/dom';
import { AppShell } from '@components/app-shell';
import { CartStore } from '@core/cart/store';
import { CatalogStore } from '@core/catalog/store';
import { CheckoutStore } from '@core/checkout/store';
import { CounterStore } from '@core/counter/store';
import { ErrorLogStore } from '@core/error-log/store';
import { ProfileStore } from '@core/profile/store';
import { createDummyJsonProductCatalog } from './adapters/dummyjson-product-catalog';
import { createFakeOrderClient } from './adapters/fake-order-client';
import { createFakeProfileClient } from './adapters/fake-profile-client';
import { createLocalStorageCounterRepository } from './adapters/local-storage-counter-repository';
import { createSavedCart } from './adapters/saved-cart';
import { Router } from './routes';

// Composition root (user-land): this is where you choose the adapters and assemble the stores.
const counter = CounterStore.create({ counterRepository: createLocalStorageCounterRepository() });
const profile = ProfileStore.create({ profileClient: createFakeProfileClient() }); // simulated server, with latency
const savedCart = createSavedCart();
const cart = CartStore.create({ quantities: savedCart.load() }); // the cart from before the reload
const checkout = CheckoutStore.create({ cart, orderClient: createFakeOrderClient() }); // a store that depends on another
const errorLog = ErrorLogStore.create();
const catalog = CatalogStore.create({ productCatalog: createDummyJsonProductCatalog() }); // the public test API dummyjson.com
// The tab title: the one set by the displayed screen (`@title`), followed by the app name.
const router = createRouter(Router, { title: { default: 'Super · examples', suffix: ' · Super' } });

// subscribe: the cart is saved on every change, and survives a page reload.
// The store knows nothing about storage: the composition root wires it in.
cart.subscribe((state) => savedCart.save(state.quantities));

createApp({
  root: document.querySelector<HTMLElement>('#app')!,
  stores: [counter, profile, cart, checkout, errorLog, catalog],
  router,
  // Every component error, caught or not: the console, and the log shown by the "Errors" example.
  onError: (error, { tag, phase, caughtBy }) => {
    console.error(`[${tag}] ${phase}`, { caughtBy }, error);
    errorLog.send('record', { message: error.message, tag, phase, caughtBy });
  },
}).mount(AppShell.create());
```

1. **Create the stores** with `XStore.create(deps)`: this is where you choose `localStorage`, an HTTP API or an in-memory version, and pass a store to the one that depends on it (`checkout` receives `cart`). `create` returns the store handle, never the class instance.
2. **Create the router** from the `Router` declared in `routes.ts`, with the frame for the tab title (`title: { default, suffix }`, see [The page title](router.html#the-page-title)).
3. **Create the application** on a root element, providing it with stores and router.
4. **Mount** the root component, created by `AppShell.create()`. `main.ts` stays a `.ts` file: it has no template, so it creates the component with `create()` instead of writing `<AppShell />`. The import `@components/app-shell`, without an extension, finds `app-shell/index.super`.

`main.ts` is user-land: Super imposes nothing on it. No injection container, no hidden configuration: the whole assembly can be read in this file. It can also use the handles directly, as here with `cart.subscribe`, which saves the cart to `localStorage` on every change (through the adapter `adapters/saved-cart.ts`): the cart read back at startup (`CartStore.create({ quantities: savedCart.load() })`) thus survives a page reload.

This is a good use of `subscribe`: syncing state with an external system (storage, analytics, another tab), outside any component, without the store knowing. `CartStore` knows nothing about storage, the composition root wires it in. The counter does the opposite: its store talks to a port, `CounterRepository`, because persistence is part of its domain (asynchronous loading, errors to display). See [subscribe](stores.html#subscribe).

## createApp

| Option | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `root` | The HTML element under which the application lives. |
| `stores` | The store handles to provide to the components rendered under `root`, each under the name of its contract. |
| `router` | The router created by `createRouter`. It is provided under the name `'router'`, clicks on internal links become navigations, and its guards read the stores of this application. |
| `onError` | Receives every error from a component rendered under `root`, caught or not: `(error, { tag, phase, caughtBy })`. See [Handling errors](errors.html#onerror). |

| Returns | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `mount(element)` | Replaces the content of the root with the element, and returns it. |
| `dispose()` | Removes the provider and the link interception, then empties the root. |
| `root` | The root element. |

## How a component finds its store

A component declares `@contract counter;`. When it mounts, it asks the DOM, walking up from itself: "who provides a store for the contract `counter`?". The nearest application that has one answers. In practice:

- A component works **anywhere under the root**, at any depth, without passing it the store as props.
- The **contract name** is the key: the one in `super({ name: 'counter' })` in `@core/counter/contract.ts`. The component imports neither the contract nor the store; the Vite plugin rejects two contracts with the same name and generates `@core/contracts.d.ts`, which types `@contract counter` (and `this.contract('counter')` in a component written in `.ts`).
- A component mounted **without a store for that name** throws an explicit error (phase `setup`): "no store provided for the contract "counter". Add it to createApp({ stores }) or to mount(..., { stores })".

## Multiple applications

You can create several applications, and even nest them: the one nearest to the component answers first. This is useful for a widget that has its own stores in the middle of a page. In the example, a user-land function mounts the timer on the element it is given, and returns a way to release everything:

```ts title="src/widgets/timer-widget.ts"
import { createApp } from '@super-ts/dom';
import { TimerWidget } from '@components/widget/timer-widget';
import { TimerStore } from '@core/timer/store';

export function mountTimerWidget(root: HTMLElement): () => void {
  const timer = TimerStore.create();
  const app = createApp({ root, stores: [timer] });
  app.mount(TimerWidget.create());
  return () => {
    app.dispose();
    timer.dispose();
  };
}
```

The `/widget` screen calls it on an element of its own template, declared with `@ref widgetSlot: HTMLElement;` and set with `ref={this.widgetSlot}`, and releases the widget if it is unmounted while open:

```ts title="src/@components/widget/index.super (excerpt)"
export class WidgetScreen extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'widget-screen';
  @title = 'Widget';

  @state local = { open: false };
  @ref widgetSlot: HTMLElement;
  #close: (() => void) | null = null;

  toggle = () => {
    if (this.#close) {
      this.#close();
      this.#close = null;
      this.local.set({ open: false });
      return;
    }
    this.#close = mountTimerWidget(this.widgetSlot.value!);
    this.local.set({ open: true });
  };

  protected override unmounted() {
    this.#close?.();
    this.#close = null;
  }

  render() {
    <main class="screen">
      <h1>Widget</h1>
      {/* … */}
      <button type="button" on:click={this.toggle}>{this.local.get().open ? 'Close the timer' : 'Open the timer'}</button>
      <div class="widget-slot" ref={this.widgetSlot}></div>
    </main>
  }
}
```

Under the widget element, `@contract timer` finds the store of the second application; `@contract counter` would walk up to the first. The timer knows nothing about this: it asks for a contract by name, and the nearest application that provides it answers.

> **Only one store per contract in an application**
>
> Providing two stores for the same contract to the same application throws an error: "two stores provided for the contract "counter"".

## Loading data at startup

Two ways, depending on where you want to see the intent:

```ts title="src/@components/app-shell/index.super (excerpt)"
// In the root component, on mount (the example's choice)
export class AppShell extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'app-shell';

  @contract counter;
  // …

  protected override mounted() {
    this.counter.send('load');
  }
}
```

```ts title="src/main.ts"
// Or directly in main.ts, on the handle
void counter.send('load');
```

---

# Ports and adapters

External data sources (localStorage, HTTP API, IndexedDB) are not a Super concept: they are plain dependencies of your stores. The [examples app](examples.html) organises them into ports and adapters, a project choice: `localStorage` for the counters, a simulated server for the form, a real HTTP API (dummyjson.com) for the kit's wired table.

## The principle

- A **port** is an interface: what the store needs, expressed in its own terms ("load all counters", "save a counter").
- An **adapter** is an implementation of that port for a given technology.
- The **store** depends on the port, never on an adapter.
- The **composition root** chooses the adapter.

The result: you change storage without touching the store, and you test the store with an in-memory adapter.

## The port

```ts title="src/ports/counter-repository.ts"
export interface CounterRepository {
  loadAll(): Promise<Record<string, number>>;
  save(id: string, count: number): Promise<void>;
}
```

## The adapters

```ts title="src/adapters/local-storage-counter-repository.ts"
export function createLocalStorageCounterRepository({
  storage = window.localStorage,
  key = 'super.counters',
}: Options = {}): CounterRepository {
  function read(): Record<string, number> {
    const raw = storage.getItem(key);
    if (raw === null) return {};
    // … parses and validates the JSON, throws an error if it is invalid
  }

  return {
    async loadAll() {
      return read();
    },
    async save(id, count) {
      storage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify({ ...read(), [id]: count }));
    },
  };
}
```

```ts title="src/adapters/in-memory-counter-repository.ts"
export function createInMemoryCounterRepository(
  initial: Record<string, number> = {},
): CounterRepository & { stored: Record<string, number> } {
  return {
    stored: { ...initial },
    async loadAll() {
      return { ...this.stored };
    },
    async save(id, count) {
      this.stored = { ...this.stored, [id]: count };
    },
  };
}
```

The in-memory adapter exposes `stored`, handy for checking what was saved in a test.

An HTTP adapter has the same shape, with `fetch` calls. The one for the product catalogue translates the page or search requested by the store into the parameters of the public test API dummyjson.com, and its response into the domain types:

```ts title="src/ports/product-catalog.ts (excerpt)"
export interface ProductCatalog {
  list(query: ProductQuery): Promise<ProductPage>;
  /** The products whose name or description contains `text`, at most `limit`. */
  search(text: string, limit: number): Promise<Product[]>;
}
```

```ts title="src/adapters/dummyjson-product-catalog.ts (excerpt)"
export function createDummyJsonProductCatalog(fetchImpl: typeof fetch = fetch): ProductCatalog {
  const get = async (url: string): Promise<Raw> => {
    const response = await fetchImpl(url);
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`dummyjson: ${response.status}`);
    return (await response.json()) as Raw;
  };
  return {
    async list({ page, pageSize, sort, order }: ProductQuery): Promise<ProductPage> {
      const params = new URLSearchParams({
        limit: String(pageSize),
        skip: String((page - 1) * pageSize),
        select: SELECT,
        ...(sort ? { sortBy: sort, order } : {}),
      });
      const raw = await get(`${API}?${params}`);
      return { products: toProducts(raw), total: raw.total };
    },
    async search(text, limit) {
      const params = new URLSearchParams({ q: text, limit: String(limit), select: SELECT });
      return toProducts(await get(`${API}/search?${params}`));
    },
  };
}
```

`fetch` is itself a parameter: the adapter's test gives it a fake one, and checks the URL built without a network. The store and screen tests take the port's other adapter, `createInMemoryProductCatalog`, which sorts, paginates and searches in memory as the server would.

## Wiring them

```ts
// The store declares its dependency through its constructor's parameters.
type Deps = { counterRepository: CounterRepository };

export class CounterStore extends SuperStore<CounterContract> implements Commands<CounterStore> {
  #repository: CounterRepository;

  constructor({ counterRepository }: Deps) {
    super({ contract: 'counter', initialState: { counts: {}, loadErrorMessage: null } });
    this.#repository = counterRepository;
  }
  // …
}

// main.ts chooses the adapter.
CounterStore.create({ counterRepository: createLocalStorageCounterRepository() });

// A test chooses another one.
CounterStore.create({ counterRepository: createInMemoryCounterRepository({ coffees: 1 }) });
```

## Where to put them

`ports/` and `adapters/` are user-land folders: Super does not know about them. You can name them differently, or put the port next to the store, in its `@core/` folder. A common-sense rule: a component never imports an adapter. The plugin does not forbid it (adapters are in user-land), but a component that called an adapter would bypass the store, and lose the shared state and the events.

## Adapter errors

An adapter can fail (quota exceeded, network down). It is up to the store to decide how to publish it: `loadErrorMessage` in the state for a load (the error must stay visible), a failure reason for a write. See [Stores: errors](stores.html#errors).

```ts
await this.#repository.save(id, next).catch(() => this.fail('storage')); // increment:failed, reason 'storage'
```

---

# Testing

Each building block is tested at its own level: the store without a DOM, the adapter on its own, the component with a fake store, the whole app with an in-memory router. And the typing guarantees have their own tests.

## Configuration

Tests run under Vitest with happy-dom, a simulated DOM. They live next to the code they test (`@core/counter/store.test.ts` next to `@core/counter/store.ts`, `@components/counter/index.test.ts` next to the screen, `index.super`).

A test stays a `.ts` file, even for a component written in `.super`. Vitest reuses the plugins from `vite.config.ts`: the Super plugin compiles `.super` files there as in dev, and `import { CounterControls } from './counter-controls'` finds `counter-controls.super`.

```ts title="vitest.config.ts"
export default defineConfig({
  resolve: { alias },
  plugins,                                       // the Super plugin also compiles the tests' .super files
  test: {
    environment: 'happy-dom',
    execArgv: ['--no-experimental-webstorage'],  // Node 25+: see below
    globals: true,
    setupFiles: ['./vitest.setup.ts'],
  },
});
```

```ts title="vitest.setup.ts"
import { cleanup } from '@super-ts/testing';
import { afterEach } from 'vitest';

// Unmounts everything `mount()` mounted during the test.
afterEach(() => cleanup());
```

> **Node 25 and later**
>
> Node exposes a native `localStorage` that hides happy-dom's ("`localStorage.clear is not a function`"). The `execArgv: ['--no-experimental-webstorage']` option disables it in the test workers.

## Testing a store

A store is tested without a DOM, with an in-memory adapter. `XStore.create(deps)` returns the handle, as in `main.ts`; `await send(…)` waits for the command to finish, then you check the state, the selectors and the events.

```ts title="src/@core/counter/store.test.ts"
import { record } from '@super-ts/testing';
import { createInMemoryCounterRepository } from '../../adapters/in-memory-counter-repository';
import { CounterStore } from './store';

test('increment persists, updates the state, and Super publishes increment:done with the result', async () => {
  const counterRepository = createInMemoryCounterRepository({ coffees: 1 });
  const store = CounterStore.create({ counterRepository });
  const done = record(store, 'increment:done');
  await store.send('load');

  await store.send('increment', { id: 'coffees' });

  expect(store.selectors.count('coffees')).toBe(2);
  expect(counterRepository.stored).toEqual({ coffees: 2 });
  expect(done.calls).toEqual([{ input: { id: 'coffees' }, result: { count: 2 } }]);
});
```

- **`store.selectors.x(…)`** reads the current state through the contract's selectors; `store.state()` gives the raw, frozen state.
- **`store.pending(…)`** tells whether a command is pending: any (`pending()`), one command (`pending('load')`), or one command for a body (`pending('increment', { id: 'coffees' })`).
- **`record(store, event)`** records the payloads, including lifecycle ones (`'increment:done'`): `calls` (all), `last` (the last one), `stop()` (stops listening).

A failure is checked in two ways: the `send` promise, rejected with a `CommandFailure` carrying the reason, and the `:failed` event. A fake adapter written inline is enough:

```ts title="src/@core/counter/store.test.ts"
test('a save failure gives the reason storage and keeps the value', async () => {
  const store = CounterStore.create({
    counterRepository: { loadAll: async () => ({ coffees: 3 }), save: async () => Promise.reject(new Error('quota exceeded')) },
  });
  const failed = record(store, 'increment:failed');
  await store.send('load');

  await store.send('increment', { id: 'coffees' }).catch(() => {});

  expect(failed.last).toEqual({ input: { id: 'coffees' }, reason: 'storage', error: null });
  expect(store.state().counts).toEqual({ coffees: 3 });
  expect(store.pending()).toBe(false); // nothing pending any more, even after a failure
});
```

A store that depends on another is tested with the real one: you create the cart, then the checkout that receives it as a dependency, exactly as in `main.ts`.

```ts title="src/@core/checkout/store.test.ts"
function setup() {
  const cart = CartStore.create();
  const orderClient = createFakeOrderClient({ delay: 0 });
  const checkout = CheckoutStore.create({ cart, orderClient });
  return { cart, orderClient, checkout };
}

test('places the order with the cart contents, then empties the cart', async () => {
  const { cart, orderClient, checkout } = setup();
  await cart.send('add', { sku: 'tshirt' });

  await checkout.send('placeOrder', { address: '12 Lilac Street' });

  expect(orderClient.orders).toEqual([{ address: '12 Lilac Street', lines: [{ sku: 'tshirt', quantity: 1 }], total: 2500 }]);
  expect(cart.selectors.isEmpty()).toBe(true);
  expect(checkout.state().lastOrder).toEqual({ orderId: 'C0001', total: 2500 });
});
```

## Testing an adapter

The `localStorage` adapter is tested against happy-dom's `localStorage`, or against any compatible object thanks to its `storage` option. Nothing from Super here: it is user-land.

```ts title="src/adapters/local-storage-counter-repository.test.ts"
test('reads back what was saved, under the chosen key, without overwriting the other counters', async () => {
  const repository = createLocalStorageCounterRepository({ key: 'test.counters' });

  await repository.save('coffees', 7);
  await repository.save('pushups', 2);

  expect(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('test.counters')!)).toEqual({ coffees: 7, pushups: 2 });
  await expect(createLocalStorageCounterRepository({ key: 'test.counters' }).loadAll()).resolves.toEqual({ coffees: 7, pushups: 2 });
});
```

## Testing a component on its own

A presentational component, without a store, is mounted with its props; its events are listened to through `on`, typed by its `emits`. The component is a `.super` file, the test a `.ts` file that imports it without an extension.

```ts title="src/@components/counter/counter-controls.test.ts"
import { mount } from '@super-ts/testing';
import { within } from '@testing-library/dom';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { CounterControls } from './counter-controls';

test('displays the value and emits increment / decrement', async () => {
  const increment = vi.fn();
  const decrement = vi.fn();
  const { container } = await mount(CounterControls, {
    props: { count: 4, canDecrement: true, canIncrement: true },
    on: { increment, decrement },
  });
  const ui = within(container);

  await userEvent.click(ui.getByRole('button', { name: 'Increment' }));
  await userEvent.click(ui.getByRole('button', { name: 'Decrement' }));

  expect(ui.getByLabelText('Counter value').textContent).toBe('4');
  expect(increment).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  expect(decrement).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
});
```

### mount

`mount(Class, options)` takes the class exported by the `.super` file (not an element already created), mounts it in `document.body` under a test application, waits for the first render and returns:

| Option | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `props` | The component's props, typed by its class. |
| `stores` | The stores to provide (real or fake), found by their contract name as with `createApp`. |
| `router` | A router, usually `createRouter(Router, { mode: 'memory', initialPath })`. A screen mounted on its own reads its route from it: `initialPath: '/counters/coffees'` gives it `id === 'coffees'`. |
| `on` | Listeners for the component's events, typed by its `emits`. |
| `onError` | Receives the errors of mounted components, like `createApp({ onError })`. See [Testing errors](errors.html#testing-errors). |

| Return value | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `container` | The container, to pass to testing-library's `within()`. |
| `element` | The mounted instance, typed by its class. |
| `setProps(props)` | Changes the props and waits for the render. |
| `unmount()` | Unmounts (done automatically by `cleanup`). |

### flush

Store notifications and renders are batched at the end of the task. After an action that changes a store without going through testing-library (an `emit` on a fake store, a `send` on a real one), `await flush()` lets the pending renders through. testing-library's `findBy*` wait on their own.

## Testing a screen with a fake store

`fakeStore('name', { state, commands? })` creates a store for the contract of that name, without an implementation. The screen finds it as it would find the real one, through `@contract counter`: that is what the rule "a component only knows the contract" allows. The given state is typed by the contract, and the contract's selectors read it normally.

```ts title="src/@components/counter/index.test.ts"
import { createRouter } from '@super-ts/dom';
import { type FakeCommands, fakeStore, flush, mount } from '@super-ts/testing';
import type { CounterState } from '@core/counter/contract';
import { Router } from '../../routes';
import { CounterScreen } from '.';

const idle: CounterState = { counts: { coffees: 2 }, loadErrorMessage: null };

type CounterCommands = FakeCommands<'counter'>;

async function setup(id: string, commands: CounterCommands = {}) {
  const counter = fakeStore('counter', { state: idle, commands });
  // The screen contains links: it needs a router (here in memory).
  const router = createRouter(Router, { mode: 'memory', initialPath: `/counters/${id}` });
  const { container } = await mount(CounterScreen, { stores: [counter], router });
  return { counter, router, ui: within(container) };
}

test('sends the commands with the counter id', async () => {
  const { counter, ui } = await setup('coffees');

  await userEvent.click(ui.getByRole('button', { name: 'Increment' }));

  expect(counter.sent).toEqual([{ name: 'increment', args: [{ id: 'coffees' }] }]);
});

test('displays the failure reason message, for its own counter only', async () => {
  const { counter, ui } = await setup('coffees');

  // The test plays the store's role by emitting the outcome.
  counter.emit('decrement:failed', { input: { id: 'pushups' }, reason: 'storage', error: null });
  counter.emit('decrement:failed', { input: { id: 'coffees' }, reason: 'below-min', error: null });
  await flush();

  expect(ui.getByText('The counter is already at zero.')).toBeTruthy();
  expect(ui.queryByText('Could not save: storage is unavailable.')).toBeNull();
});
```

| Fake store member | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `sent` | The commands received, in order: `{ name, args }`. |
| `setState(patch)` | Changes the state, as the store would. |
| `emit(name, payload)` | Emits a contract event, or a command's outcome (`'decrement:failed'`), as the store and Super would. |
| `selectors`, `state()`, `on`… | The rest of a store's handle, like a real one. |
| `commands` (option) | Implementations for some commands. The others are recorded and finish without publishing an outcome: it is up to the test to emit `:done` or `:failed`, with values that match the contract. |

`FakeCommands<'counter'>` types these implementations by the contract name. Each one receives the body, then `{ fail }`, and returns the result declared by the `Outcome`: Super then publishes the outcome as for a real store.

```ts
const counter = fakeStore('counter', {
  state: idle,
  commands: {
    increment: () => ({ count: 3 }),                 // publishes increment:done with { count: 3 }
    decrement: (_input, { fail }) => fail('storage'), // publishes decrement:failed with the storage reason
  },
});
```

## Testing the whole application

The app is assembled as in `main.ts`: real stores, adapters without latency, in-memory router. `mount` receives the shell, `AppShell`, which shows the route's screen.

```ts title="src/app.test.ts"
async function startApp(initialPath = '/') {
  const counter = CounterStore.create({ counterRepository: createLocalStorageCounterRepository() });
  const profileClient = createFakeProfileClient({ delay: 0 });
  const profile = ProfileStore.create({ profileClient });
  const cart = CartStore.create();
  const orderClient = createFakeOrderClient({ delay: 0 });
  const checkout = CheckoutStore.create({ cart, orderClient });
  const errorLog = ErrorLogStore.create();
  const router = createRouter(Router, { mode: 'memory', initialPath });
  const { container } = await mount(AppShell, {
    stores: [counter, profile, cart, checkout, errorLog],
    router,
    onError: (error, { tag, phase, caughtBy }) => errorLog.send('record', { message: error.message, tag, phase, caughtBy }),
  });
  await flush(); // lets `load` finish
  return { router, profileClient, orderClient, cart, ui: within(container) };
}

test('full counter journey: list, detail, increment, back', async () => {
  const { router, ui } = await startApp('/counters');

  await userEvent.click(ui.getByRole('link', { name: 'Coffees' }));
  expect(router.state()).toMatchObject({ path: '/counters/coffees', name: 'counter', params: { id: 'coffees' } });
  expect(ui.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Coffees' })).toBeTruthy();

  await userEvent.click(ui.getByRole('button', { name: 'Increment' }));
  await userEvent.click(ui.getByRole('button', { name: 'Increment' }));
  expect(await ui.findByText('Incremented: 2')).toBeTruthy();

  await userEvent.click(ui.getByRole('link', { name: '← All counters' }));
  expect(ui.getByRole('link', { name: 'Coffees' }).parentElement!.textContent).toContain('2');
  expect(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('super.counters')!)).toEqual({ coffees: 2 });
});
```

## Type tests: the *.test-d.ts files

Part of what Super promises is compile errors: an unknown route, a missing parameter, a screen with the wrong props. A Vitest test cannot observe that a line is rejected by the compiler. The `*.test-d.ts` files are there for that.

```ts
import { expectTypeOf, test } from 'vitest';

test('Router.href is typed by the paths', () => {
  expectTypeOf(Router.href('home')).toBeString();
  // @ts-expect-error `id` parameter required
  Router.href('counter');
});
```

- **The "d"** comes from `.d.ts`: these files test typing, not behaviour. It is the Vitest convention.
- **They are never run**. It is `npm run typecheck` (`super-tsc`, which runs `tsc`) that compiles them.
- **Each `// @ts-expect-error`** asserts "this line must be rejected". If a change makes it acceptable, compilation fails ("Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive").
- `npm run check` runs the type check then the tests: these files are checked on every run.

The template of a `.super` file does not need type tests: `npm run typecheck` checks it directly (a child's props, attributes, events, interpolations). The types a test sees of a `.super` component (its props for `mount`, its `emits` for `on`) come from the virtual TypeScript, through the declaration `super-tsc` writes into `.super/types/` (see [Tooling](tooling.html#type-check)).

## Who tests what

| What is tested | Where |
| --- | --- |
| How Super works (router, selectors, re-renders, contract typing…) | The package tests, in `packages/`. Your app does not have to redo them. |
| Your app's behaviour (store rules, screen display, journeys) | Your app's tests, next to your code. |

---

# Tooling

A `.super` file is not TypeScript that `tsc` or your editor can read on their own. Three tools handle it: the command-line check, the Vite plugin that compiles it, and a language server for the editor. All of them rest on the same principle: a **virtual TypeScript**.

## The principle: a virtual TypeScript

Each `.super` file is translated into equivalent TypeScript for the compiler: the file's code is copied as is, each element becomes a sequence of typed calls, and a mapping table links each position in the virtual TS to its position in the `.super` file. The compiler checks this virtual TS, and errors are reported at the right line and column of the `.super` file.

- **Statements are copied as is** (`if`, `for`, `switch`, declarations): TypeScript's type narrowing applies to the template.
- **A child component becomes a call to its `create` method**, whose typing already checks props and events.
- **The virtual TS is also written to disk**, in `.super/virtual/` next to the tsconfig (ignored by git), with, in `.super/types/`, a declaration (`.d.ts`) of the file's exports and its source map back to the `.super` file.
- **The tsconfig files declare these folders** (`rootDirs`, `paths`): a `.ts` file that imports a `.super` component, such as `routes.ts`, sees its types through the declaration. The editor's TypeScript server follows its source map: "go to definition" opens the `.super` file, in any editor.

## Type check: super-tsc

```bash
npm run typecheck
# or, for a specific project:
node packages/lang/src/cli.ts examples/demo/tsconfig.json
```

`super-tsc` writes the virtual TS of each `.super` file covered by the tsconfig (its `include` and `exclude`), runs the project's `tsc` (TypeScript 7), then reports each error in the `.super` file. Syntax errors in `.super` files (ambiguous text, an unclosed tag) are reported too. The project's `.ts` files are checked in the same pass.

```text
src/@components/shop/index.super(29,48): error TS2339: Property 'pirce' does not exist on type 'Product'.
src/@components/shop/index.super(42,10): error SUPER: Text read as `for`, which is not valid (…). If it is text, wrap it in braces: {'for (more info) see below'}
```

What is checked is detailed in [What the compiler checks](guarantees.html).

## Compiling: the Vite plugin

`superPlugin` compiles each `.super` file into lit-html code, in dev, at build time and in tests (Vitest goes through the same plugins). An import without an extension finds a `.super` file: `@components/shop` resolves to `shop/index.super`. The plugin's architecture rules apply to the compiled code, and hot replacement works as it does for a `.ts` component.

- **A syntax error** in a `.super` file stops the module from loading, with its position: overlay in dev, failed build or test.
- **In dev**, the plugin also rewrites the virtual TS to disk on each change.

### Source maps

The compiled code keeps the line numbers of the `.super` file, and the plugin provides a source map down to the column: an error trace in the browser or a debugger breakpoint points to the source.

## In the editor: the language server

`packages/lang-server` is a language server (LSP) built on Volar. It serves `.super` files, and only them.

- **Errors** from TypeScript and syntax, as you type, with the quick fix "Wrap in braces" for ambiguous text.
- **Completion** in expressions, including while typing (`if (this.`, a loop key, an unfinished declaration).
- **Completion in tags**: after `<`, components (those of the project not yet imported add their import) and HTML tags; after `</`, the tag to close; inside a tag, its attributes, `ref` and its events, or a component's props (required ones first) and events.
- **Hover and go to definition**; hovering `@tag`, `@title`, `@prop`, `@emit` and the setup declarations (`@contract`, `@on`…) shows their documentation (form, allowed values, example).
- **File formatting** (see [Formatting](tooling.html#formatting)).
- **The virtual TS written to disk on each keystroke**: a `.ts` file open alongside sees a new prop straight away.

> **TypeScript 6 in the editor, TypeScript 7 on the command line**
>
> Volar cannot drive TypeScript 7 yet. The language server therefore has its own package (`packages/lang-server`, with its dependencies) and runs on TypeScript 6, while `super-tsc` uses the project's TypeScript 7. Both give the same errors on what the demo does.

## Formatting

```bash
npm run format   # Biome for .ts files, the .super formatter for .super files
npm run lint     # checks both (also run by npm run check)
```

The TS of a `.super` file is formatted by Biome, with the repository's configuration: each top-level element is replaced by a placeholder statement, which Biome places and indents like the others. The `.super` formatter then prints the templates at those positions:

- **A tag on one line** if it fits within the width (140 columns), otherwise one attribute per line and indented children.
- **A component that receives children, and an `<:name>` slot**, always on several lines, even if they fit: what goes into which slot is readable at a glance.
- **Running text** fills the lines, with its inline elements (`<code>`, `<strong>`); a list of elements without text keeps one element per line.
- **Statements** (`if`, `for`, `switch`, declarations) and their blocks are indented, blank lines between children are kept (one at most).
- **A component's declarations** (`@tag = …;`, `@title = …;`, `@prop`, `@emit`) are kept and indented like the other class members, even though `@tag` and `@title` are not valid TS.

**The rendering never changes**: a line is only broken where there is already whitespace, or at the edge of an element, a block or a statement, where whitespace renders nothing (see [whitespace](templates.html#whitespace)). The tests check this on every `.super` file in the repository. A file with syntax errors is not formatted.

In the editor, the language server formats the file (format on save in Zed, see below).

## Zed

The extension in `editors/zed` declares the "Super" language for `.super` files and starts the server: the one from the `super-language-server` package if it is installed in the project, otherwise `packages/lang-server`, with the Node on the PATH. Since `.super` files have their own language, vtsls, Zed's usual TypeScript server, does not see them.

- **Installing**: Rust via rustup, then `zed: install dev extension` on the `editors/zed` folder (see its README). You can follow the build in `zed: open log`.
- **Highlighting**: the Tree-sitter grammar for `.super` files (`editors/tree-sitter-super`), the TSX one extended to statements written between tags: `if`, `for … ; key`, `switch` and declarations are highlighted as code, not as text. It also knows `@tag = …;` and `@title = …;` in a class body (rule `super_declaration`), which TSX would reject.
- **Comments**: between tags, `cmd+/` writes `{/* … */}`.
- **Formatting**: by the server, on save; never by Prettier.
- **Go to definition from a `.ts` file**: vtsls follows the source map of the component's declaration and opens the `.super` file (see [the principle](tooling.html#virtual-ts)).

After a server update, restart it from an open `.super` file: `editor: restart language server`. After a change to the extension itself: *Rebuild* in the extensions panel. After a grammar update (such as the addition of `@tag` and `@title`), reinstall the extension: `zed: install dev extension` on `editors/zed`.

The limitations of this setup are listed in [Limitations](limitations.html).

## The packages

| Package | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `packages/lang` | Parser, virtual TS, compiler, source maps, formatter, `super-tsc`, and the specification (`SPEC.md`). |
| `packages/lang-server` | Language server. |
| `packages/vite` | The plugin that compiles `.super` files. |

---

# Guarantees

Most misuses of Super are caught before run time: by TypeScript, or by the Vite plugin. This page lists what is checked, where, and what is not.

Except for the section on [templates](guarantees.html#super-templates), each excerpt below comes from the repository's type tests (`packages/*/src/*.test-d.ts`): each `@ts-expect-error` there makes `npm run typecheck` fail if the expected error disappears. The excerpts use their test contract `basket`: commands `add({ sku })`, `clear()` and `save({ id })` (which declares `Outcome<{ count: number }, 'empty' | 'offline'>`), events `emptied` and `saved: { id }`, selectors `quantity(sku)`, `count()`, `entries()`.

## Contracts and stores

```ts
// @ts-expect-error a command does not return data
class Async extends SuperContract<{ state: {}; commands: { add(): Promise<number> } }> {}
// @ts-expect-error two parameters: a command has only one body
class Bad extends SuperContract<{ state: {}; commands: { add(a: number, b: number): void } }> {}
class Typo extends SuperContract<{ state: {}; command: { add(): void } }> {
  constructor() {
    // @ts-expect-error unknown key in the contract types: command (expected: state, commands, events)
    super({ name: 'typo' });
  }
}

class BadName extends SuperStore<BasketContract> {
  constructor() {
    // @ts-expect-error no contract 'cart'
    super({ contract: 'cart', initialState: { items: {} } });
  }
}
// @ts-expect-error initialState does not match the contract's state
super({ contract: 'basket', initialState: { items: 'none' } });

// @ts-expect-error the first parameter of a selector is the contract's state
abstract class WrongStore extends SuperStore<WrongState> {} // WrongState: count(s: { total: number })
// @ts-expect-error "pending" is reserved: Super provides it along with the selectors
abstract class PendingStore extends SuperStore<Pending> {}  // Pending declares a pending selector

// @ts-expect-error clear and save are missing
class Missing extends SuperStore<BasketContract> implements Commands<Missing> {
  constructor() { super(init); }
  add(_: { sku: string }) {}
}

class Wrong extends SuperStore<BasketContract> implements Commands<Wrong> {
  // @ts-expect-error parameters differ from the contract's
  add(_: { sku: 'mug' }) {}
  // @ts-expect-error clear is declared void
  clear() { return 42; }
  // @ts-expect-error the declared result is { count: number }
  async save(_: { id: string }) { return { total: 0 }; }
  // @ts-expect-error public method outside the contract
  increment() {}
}

// In a store method:
// @ts-expect-error unknown event
this.emit('nope');
// @ts-expect-error payload required
this.emit('saved');
// @ts-expect-error undeclared failure reason
this.fail('nope');
// @ts-expect-error unknown command
void this.send('nope');

// @ts-expect-error missing dependency
WithDeps.create();
// @ts-expect-error wrongly typed dependency
Store.create({ api: { fetchCart: () => 42 } });
// @ts-expect-error a store without dependencies receives none
NoDeps.create({ api: 1 });
```

- A command declared with a direct response, or with several parameters.
- A `super({ contract })` that names an unknown contract, or a non-conforming initial state.
- With `implements Commands<Self>`: a command without a method, a method whose parameters differ from the contract's, a method that returns something other than the declared result (or forgets it), a public method outside the contract.
- An unknown event, a payload wrongly typed or forgotten; a failure reason unknown to the contract; an unknown command in `this.send`.
- Missing or wrongly typed dependencies at creation.

## Reading and sending

On a store handle (tests, composition root, other stores):

```ts
const basket = Ok.create();
// @ts-expect-error the instance does not leak out: no add method on the handle
basket.add({ sku: 'mug' });
// @ts-expect-error wrongly typed body
basket.send('add', { sku: 42 });
// @ts-expect-error selector parameter required
basket.selectors.quantity();

// @ts-expect-error unknown command
void shop.send('remove');
// @ts-expect-error missing body
void shop.send('add');
// @ts-expect-error extra argument
void shop.send('load', 1);
// @ts-expect-error unknown event
shop.on('removed', () => {});
// @ts-expect-error unknown command
cart.on('remove:done', () => {});
// @ts-expect-error field absent from the body
cart.pending('add', { id: 'a' });
```

In a component, through the contract view (excerpt from the type tests, written in `.ts`: in a `.super`, `@contract basket;` and `@selector` give the same checks):

```ts
basket = this.contract('basket');
// @ts-expect-error no contract 'cart'
other = this.contract('cart');

// @ts-expect-error a selector with a parameter is read inside a function
raw = this.selector(this.basket.selectors.quantity);
// @ts-expect-error 0 does not come from a selector: the condition goes in render
shown = this.selector(() => (this.props.show ? this.basket.selectors.count() : 0));
// @ts-expect-error a calculation on the value goes in render (or in a contract selector)
double = this.selector(() => this.basket.selectors.count() * 2);
// @ts-expect-error a derived array is no longer the selector's value
skus = this.selector(() => this.basket.selectors.entries().map(([sku]) => sku));
// @ts-expect-error no selector
constant = this.selector(() => 42);

render() {
  // @ts-expect-error the raw state is not exposed
  this.basket.state();
  // @ts-expect-error wrongly typed body
  this.basket.send('add', { sku: 1 });
  // @ts-expect-error unknown command
  this.basket.send('nope');
  // …
}
```

## Components

These tests write `Dialog.create(…)`: that is what `<Dialog … />` becomes in the virtual TypeScript of a `.super`, hence the same errors in a template (see [below](guarantees.html#super-templates)).

```ts
class Dialog extends SuperElement<{ props: { question: string }; emits: { answered: { confirmed: boolean }; closed: void } }> {
  static tag = 't-dialog';
  render() {
    // @ts-expect-error undeclared event
    this.emit('nope');
    // @ts-expect-error payload required
    this.emit('answered');
    // …
  }
}

// @ts-expect-error props required
Dialog.create();
// @ts-expect-error wrongly typed prop
Dialog.create({ question: 42 });
// @ts-expect-error listener for an event the child does not emit
Dialog.create({ question: 'ok?' }, { on: { nope: () => {} } });
// @ts-expect-error missing `static tag`
NoTag.create();

// @ts-expect-error render is required
class NoRender extends SuperElement {
  static tag = 'cmp-no-render';
}
```

### Forms

```ts
// @ts-expect-error unknown field
edit.field('nope');
// @ts-expect-error a list is not bound like a simple field
edit.field('phones');
// @ts-expect-error radio value outside the union
edit.field('plan', 'gold');
// @ts-expect-error incomplete row
phones.add({ label: 'work' });
```

`this.form({ … })` also checks that `failures` distributes exactly the failure reasons of the submit command (a reason forgotten, present twice or unknown to the contract does not compile, nor does an unknown field in `fields`), that `submit.toInput` produces the command's body, and that the `toInput` of an asynchronous check (`checks`) produces that of its own command.

## Templates in .super files

The template of a `.super` component is checked by `npm run typecheck` (`super-tsc`), and each error is reported at its position in the `.super`. The excerpt comes from the test project in `packages/lang`: each line marked `ERROR` must be reported, and no other (`packages/lang/src/check.test.ts`); there are 16 of them. `Greeting` there is a component with props `{ name: string }`, which emits `closed`; `Panel` declares `@prop heading: string;`, `@prop content: Children;` and `@prop footer?: Children;`.

```ts title="errors.super"
export class ErrorsFixture extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'lang-errors';
  @ref input: HTMLInputElement;
  @state local = { user: null as { name: string } | null, status: 'idle' as Status, items: [] as Item[] };

  render() {
    <main>
      <dvi>typo</dvi> {/* ERROR unknown tag */}
      <p>{this.local.get().user.name}</p> {/* ERROR possibly null */}
      const user = this.local.get().user;
      if (user) {
        <p>{user.name}</p>
      }
      for (const item of this.local.get().items; key item.idd) { {/* ERROR key */}
        <li>{item}</li> {/* ERROR interpolated object */}
      }
      <button on:clik={() => {}}>x</button> {/* ERROR unknown event */}
      <input on:input={(e) => e.currentTarget.value.toFixed()} /> {/* ERROR value is a string */}
      <div ref={this.input}></div> {/* ERROR ref on the wrong element */}
      <input ref={this.input} />
      const status = this.local.get().status;
      switch (status) {
        case 'idle': <p>idle</p>
        default: {assertNever(status)} {/* ERROR non-exhaustive switch */}
      }
      <Greeting nam="Ada" on:closed={(e) => e.reason} /> {/* ERROR unknown prop */}
      <Greeting name={42} /> {/* ERROR wrongly typed prop */}
      <Greeting name="Ada" on:open={() => {}} /> {/* ERROR event unknown to the component */}
      <p>for (more info) see below</p> {/* ERROR ambiguous text */}
      <Greeting name="Ada"><p>Greeting takes no children</p></Greeting> {/* ERROR children rejected */}
      <Panel heading="No children" /> {/* ERROR children required */}
      <Panel heading="x"><p>a</p><:header>h</:header></Panel> {/* ERROR unknown slot */}
    </main>
  }
}

export class NativeName extends SuperElement {
  @tag = 'lang-native-name';
  @prop title: string; // {/* ERROR name already taken by HTML elements */}
  render() {
    <p>{this.title}</p>
  }
}
```

- A tag without a hyphen that is not a known HTML tag.
- A possibly `null` value read without a test; the narrowing of an `if` applies to the elements it contains.
- A loop key (`key`) that does not exist on the iterated item.
- An object displayed with `{…}` (no more `[object Object]`).
- An `on:` listener for an event the tag does not have, and the type of the received event (`e.currentTarget` is the `HTMLInputElement`).
- A `ref={…}` reference set on an element of a different type from its own.
- A non-exhaustive `switch`, with `default: {assertNever(x)}`.
- On a child component: an unknown prop, a wrongly typed prop, an `on:` for an event missing from its `emits`.
- Children for a component that does not declare `content`, required children that are missing, a `<:name>` slot that is not a prop of the component.
- Text that starts like a statement without being one, with the suggested fix: `{'for (more info) see below'}`.
- A prop named after a property of HTML elements (`@prop title`, `id`, `hidden`…): "`'title' is already a property of HTML elements: choose another name`".

The TypeScript message is reported as is ("`'nam' does not exist in type 'Props'. Did you mean to write 'name'?`"). The parser also rejects, with the message and often the fix (`packages/lang/src/parser.test.ts`, `packages/lang/src/compile.test.ts`):

- lit syntax: `@click`, `?disabled`, `.value` ("lit syntax: write `on:click={…}`");
- `<` and `}` in text, with the fix `{'<'}`, `{'}'}`;
- a closing tag that does not match ("`</i> closes <b>`");
- `return x;` in a method that emits elements (`return;` remains allowed, as does `return x;` in a nested function);
- an element outside a class method;
- a block whose `}` is missing before the parent's closing tag;
- a `<:name>` slot outside a component, with attributes, filled twice, or named `content`.

### Component declarations

The `@tag`, `@title`, `@prop` and `@emit` declarations are read by the parser, which rejects (`parser.test.ts`, "parse: component declarations"):

- a component without `@tag` ("`` A component declares its tag: `@tag = 'my-component';` ``"), except an `abstract` class;
- `static tag = '…';` in a `.super` ("`` In a `.super` file, the tag is declared with `@tag = '…';` ``");
- a tag that is not a literal string, in lower case, with a hyphen;
- a hand-written `SuperElement<…>` generic ("`` In a `.super` file, props and events are declared in the class: `@prop name: Type;` and `@emit name: Type;` ``");
- a duplicate declaration ("`` `@tag` declared twice ``", "`` `@prop a` declared twice ``");
- a prop without a type (`@prop label;`), an optional prop with a default value (`@prop size?: number = 2;`: "remove the `?`"), an event with a value;
- a declaration outside a component ("`` `@prop` is only written in a component (`extends SuperElement`) ``").

The component's types are derived from them (`virtual.test.ts`): `@prop question: string;` becomes a required prop, `@prop tone: … = 'neutral';` and `@prop size?: number;` optional props, `@emit answered: { confirmed: boolean };` an event. These are what the tags that use the component are checked against (unknown prop, wrongly typed prop, unknown `on:`, above).

Setup declarations (`@contract`, `@selector`, `@state`, `@form`, `@ref`, `@on`) are read too, and the parser rejects (`parser.test.ts`, "parse: setup declarations and listeners"):

- a contract declared twice, even under another field name ("`` The contract `cart` is already declared by `@contract cart` ``");
- `@contract router;` ("`` The router is read through `this.router`, without `@contract` ``");
- a contract that is not a literal string (`@contract cart = name;`);
- a type on `@selector` ("``No type on `@selector`: it comes from the value``");
- a `@ref` without a type ("`` A ref declares the type of its element: `@ref input: HTMLInputElement;` ``");
- a badly written `@on` (`@on('cart')`: "`` `@on` is written `@on('contract', 'event')`, above a method ``");
- the old form in a component (`cart = this.contract('cart');`, `this.selector(…)`, `this.state(…)`, `this.ref<T>()`), with the rewritten line as the fix (`@contract cart;`, `@state local = { open: false };`…); outside a component, the same line remains ordinary TypeScript;
- a listener set in the constructor ("`` In a `.super` file, a listener is declared on a method: `@on('cart', 'event') onEvent(payload) { … }` ``").

The virtual TypeScript derives from them the fields that used to be written by hand (`virtual.test.ts`): `@contract cart;` becomes `readonly cart = this.contract('cart');`, `@selector`, `@state` and `@ref` become the fields `this.selector(…)`, `this.state(…)`, `this.ref<T>()`, and `@on('profile', 'save:done') onSaved(…)` a listener `this.contract('profile').on('save:done', …)`: the method's parameter therefore has the type of the event's payload, checked as in a hand-written listener. `@on('router', 'navigated')` becomes `this.router.on('navigated', …)`.

### Page title

`@title = …;` and `this.page.title = …` are checked at run time (`packages/dom/src/page.test.ts`):

- a title set during `render` throws "`` `this.page.title` cannot be set during render ``";
- `this.page.title` cannot be read: "`` `this.page.title` is set, it cannot be read ``";
- the stack is tested: the last mounted component that sets a title wins, the one below follows its data without being displayed and comes back on unmount; a title written as a function follows the values it reads, like `render`.

The compiled code keeps the source's line numbers, and its source map maps the final JS back to the line and column of the `.super` (`compile.test.ts`). See [Templates](templates.html) and [Tooling](tooling.html).

## Router

With `defineRouter({ home: '/', item: { path: '/items/:id', params: params<{ id: number }>({ id: Number }) }, list: '/list?sort&tag[]' })`:

```ts
// In a component, through this.router:
// @ts-expect-error the router is read through this.router
this.contract('router');
// @ts-expect-error missing `id` param
this.router.href('item');
// @ts-expect-error `id` is a number
this.router.href('item', { params: { id: '1' } });
// @ts-expect-error unknown route
this.router.href('nope');
// @ts-expect-error params required
this.router.send('navigate', { to: 'item' });
// @ts-expect-error unknown route
this.router.send('navigate', { to: 'nope' });
// @ts-expect-error no route has this param
this.router.current.params.nope;
// @ts-expect-error in the `item` screen, `sort` is another route's query
this.router.current.query.sort;
// @ts-expect-error unknown route
this.router.at('nope');
```
